about: An example shape already split into equal parts appears, and the child taps another shape split into the same number of equal parts — even when the pieces are shaped differently, like a square cut corner-to-corner and a square cut straight down the middle that both show two equal halves. It's an interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

The big idea is that equal shares of the same whole do not have to look alike. The other choices show the shape split into unequal parts, split into the wrong number of parts, or not split at all, so the child has to focus on the count of equal pieces rather than on the picture matching exactly. The child recognizes the matching partition; the child does not cut the shapes.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.3 — recognizing that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape, and naming shares as halves, thirds, and fourths. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Recognize that equal shares of one shape can look different and still be equal
Match by the number of equal parts, not by pictures that look identical
Tell equal parts from unequal parts, and the right number from the wrong number
Use the words halves, thirds, and fourths for equal shares
howToPlay: Look at the example shape and see how many equal parts it is split into.
Tap the other shape split into the same number of equal parts, even if the pieces look different, then press Check.
Try again any time; there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Recognize shapes split into two, three, or four equal shares — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.3
Understand that equal shares can have different shapes as long as the parts are the same size
Strengthen the fair-share thinking that names and compares fractions later

about: Four cards lie on a shelf, each the same shape cut into pieces. The child hangs a card on a mobile that has one hook for every share. Cardboard weighs by its size, so the mobile measures what "equal" means: fair shares hang perfectly level, an unfair cut tips the bar, extra pieces drop into a spare tray, and missing pieces leave a hook bare. A pin holds the bar still until Check pulls it out and the mobile swings to its true tilt.

The first level asks for halves and fourths of circles, squares and rectangles. The second adds thirds on a bar pivoted at a third, and fair shares that look different, such as fourths cut corner to corner or a triangle cut into three from its center. The third level turns it around: three mobiles carry name plates for one half, one third and one fourth, and the child hangs a card with one shaded share on the mobile it belongs to. When every share is equal, a stacked fraction appears on each piece.

After a first miss the mobile shows what is wrong: it tips, a hook stays empty, or pieces land in the tray, and the heaviest share glows. After a second miss the springs under the hooks are measured against a dashed fair line, so the share that is too big stands out; in the third level the mobile with the right number of hooks bobs. Aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.3 (halves and fourths), with thirds from 2.G.A.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Telling equal shares from unequal ones by their size, not by the number of lines
Matching the number of equal shares to halves, thirds and fourths
Seeing that equal shares of the same whole can look different
Naming one share as one half, one third or one fourth
howToPlay: Tap a card, or drag it onto the mobile, to hang it. Tap the mobile to take the card down.
Press Check to pull the pin. Fair shares hang level; an unfair card tips the bar.
Pieces in the spare tray mean too many pieces; a bare hook means too few.
In "Name the share", tap the card, then tap the mobile whose name plate matches the shaded share.
In the settings choose the level (Halves and fourths · Thirds and fair shares · Name the share) and turn the spirit level on the bar on or off.
learningGoals: Recognize circles, rectangles and other shapes cut into two, three or four equal shares, and tell when shares are not equal.
Describe the shares as halves, thirds and fourths (quarters).
Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.
Name one share of a whole as one half, one third or one fourth.

about: Every picture rides a kite, and the kite needs a tail with one bow for every beat of its word. The child taps the picture to hear the word, ties bows onto the tail, and presses Check for a gust of wind. It is an interactive phonics activity for Kindergarten and first grade that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The kite gives the verdict. With the right number of bows in the right order it climbs and flies steady, lighting each syllable in turn: rab … bit, rabbit. With too few bows the last bow carries two beats and the kite spins; with too many, a blank bow drags it down into the grass; with the syllables out of order the tail knots at the first bow that is out of place. The tail always starts with one bow, and every bow is the same size, so nothing on the screen gives the count away.

It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.B: count, pronounce, blend and segment the syllables of spoken words. Five levels use the same kite: count the beats, tie the syllables to spell the word (or write each syllable on its own bow), find a missing syllable or put scrambled ones in order, sort picture cards onto kites with one, two, or three bows, and hang one tassel for each sound inside a syllable. Every syllable split shown is one a child says aloud and one that several dictionary sources agree on. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting the syllables in a spoken word
Blending syllables into a word
Finding a missing syllable and putting syllables in order
Sorting words by how many syllables they have
howToPlay: Tap the picture to hear the word.
Tie one bow on the tail for every beat you hear, or drag the syllable bows into place.
Press Check and watch the kite: steady means right, a spin or a sag tells you what to change.
On the kite fence, drag the picture card onto the kite with the right number of bows.
learningGoals: Count, pronounce, blend and segment syllables in spoken words, the focus of Common Core RF.K.2.B
Put the syllables of a word in the right order
Hear how many sounds are in each syllable

about: Which one is taller, longer or shorter? Here the things stand on folding stands of different heights, or lie on rails a little way from a start wall, so their tops and ends can trick the eye: the shorter palm tree may stand on the higher stand. The child can drag a picture down and its stand folds under it, or drag a lying pencil left until it touches the wall, then taps the one they choose and presses Check. It is an interactive Kindergarten measurement activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is the honest stand and the level beam. On Check every stand folds and every lying thing slides to the wall, so all of them share one floor or one start line, and a golden beam comes to rest on the true tallest top or longest end; every shorter one shows the gap between its top and the beam. In most rounds the stands make the wrong answer look right, so children soon bring everything down to the floor first: that is the measuring move, lining up the ends. A wrong choice is answered by the beam itself, and a second wrong choice makes the right picture glow. The same object appears at two or more sizes, so the child compares a thing with itself, not two different things.

It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.A.2: directly comparing two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which has more of it and which has less. "A whole row" asks for the tallest, longest, shortest or biggest of three or four. "On the floor" starts with everything already lined up, for the youngest. The pictures come from the illustrated library and stand or lie along their own drawn shapes. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing two things by height or by length
Lining up the bottoms or the ends before comparing
Finding the tallest, longest, shortest or biggest in a row
Telling taller from longer and the two kinds of shorter
howToPlay: Look at the question: taller, longer, shorter, or the tallest, longest, shortest or biggest in a row.
Drag a picture down to fold its stand, or drag a lying thing left to the wall.
Tap the one you choose, then press Check.
Watch the beam: it rests on the true tallest top or longest end.
learningGoals: Directly compare two objects by height or length, the focus of Common Core K.MD.A.2
Line up a common starting point before comparing
Find the tallest, longest or shortest in a small set

about: A ticket shows a number, and a train with ten seats waits at a platform full of animals. The child taps the animals one at a time — each one hops into the next seat — and presses Go when the train holds exactly as many as the ticket says. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity for numbers to 10 that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The hard part of making a number is knowing when to stop, and the train is built around it: more animals wait than any ticket asks for, so the child has to keep the count and decide. The ten seats are a ten-frame — two rows of five, filled from the front — so seven reads as a full row and two more. When the count is wrong, the train numbers its passengers so the child can see why, and the child fixes it; the help never moves an animal. On some rounds the train stops again and the new ticket is one more or one fewer, so the child puts on or lets off just one animal instead of starting over.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4 — one number for each object, the last number said tells how many, and each next number is one more. Teachers can choose tickets up to 5 or up to 10, and counting numbers shown as the animals get on or said aloud by the child. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting out exactly as many animals as the ticket shows
Putting one animal in each seat and saying one number for each
Stopping at the right number — the last number counted tells how many
Changing the train by just one when the ticket is one more or one fewer
howToPlay: Read the number on the ticket.
Tap animals on the platform to put them on the train, one at a time. Tap the train to let the last animal off.
When the train holds as many animals as the ticket says, press Go.
Too many or too few? The train says how many are on board — let some off or put more on and press Go again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Connect counting to how many: one number for each object, and the last number tells how many — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.4
Know that the last number counted tells how many, and stop there
See that the next number is one more, and the number before is one fewer

about: An order slip shows a number, and two market trays of ten spaces wait at the fruit stand. The child taps the space where the order ends — the fruit tumbles in, space after space, up to there — and presses Check when the trays hold exactly as many fruits as the order says. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity for numbers to 20 that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

Making a number is mostly about knowing where it ends. The two trays are a double ten-frame, so 17 is a full tray and 7 more, and the child can find the seventeenth space by counting one by one or by tens and fives. A tap on a fruit takes back that fruit and every fruit after it, so each next space is one more, and taking back the last fruit makes one fewer. When the count is wrong, the stand numbers its fruit so the child can see why; a second wrong Check marks the extra fruit or the spaces still waiting, and the help never moves a fruit. The two mistakes teachers see most with numbers past ten are named: only the part after ten (7 for 17) and only the full tray (10 for 17).

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4 — one number for each object, the last number said tells how many, and each next number is one more. Teachers can choose orders up to 10 (one tray) or up to 20, and whether a tap fills up to the space or adds one fruit at a time (then the child says one number for each fruit). No timer, no score.
practices: Putting exactly as many fruits in the trays as the order shows, up to 20
Finding where a number ends on a double ten-frame: a full tray and some more
Knowing that the last number counted tells how many
Changing the trays by one: one more, one fewer
howToPlay: Read the number on the order slip.
Tap an empty space: the fruit fills up to it. Tap a fruit to take that fruit and the ones after it back.
When the trays hold as many fruits as the order says, press Check.
Not quite? The stand numbers its fruit — add or take back fruit and press Check again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Make a number from 1 to 20 with objects — the K.CC.B.4 idea that the last number counted tells how many
See a number past ten as a full ten and some more
Know that the next number is one more and the number before is one fewer

about: A table of animals and one question: how many? The child taps each animal to count it — a numbered tag drops on it — then taps the numeral on the rail that tells how many. The animals sit in a line, in rows, in a circle or scattered, exactly the four arrangements Kindergarten counting asks for. It runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

This is counting with the three principles built into the material. An animal can be tagged only once (one-to-one), the tags are numbered in the order they were given (stable order), and the last tag glows because the last number said is the answer (cardinality). If something is skipped, the hint names it and the uncounted animal pulses. Two extra moves — Count again and Mix them up — let a child discover that the order does not matter and that the number stays the same when the animals move.

It is the first half of Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer "how many?" about things arranged in a line, an array or a circle, or scattered; this table runs 1 to 10, the standard continues to 20. No timer, no score — just calm, hands-on counting.
practices: Tagging each animal once while counting out loud
Answering "how many?" with the numeral on the rail
Counting things in a line, in rows, in a circle and scattered
Checking that a group counted in a new order is still the same number
howToPlay: Tap each animal to count it and say its number. A numbered tag lands on it.
When every animal has a tag, the last tag glows — tap that number on the rail, then press Check.
Try Count again or Mix them up: the order changes, the number stays the same. There is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count to answer how many about up to ten objects — the first half of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Use one-to-one tagging and name the last number as the total
Count objects in a line, an array, a circle and a scattered group

about: Two wooden fruit crates, ten boxes each — the double ten-frame of the classroom, filled with real fruit pictures. The fruit drops in box by box, one row of five, then the next, and the child writes how many on a slate with number keys, from 1 to 20. When the number is right the slate turns gold, the last fruit carries the number and it is spoken. This interactive Kindergarten counting activity runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The crates are built for the teen numbers. A full crate is ten, so fourteen is a full crate and four more — and in the written 14 the 1 is for the full crate and the 4 for the rest. A wrong number is named the way a teacher would name it: 41 for 14 has the digits the other way round, 4 for 14 counts only the second crate, and 10 for 14 only the first. Then the crates help without giving the answer away: first, from six fruits up, the numbers 5, 10 and 15 appear on the fruit, so the child can start there and count on; after a second miss the count-on numbers run along the fruit and stop at a question mark on the last one. The child still says the final number.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.3 — writing numbers to 20 and representing a number of objects with a written numeral. Teachers can choose numbers to 10 (one crate) or to 20, and a quick look: a cloth covers the crates after a moment and Peek lifts it again, so the fruit is read by its rows of five rather than one by one. No timer, no score.
practices: Reading a double ten-frame: a full crate is ten, a full row is five
Writing the numeral 1 to 20 for the amount in the crates
Counting on from 5, 10 or 15 instead of starting again at one
Writing teen numbers with the digits in the right order
howToPlay: Look at the crates and count the fruit — a full crate is ten.
Write the number on the slate with the number keys and press Check.
Not yet? Read what the crates show: start at the number on a fruit and count on. After a second try the numbers run to a question mark — say the number that goes there.
A right number turns the slate gold; Next brings new crates.
learningGoals: Represent a count of up to 20 objects with a written numeral — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.3
Read a teen number as ten and some more ones, and write its two digits in order
Count on from a known row of five or a full ten

about: A number from 11 to 19 appears with its word — say 14, fourteen. The child holds a little spout and counters pour out, about four a second, each rolling into the next cell of a ten-frame tray; a tap pours exactly one. Nothing can reach the second tray until the first is full: on the tenth counter the top tray shivers, its rim flashes and a chute opens, and the eleventh rolls down into the tray below. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that gravity puts the ten first, so 14 is literally a full ten that overflowed plus four. No count is shown while the child pours — they stop where they think the number is and press Check. Too few or too many, and the target's shape appears as dotted cells over the trays, so the gap or the extra counter is plain to see; after a second miss the dotted cells count themselves along the pour. A tap on a counter takes the last one back (a counter in the full top tray stays while the bottom tray has any). On success the 1 of the numeral floats onto the full tray and the 4 onto the four counters below. The "Number of the day" level goes further: every full tray seals and slides onto a tens shelf, a tray stack adds a whole sealed ten with one tap, and a day card fills step by step — build 37, add ten more (47), take ten away from 37 (27); in three rounds one more or one less as well, where 49 + 1 seals a new ten and 30 − 1 opens one.

It is aligned to Common Core K.NBT.A.1 — composing and decomposing the numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones — and the Number of the day level follows the grade 1 number-of-the-day routine: tens and ones, the number word, a tally up to 20, ten more and ten less. The number words come from the same reviewed tables as the printable worksheets. Teachers can choose to show the dotted shape from the start. "Just pour" is open play, with a day card that counts along. No timer, no score.
practices: Building 11–19 as a full ten and some more
Seeing the 1 in a teen number as a whole ten
Showing a number up to 99 as full tens and ones
Finding ten more, ten less, one more and one less
howToPlay: Look at the number on the card.
Hold the spout to pour, or tap it for one counter. Tap a counter to take the last one back.
Stop where you think the number is and press Check.
Not yet? The dotted places show the number's shape. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Compose and decompose numbers 11–19 into a ten and some ones — the focus of Common Core K.NBT.A.1
Read a two-digit number as tens and ones
Find ten more and ten less without counting by ones

about: Every card becomes one rail of a ladder. An addition is two short rails clicked together end to end: 2 + 3 is a rail of 2 holes and a rail of 3. A subtraction is a tall rail with its top sawn off: 9 − 4 is a rail of 9 holes, and the top 4 fall away. The child taps an addition and a subtraction, and the two rails stand side by side.

Then the child taps the squirrel. It climbs a rung at every height that has a hole on both rails. If the rails are the same height, it reaches the gold top rung and the acorn, and the ladder folds into a tag that reads 2 + 3 = 9 − 4: work on both sides of the equals sign, shown to be equal. If one rail is taller, the squirrel stops, and the extra holes on the taller side glow and are numbered. If it stops a second time, little rails appear on the cards to compare.

In the Undo it level, the four cards are one fact family, such as 3 + 5, 5 + 3, 8 − 5 and 8 − 3. Every rail is 8 holes tall, so height cannot decide. Each rail is two colours, and the squirrel climbs only where the colours match, so 3 + 5 goes with 8 − 5, the subtraction that takes away the part added last. The Same answer level is aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.7; Undo it practises the link between addition and subtraction. No timer and no score.
practices: Understanding the equals sign as “the same as”: 2 + 3 = 9 − 4
Working out additions and subtractions within 20
Deciding whether two expressions are worth the same
Pairing each addition with the subtraction that undoes it
howToPlay: Tap an addition card and a subtraction card. Their rails appear in the ladder yard.
Tap the squirrel to send it up the ladder. If it reaches the acorn, the pair is right and its tag hangs on the rack.
If it stops, look at the glowing holes (in Undo it, the ringed holes), then tap another card to try again. Tap a tag on the rack to take that ladder apart.
In the settings, choose the pairs (Same answer or Undo it) and when to show the rails (After I choose or On the cards). “On the cards” is the easier setting.
learningGoals: Understand the meaning of the equals sign
Decide whether an equation with + and − on both sides is true
Add and subtract within 20
Link each addition to the subtraction that undoes it

about: A mixed pile of animals, fruits and vehicles rides a conveyor belt one picture at a time, and the child drops each one down the right chute. The little pictures on each chute show what belongs there; a picture dropped down the wrong chute bounces back to the belt, so every thing is sorted, and sorted only once. It is an interactive Kindergarten activity about sorting and counting that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the glass tubes turn into a picture graph while the child works. Every picture takes one slot of the same height, a big elephant as much as a small kiwi, so the height of a tube IS how many are in it. When the belt is empty a question follows: how many are in one group, which group has the most or the fewest, how many more one group has than another, or the tubes must be dragged into order from most to fewest. A wrong answer brings help that shows instead of tells: the asked tube lights up slot by slot, a dashed line shows how high each tube reaches, the tubes that are the wrong way round lean together, or lines pair up two tubes so the extras stand out. In the two-way level the tubes also ask whether a thing flies, and the penguin, a bird that does not fly, belongs with the things that do not fly.

It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.B.3: classifying objects into given categories, counting the number in each category and sorting the categories by count; the "how many more" and two-way questions reach towards first-grade comparisons. Teachers choose two groups, three groups, or the two-way table, and whether the numbers beside the tube slots are shown (reading a graph) or hidden (counting). The pictures come from the illustrated library. No timer, no score.
practices: Sorting a mixed set into groups
Counting each group without skipping or counting twice
Comparing groups: most, fewest, how many more
Putting the groups in order by how many
howToPlay: Drop the picture on the belt down the right chute (tap the chute or drag the picture).
A wrong chute bounces it back: look at the little pictures on each chute.
When the belt is empty, answer the question: tap a number, tap a tube, or drag the tubes into order.
Press Check.
learningGoals: Classify objects into given categories and count each, the focus of Common Core K.MD.B.3
Sort the categories by count and find the most and the fewest
Read a simple picture graph and compare two groups

about: Long, tall and heavy are three different ways to measure, so here the child answers by choosing a measuring station. A sign card asks the question with no words: a sideways arrow for how long, an upright arrow for how tall, a weight for how heavy. The picture can be laid on the track (a slider runs to its far end and leaves a bar), stood at the post (a cap clunks down onto its top) or hung on the spring (the pan drops and bobs, far for a heavy thing, hardly at all for a light one). It is an interactive Kindergarten measurement activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that a wrong station still measures, honestly, the wrong thing. Put the giraffe on the track when the question is how tall and it tips over and lies down: the track shows how long it is lying down, and the track’s sign pops up next to the question’s, two different signs side by side. A second wrong try makes the right station glow. The pencil lies long and low at the post; the rock stretches the spring far. On the harder level one picture is measured two ways and a measure card drops into an album: the sunflower is light on the spring and tall at the post, so tall does not mean heavy. "Big or small" is a second instrument: a square size window glides over the pictures after Check, a big one pokes out of it and a small one fits inside with room to spare, so "big" is proved, not told.

It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.A.1: describing measurable attributes of objects, such as length, height and weight, and describing several of them for one object. The pictures come from the illustrated library, and each one is laid flat or stood up along its own drawn shape. Teachers choose "Long, tall, heavy" or "Big or small", and an easier or harder level. "Try anything" is open play: put any of 17 pictures on any station and watch what it measures. No timer, no score.
practices: Telling how long, how tall and how heavy apart
Choosing the right way to measure a thing
Describing one object two ways (long and light)
Telling big from small with a size window
howToPlay: Look at the sign on the question card.
Drag the picture onto a station, or tap the picture and then a station.
A wrong station still measures: compare its sign with the question.
No timer, no score: try another station.
learningGoals: Describe measurable attributes such as length, height and weight, the focus of Common Core K.MD.A.1
Describe several measurable attributes of one object
Tell big from small by comparing with a window

about: Marigold the mole runs a Knowing Machine that builds new words by snapping a prefix or suffix onto a root: kind, lucky, tell, color, fear, or help drops in, a cog stamped un-, re-, -ful, or -less clicks on, and the child reads what it makes — unkind, retell, colorful, fearless — then taps what it now means. It's a browser-based Grade 2 reading activity that needs no account or download.

The work is meaning, not memorizing. For unkind the choices are 'kind,' 'not kind,' and 'full of kindness,' so the child has to know that un- flips a word to its opposite, while -ful means 'full of' and -less means 'without.' Later rounds turn it around: the machine shows a meaning like 'to tie it again' or 'without any use,' and the child taps the affix (re-, less) that builds it, proving the part-to-meaning link both directions.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.b — using a known affix as a clue to the meaning of a new word. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Knowing that un- means not, re- means again, -ful means full of, and -less means without
Reading a built word like unhappy or spotless and choosing the meaning that fits
Working backward from a meaning to the prefix or suffix that makes it
Telling apart -ful and -less, which attach to the same root but mean opposite things
howToPlay: Read the word Marigold's Knowing Machine has built, and look at the cog that made it.
Tap the choice that tells what the new word means; in the 'which one' rounds, read the meaning first and tap the affix that builds it.
Not quite? That choice fades and you pick from the ones that are left — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use common prefixes and suffixes as clues to a word's meaning — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.b.
Understand that un- reverses a word while -ful and -less point in opposite directions.
Build the word-part habit that helps a child unlock new vocabulary while reading independently.

about: Every row of fruit on the plate is threaded on one skewer, so a row can only come out whole. The child lifts the skewers off one by one into a rack, and each skewer gets a box: three skewers of four raspberries read 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. A tap on the skewer pot turns the sticks the other way without moving a single piece of fruit, and the same plate reads 3 + 3 + 3 + 3.

Rows plus columns is the classic slip: typing 7 for 3 rows of 4 lights one row and one column while the rest pulse, so the child sees what was added. A box that disagrees with its skewer wobbles. In Build the child grows the plate for a sum like 4 + 4 + 4; in Find the child picks the plate that is 3 rows of 4 among plates that differ by one row or one column. Big arrays go to 10 rows of 10 with square tiles, and success ends with the sentence 3 × 4 = 12.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.4: use addition to find the total number of objects in a rectangular array with up to 5 rows and 5 columns, and write an equation as a sum of equal addends. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Find the total of an array by adding equal rows
Write an array as a sum of equal addends
Build the array for a repeated addition
Pick the array that shows rows of a number
howToPlay: Tap a skewer to lift it into the rack; tap it in the rack to put it back.
Type how many each skewer holds and how many in all, then press Check.
In the settings, choose Count, Build or Find, and arrays up to 5 by 5 or big arrays.
learningGoals: Find the total of a rectangular array by repeated addition.
See that every row of an array holds the same number.
Connect rows of a number with a multiplication sentence.

about: The adding sentence is printed on a paper accordion under the bead trays: one pleat for each group, each pleat as tall as its group. The child fills the trays and squeezes the strip. When every group holds the same, the pleats fold flat into one panel, and 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 becomes 3 × 4 = 12: one face that shows how many are in each group, three pleat edges behind it for the three groups.

When one group is different, the strip springs back open and the odd pleat stands out, so equal groups are not a rule the child is told but something the paper refuses to do without. Easy groups arrive filled, sometimes with one tray off by one to fix, and the child types the total after each group. Tricky groups and arrays go up to 6 rows of 8, and the child writes the times sentence. Every fair fold adds a page to a small times book.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.4: use addition to find the total number of objects in equal groups and arrays, and write an equation as a sum of equal addends. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Make equal groups of a given size
Find the total of equal groups by repeated addition
Keep a running total group by group
Write equal groups as a multiplication
howToPlay: Tap a tray to add a bead; hold it to take one out.
Squeeze the strip with the handle: equal groups fold flat, unequal ones spring back.
Type how many in all (or the times sentence) and press Check. In the settings, choose the level and whether the running totals are shown.
learningGoals: Find the total of equal groups by adding the same number again and again.
Notice that only equal groups can be written as a multiplication.
Connect a sum like 4 + 4 + 4 with 3 groups of 4.

about: Atlas the armadillo keeps fact files. The child reads a short fact, "Bees live in a hive. They make sweet honey.", and answers "Where do bees live?" by swiping a highlighter over the words in the text. The caught words drop into the question’s own sentence on the answer card: only the words that answer make it read true, and the card snaps into the drawer. Highlight the wrong words and the card reads them back so the child can see they do not fit. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

Every fact has two questions, one answered in each sentence, so the answer is never always in the same place. In Fill the fact file, the child sorts the five sentences of an animal’s text into drawers (eats, lives, moves, is covered in, babies) and then decides whether three claims are in the file. In Word-bank file, the child puts the key words back into the text’s own sentences and picks three favourite facts. Pictures can be turned off so only the words count.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.K.1: asking and answering questions about key details in a text. Every picture comes from the picture library. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the words in a text that answer a question
Answering with evidence from the text
Sorting facts about an animal by what they tell
Deciding whether a claim is in the text
howToPlay: Read the fact, or tap Atlas to hear it.
Swipe the highlighter over the words that answer the question, then check.
In the fact file, drag each sentence into its drawer.
Put each word back in its sentence and pick three facts.
learningGoals: The child finds the key detail that answers a question
The child shows where in the text the answer is
The child tells which facts are in a text and which are not

about: At The Harbor Post, Marlow the pelican hands the child short notes to sort by why their author wrote them: a note about owls hunting at night is there to inform, one about Pip the puppy chasing his tail is there to entertain, and one that begins 'To make a paper boat, first fold the paper in half' is there to instruct. It's a Grade 2 reading activity that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

The three bins — 'To tell facts,' 'To tell a fun story,' and 'To show how to do it' — make the author's job visible. The child reads each note and decides its purpose from how it is written: real-world facts, a silly little tale, or step-by-step directions with words like first, next, and then. They are judging the writer's intent, not just the topic, which is what makes author's purpose a thinking skill rather than a guess.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.2.6 — identifying the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Deciding whether a note is meant to inform, entertain, or instruct
Spotting real facts versus a made-up, playful story
Recognizing how-to directions by their step words like first, next, and then
Judging why a writer wrote something, not just what it is about
howToPlay: Read the short harbor note Marlow hands you.
Send it to the right bin — to tell facts, to tell a fun story, or to show how to do it.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify whether a text is written to inform, entertain, or instruct — the focus of Common Core RI.2.6.
Use clues in the writing, such as facts or step-by-step directions, to find the author's purpose.
Build the reader's awareness of why authors write, which supports comprehension across texts.

about: Bea the bookworm has two shelves that test a book the way it is made. The ribbon shelf threads a ribbon through a book's pages from the first to the last: only a story, with a beginning, a middle and an end, can be tied with a bow. The shaker shelf shakes the pages into a new order: a fact book still makes sense, because every page stands on its own. Bea's Two Bookshelves is a Grade 1 reading activity about telling stories from books that give information.

Every book opens to three pages. Shaken onto the wrong shelf, "Bunny's Lost Mitten" comes out ending first ("At last she found it on her own front step.") and hops back to the desk, while "How Bees Make Honey" shrugs it off: "Bees drink sweet nectar from flowers." reads just as well on any page. In Same topic, a story and a fact book share a subject, so the topic can never decide, and "How Buzz Got to the Moon" shows that a title can sound like a fact book and still be a story.

It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.5: explain major differences between books that tell stories and books that give information. Bea's fact books are all-about books; how-to and life-cycle books do go in order, and the shelves teach the main difference at Grade 1. No timer and no score.
practices: Read the inside pages to tell a story from a fact book
Notice that a story needs its beginning, middle and end
Notice that each page of a fact book stands on its own
Look past the topic, the picture and the title
howToPlay: Read Bea's ask, then tap a book to open it. The round knob shakes its pages.
With the book open, tap the shelf it belongs on, then press Check and watch the shelf test it.
Choose the books in the settings: Bea asks, Same topic, or Fill both shelves. Inside pages can also lie open on the desk for the whole class.
learningGoals: Tell books that tell stories from books that give information, the focus of Common Core RL.1.5.
Explain the difference: a story goes from a beginning to an end; a fact book teaches a true fact on every page.
Decide by reading, not by the topic, the picture or the title.

about: Bingo the dog calls a picture, and the child finds its word on a bingo card full of look-alike words: cat, cot, cut, pot, hit, hut, cap, cop and cup. A chip goes on the word that names the picture, and every word read right flips over into its picture, until a whole line is pictures and Bingo hops – BINGO. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

A chip on a look-alike slides off, and the letters that differ light up, so the child sees that cot is not cat because of one letter. After two tries the card dims all but the right word and its two nearest look-alikes; after three the right square pulses. When the card is full, the words left over are the ones Bingo never called. Other cards hold word families (cat, hat, bat, mat), words that start with two consonants, and two-syllable words. In You call the roles swap: Bingo holds the pictures, the child holds three word cards – cat, cap and cot – and Bingo covers exactly what the chosen card says.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3.d, telling apart similarly spelled words by the letters that differ. A setting adds the first letter to the call card. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading short words letter by letter
Telling apart words that differ by one letter, such as cat and cot
Matching a written word to its picture
Reading words of one family, and two-syllable words
howToPlay: Look at the picture Bingo calls.
Tap a word on the card, or drag the chip onto it.
Press Check. If the chip slides off, look at the letters that light up and try again.
learningGoals: The child reads a short word exactly, letter by letter
The child tells a word apart from look-alikes that differ by one letter
The child matches a written word to the picture it names

about: Booker the bear keeps the glossary and shows the child what the two words at the top of a dictionary page are for: two guide words sit at the top — like cap and cot — and the child taps the one word, from choices such as car, can, and cup, that would actually appear on that page because it falls between them in ABC order. It's a Grade 2 vocabulary activity that runs in the browser with no account.

Guide words are a real reference tool, and the only way to use them is to compare letters in order. Between cap and cot, the word car fits (it comes after cap and before cot), while can comes too early and cup comes too late. Because the choices share their first letters, the child has to look at the second and third letters to decide — the exact alphabetizing skill that makes a dictionary or glossary usable.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.e — using glossaries and beginning dictionaries to find the meaning of words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading the two guide words at the top of a glossary page
Putting words in alphabetical order by their second and third letters
Deciding which word falls between the guide words
Ruling out words that come too early or too late in ABC order
howToPlay: Look at Booker's two guide words at the top of the page.
Tap the word from the three choices that belongs on this page — the one that comes between them in ABC order.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use guide words to find a word in a glossary or dictionary — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.e.
Alphabetize words by looking past the first letter to the next ones.
Build the reference-skill confidence that helps a child look up word meanings on their own.

about: Bo the bunny is filling his pantry. On the shelf, sealed crates stand on the left (each crate holds exactly ten berries) and loose berries sit in a bowl of nine on the right. Above them hangs the door tag. In some rounds the child slings crates and berries onto the shelf to make the number on the tag; in others the shelf comes stocked and the child writes its number on two wheels, hangs a tens plaque and a ones plaque, or works out a shelf where berries have spilled out of the bowl.

On Check, the door tag stretches apart: 34 becomes 30 and 4, a hidden 0 rolls out behind the tens digit, and each part hangs over the crates or the bowl it counts. The crates are counted by tens and the loose berries by ones, and a part that does not match turns coral. So 4 crates and 3 berries for 34 shows a crate count of 40 under the 30. Ten loose berries are a crate: when a right total has spilled, Bo packs ten of them into a crate.

The order card can show numerals or number words, and the numbers go to 50 or to 99. After a second wrong try the crates open to show their ten berries each, and the loose berries are numbered. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.2. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading a two-digit number as tens and ones
Building a number from tens and ones, and writing the number for a set of tens and ones
Writing a number in expanded form, such as 34 = 30 + 4
Seeing that ten ones make a ten, that 13 is a ten and three ones, and that 70 is seven tens and no ones
howToPlay: Read the task and the door tag.
To fill the shelf, tap the crates or the basket to load the sling, then pull the sling back and let go (or tap the same pile again). Tap the last crate or berry on the shelf to take it back.
To write a number, turn the two wheels with the arrows: tens on the left, ones on the right. To hang plaques, tap a plaque, then a hook.
Press Check and watch the tag stretch over the crates and the bowl. If a count turns coral, change that part and check again.
In the settings, choose the order card (numerals or number words) and the numbers (to 50 or to 99).
learningGoals: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for tens and ones
Make a number from tens and ones and write the number they show
Write two-digit numbers in expanded form
Recognise a ten as ten ones, the teens as a ten and some ones, and decades as tens with no ones

about: In Bram's Board Shop every order is a length story: a scarf that grows, a board that is sawn, a shelf that is longer than a board. The child puts the two lengths the story gives on Bram's bench. The longest length of the story goes on the top rail, and the pieces go end to end on the bottom rail. Every story, whatever its shape, becomes the same picture: two rails that have to end together. The rack also holds a third board, the one a child gets by just adding or subtracting because of a word like "longer" or "saws off".

Once the bench is built, the child types how long the mystery board is and presses Check. The saw cuts a board exactly that long and drops it into the empty place, and a spirit level stands against the two rail ends. If the rails end together, the level stands straight and the bubble sits in the middle. If not, it leans, and the gap or the overhang is shaded. A board that is not in the story, or a length on the wrong rail, gets its own hint, even when the numbers happen to balance. After a second miss the bench ruler marks where the mystery board starts and where it has to reach. When the story balances, the success line shows the equation in the story's own shape.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.B.5 (use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths given in the same units). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Solve length word problems with the unknown at the start, the change or the result
Model a story with a drawing of a ruler: the whole on top, the parts below
Add and subtract lengths in centimeters within 100
Look past keywords like "longer" to the structure of the story
howToPlay: Read the order, then tap a board and tap a rail to put it there, or drag it: the longest length on the top rail (it can be the mystery board), the pieces on the bottom rail.
Type how long the mystery board is on the keypad and press Check. Tap the spirit level at any time to test the bench.
In the settings, choose numbers within 80 in fives or within 100, and whether the bench ruler is shown.
learningGoals: Solve length word problems within 100 with the unknown in any position, the focus of Common Core 2.MD.B.5.
Represent a length story as two equal lengths: the whole, and the parts end to end.
Write the equation that matches the story, with the unknown where the story puts it.

about: Which holds more? Here the child finds out the way it is really done: by pouring one container into the other. First the child makes a call: the raspberry goes on the one they think holds more, on the one that holds less, or on the "same" coaster. Then they fill the left one at the juice tap, pick it up and tip it into the other with their own hand: the further they tip, the faster the juice runs. It is an interactive Kindergarten measurement activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the juice decides, and it can only do one of three things. It spills over the rim into the drip tray, so the first one held more; it leaves a gap at the top, marked with a dashed line, so the second one holds more; or it fills the other one exactly to the brim, and the brim sparkles: they hold the same. Every glass, jug, bowl and pot holds what its drawn shape really holds, so the illusions are real ones: a tall thin glass can leave a gap in a low wide bowl, and a thick stoneware pot is big outside and small inside. On the tricky level no single look wins: sometimes the taller one holds more, sometimes the wider one, so the only sure way is to pour. A wrong call is answered by the evidence (the puddle, the gap or the brim is ringed), and a second wrong call makes the right place glow.

It is aligned to Common Core K.MD.A.2: directly comparing two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which has more of the attribute and which has less; here the attribute is capacity. Teachers choose easy or tricky cups and the question: holds more, holds less, or mixed; one round also asks whether the juice will fit in the other one. After each call the child can pour back and forth as long as they like, and the juice never gets more or less. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing two containers by how much they hold
Predicting first, then checking by pouring
Seeing that tall does not always mean more
Telling more, less and the same apart
howToPlay: Put the raspberry on the one you think holds more (or less, or on "the same").
Press the tap to fill the left one.
Drag it over the other one and tip it by dragging down, or use the tip button.
Watch the juice: it spills over, leaves a gap, or fills to the brim.
learningGoals: Directly compare two containers and say which holds more or less, the focus of Common Core K.MD.A.2
Say when two containers hold the same
Use pouring as the test, not how a container looks

about: Bolt the robot has a machine that bundles cubes, but only the child can pull its lever. A hopper drops small clumps of cubes onto a press plate. When the child pulls the lever, a band with exactly ten pockets wraps around the loose cubes. Ten cubes fill it, and it clasps into one ten that rolls onto the rack. With fewer, the band springs open, and by default it first shows its empty pockets. With more, it takes ten and pushes the rest back out.

In most rounds the child makes a number, such as 34 as 3 tens and 4 loose cubes. One round starts with nine cubes laid out to look like ten; another drops cubes in threes, so they overshoot ten. In an unbundle round the child taps the scissors button to snip a ten open into ten loose cubes, and the number stays the same. Other rounds ask how many cubes there are, or ask the child to bundle every ten and fill in the tens and the ones. On Check, Bolt counts the tens by tens and then the loose cubes, and ten loose cubes left on the plate are a ten still waiting to be bundled.

Numbers go to 49 or to 99, and the band can show its empty pockets or just spring open. After a wrong try, the tens are labelled 10, 20, 30. After a second, the loose cubes are numbered too, and in the rounds where the child makes a number, the number card splits into its tens and ones. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.2.a. No timer and no score.
practices: Bundling ten ones into one ten
Building two-digit numbers with as many tens as possible
Breaking a ten into ten ones without changing the number
Reading a number shown as tens and ones, including a ten and more than ten ones
howToPlay: Read the task and the number card.
Tap the hopper to drop cubes onto the plate. Tap the minus button to take one back.
Pull the lever when you think there are exactly ten loose cubes. To snip a ten open into ten loose cubes, tap the scissors button.
When the task asks for a number, type it on the keypad, or tap Tens or Ones and type the digit. Then press Check.
In the settings, choose the numbers (to 49 or to 99) and what the band does when it can’t close (show the empty pockets, or just spring open).
learningGoals: Understand that ten ones make one ten
Show a two-digit number as tens and ones
See that a ten can be opened into ten ones and the number stays the same
Recognise the decades as tens with no ones

about: The letter d hangs on a red horseshoe magnet above four pictures: a dog, a fish, a rabbit and a tiger. The child moves the pictures they think start with the sound of d under the magnet and switches it on. The dog flies up onto the hook; anything else shivers and stays on the table. The empty hooks show how many pictures are still to find. It is an interactive Kindergarten phonics activity that plays in the browser.

In Letter of the week the m magnet has three hooks, and a nose waits among the pictures, because m and n sound alike. Two magnets, m and n, share one table, so every picture has to be heard and placed. With letter teams the magnets read sh, ch and th: ship, chair and tooth each go to the team they hear, then the teams drop into gaps in the written words, and in two rounds whole words hang on the magnets to be read. After two misses, small letters appear on the pictures.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3.a, the primary sound of each consonant. No timer and no score.
practices: Hearing the first sound of a word
Matching a letter to its most common sound
Telling apart letters that sound alike, like m and n
Hearing and writing letter teams like sh, ch and th
howToPlay: Say the name of each picture and listen to its first sound.
Move the pictures that start with the magnet’s sound under it.
Switch the magnet on: the right pictures fly up, the others stay down.
learningGoals: The child names the first sound of a pictured word
The child links each consonant letter to its primary sound
The child sorts words by the letter they begin with or the letter team they contain

about: Each number stands on a podium as a little wooden cabinet with a tens drawer and a ones drawer. Under the podium there is one knob for each place, and pulling it opens that drawer in both cabinets at once. The tens drawers open first, and their rods stand up as a column beside each cabinet. If the tens are the same, the ones drawers unlock and their cubes join the columns. If the tens are different, the ones drawers lock shut, because nine ones can never reach the next ten.

Once the deciding drawers are open, the sign between the cabinets stands up and the child taps it to turn it to <, > or =. On Check every drawer opens and the sign stretches out to the two columns: its open side has to hold the taller column, and = only lies level on two columns of the same height. In order rounds, three cabinets go onto a staircase, smallest first or biggest first, and on Check their columns rise above them; a cabinet in the wrong place hops back to the waiting row.

The numbers can be groups of fruit up to 20 (packs of ten and loose counters), two-digit numbers, or four-digit numbers with four drawers, compared from the left. After a wrong try, the drawers that decide glow. After a second, in the group and two-digit rounds, the tens are counted 10, 20, 30 up each column, and a dotted line shows the gap between the two columns. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Comparing two-digit numbers by the tens first, then the ones
Seeing why nine ones can never beat one more ten
Turning the sign so that its open side faces the bigger number
Putting three numbers in order, smallest first or biggest first
howToPlay: Pull the tens knob: the tens drawers open in both cabinets and their rods stand up.
If the tens are the same, pull the ones knob too. A locked knob only rattles.
Tap the sign to turn it until it is true, then press Check.
In order rounds, drag a cabinet onto a step (or tap it, then tap the step) and press Check.
In the settings, choose the numbers (groups to 20, two-digit or four-digit) and the task (compare two or order three).
learningGoals: Compare two two-digit numbers using the meaning of the tens and ones digits — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.B.3.
Record the comparison with >, = and <.
Put three numbers in order by their place value.
Compare bigger numbers place by place, starting from the left.

about: A red post box stands under a play mat, and its doors carry numbers from 3 to 6 (to 8 with more shapes), each with that many sticks and corner dots underneath. The shapes on the mat come turned, stretched and uneven, never just the tidy upright ones. The child drags a shape to a door, or taps the shape and then the door. It is an interactive geometry activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is the door. Offered a shape, it lays its sticks down one on each side. When they fit, the shape drops through into the drawer. When the door has too many sticks, one is left over and tumbles off; when it has too few, a side stays bare and glows; and a short line under the box says what happened, such as "4 sticks for 3 sides". Trying a door is always allowed, because every bounce shows the difference stick by stick. Tapping a side plants a numbered peg on it, and only the last peg lifts off, so each side is counted once. After two bounces every side gets a tick and every corner a dot; after four the pegs plant themselves and the right door breathes.

It is aligned to Common Core K.G.B.4: analysing shapes by their parts, such as the number of sides and corners, whatever their size or turn. Three more modes widen it. Sort by sides gives a tray of shapes and three or four numbered doors. Real or not has one big door for a triangle, a square or a rectangle: an open figure falls apart at it, a straight stick slides off a curved side, a long rectangle leaves gaps against the square door's equal sticks, and a rhombus cannot hold the square-corner marks; the harder level asks by properties instead of names. Name the doors puts shape names on the doors to read. A square fits the rectangle door (and the rhombus door), because it is one, so no round asks that question and the conversation stays with the teacher. At the end the drawer shows each posted shape with its name. Teachers choose the mode and the shapes. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting the sides and corners of a shape, each one once
Recognising shapes that are turned, stretched or uneven
Sorting shapes by their number of sides
Telling real triangles, squares and rectangles from open, curved and lopsided look-alikes
howToPlay: Drag a shape to a door, or tap the shape and then the door.
Tap the sides to plant pegs if you want to count them.
In the tray modes, post every shape that fits and then press Check.
Double-tap a shape to turn it.
learningGoals: Describe shapes by their parts, the focus of Common Core K.G.B.4
Count sides one to one, whatever the turn or size
Explain why an open or curved figure is not a polygon

about: The child pours a bag of bricks into a glass tower two bricks wide, and every brick rolls into the lower column. An even number ends flat and takes the flat roof; an odd number leaves one brick sticking up that only the roof with a chimney can cover. The wrong roof tips and slides off, so the verdict is never a guess between two buttons: the tower shows why.

Then the child writes the two columns as two equal parts: 14 = 7 + 7, or 15 = 7 + 7 + 1 with the chimney brick as the one left over. Two different numbers in the boxes never pass. For numbers to 99 the tens arrive as finished slabs, five pairs each and always flat, so the child roofs four bags before the ones are poured and sees that only the ones decide.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.3: determine whether a group of objects has an odd or even number of members, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Tell even from odd by pairing objects
Write an even number as two equal parts
Show an odd number as two equal parts and one more
Decide even or odd up to 99 from the ones
howToPlay: Tap the bag to pour the bricks; hold it to pour faster.
Put a roof on the tower. If it slides off, look at the top and try the other roof.
Type the two equal columns and press Check. In the settings, choose numbers to 10, to 20 or to 99, and whether the roof comes before or after the tower.
learningGoals: Know that an even number of objects pairs up with none left over.
Write an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
Use the ones digit to decide whether a number to 99 is even or odd.

about: A red letterbox stands at the end of a post office counter, and the mail bag is full of shapes: circles, squares, triangles and stars, and spheres, cubes, cylinders, cones and pyramids, some turned and some tiny. The child drags each one onto the letter tray or the parcel tray, or taps it and then taps the tray. Nothing is judged while the child sorts, and nothing turns over to give the answer away. It is an interactive geometry activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is the slot. At Check each letter is turned on its edge in front of the slot: a flat shape becomes a thin line and slips through, while a solid stays thick, jams and drops back into the bag. Each parcel goes to the shelf, where a small window shows it from the side, and a flat shape put there topples into a line and slides off. A shape that comes back shows its edge-on view, a line beside a thick block, and the hint says why: flat shapes turn into a thin line on their edge, solids stay thick. A second miss puts an arrow on each shape that points to its tray. The twins are deliberate: a circle and a sphere, a square and a cube, a triangle and a pyramid share a bag.

It is aligned to Common Core K.G.A.3: identifying shapes as two-dimensional (flat) or three-dimensional (solid). Two counting tasks take the idea further. A solid stands see-through on a turntable with its hidden edges dashed; the child can turn it, then pulls its tab and it opens out into its flat net. Every flat face needs a postmark before the net may go through the slot, and the child taps how many with the chips from 1 to 9: a cube has six, not the three you can see. A cylinder's curved side unrolls into a striped sheet that takes no stamp. In the everyday-things task a dice, a book, an eraser, a present, a can and a drum from the picture library wear the outline of their solid. Teachers choose the task. No timer, no score.
practices: Telling flat shapes from solid ones
Seeing that a flat shape has no thickness and a solid always has some
Telling twins apart: a circle and a sphere, a square and a cube
Counting the flat faces of cubes, rectangular prisms, pyramids, other prisms and cylinders
howToPlay: Drag each shape onto the letter tray or the parcel tray, or tap it and then the tray.
Press Check and watch the slot and the shelf.
In the counting tasks, pull the tab, stamp every flat face and tap how many.
Press Check to post the net through the slot.
learningGoals: Identify shapes as flat or solid, the focus of Common Core K.G.A.3
Explain that a flat shape has no thickness
Count the flat faces of a solid by opening it out

about: A little window with two shutters: they swing open, a group of pictures looks out — ducks, apples, carrots — and the shutters close again. How many were there? The child taps a number from 1 to 10, can look again as often as they like, and presses Check. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The short look is the point. Small groups can be seen at a glance, and bigger ones are shown in the shapes teachers use in number talks: dice faces up to six, five in a line and some more, pairs, a short line, a small scatter. So the child learns to see seven as five and two instead of counting one by one — and counting is always there to check. After a wrong number the window stays open and the child counts; after a second, the numbers run along the pictures to a question mark on the last one, so the child still says how many.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer "how many?" about up to 10 things. Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 or up to 10, and whether the window opens for a moment, a little longer, or stays open for plain counting. No timer, no score — looking again is never counted against the child.
practices: Seeing small groups at a glance
Reading bigger groups by their shape: a dice face, five and some more, pairs
Counting to check, and knowing that the last number counted tells how many
Answering "how many?" for groups up to 10
howToPlay: Watch the window: it opens and shows a group, and in a quick look it closes again.
Tap the number that tells how many you saw. Tap Look again whenever you want another look.
Press Check.
Not quite? The window stays open — count them and tap the number again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Answer "how many?" about up to 10 things — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
See small amounts at a glance and bigger ones as five and some more
Use counting to check what you saw

about: Every letter has two forms, and this activity keeps them in a real printer's type case: the capitals live in the upper drawer and the small letters in the lower one, which is where the words uppercase and lowercase come from. One form stands in its drawer, and the child drags its other form from the composing tray into the empty compartment, or simply taps it. The letters are set in a school typeface with the a and g that children learn to read, and a capital I, a small l and a 1 that never look alike. It is an interactive reading activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is the back of each metal letter: every sort carries its other form there. A wrong letter dropped in the slot tips over and shows its own other form, so a D lies under the B and the column plainly holds two different letters. After that first slip the child may turn any sort over with a long press to check it; after a second, the given letter turns too and shows exactly the shape to look for. A right pair is pulled on a little press and printed onto an alphabet poster in the page's own language.

It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.1.d: recognising and naming all upper- and lowercase letters. Two more levels go further. Look-alikes lays eight sorts on a composing stick, such as b, d, p and q, n, u, m and h, or M, W, N and H, and the child taps every copy of one letter; a wrong mark turns over to show whose letter it really is. In words sets three short words under their pictures, and the child taps every copy of a letter and taps how many. Teachers choose the level and which form is given first. No timer, no score.
practices: Matching each capital with its small letter, both ways
Telling apart letters that look alike, such as b, d, p and q
Finding a letter inside words, in capitals and in small letters
Counting how many times a letter appears
howToPlay: Drag the letter's other form from the tray into the empty slot, or tap it.
Pull the press when the pair is right.
In Look-alikes and In words, tap every copy of the letter; in words, also tap how many. Then pull the press.
After a miss, press and hold a letter to see its back.
learningGoals: Recognise and name upper- and lowercase letters, the focus of Common Core RF.K.1.d
Know that a capital and its small letter are the same letter
Find a letter among look-alikes and inside words

about: A number from 1 to 9 (or 9 to 19 with the wider setting) stands open on a path of lidded stones, with a counter resting on it. The child writes the number that comes right after it on the number keys — stand on 7, write 8 — and the counter hops forward onto the stone as it opens. It is an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser on tablets, phones and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is counting on from a number you are given instead of starting over at one. The stones before the counter are hidden under lids, so the child cannot read the answer off a line of numbers; a lid can be lifted to peek at an earlier number when that helps, and the teacher can show the whole path up to the counter. A wrong answer is named for what it is — the same number, the one before, or too far — and the path opens up to the counter so the child can count on from it.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.2 — counting forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Name the number that comes right after a given number, to 10 or to 20
Count on from the middle of the sequence instead of starting at one
Cross from 9 to 10 and from 19 to 20 (wider setting: the numbers to 20)
Write a numeral on the number keys, with one or two digits
howToPlay: Look at the number the counter stands on. The next stone is open and waiting.
Tap the digits to write the number that comes next, then press Check. The counter hops onto it.
Not sure? Tap a lid to peek at an earlier number. Not quite right? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count forward from a given number — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.2
Know which number comes next in the sequence to 10, and to 20
Build the counting fluency that addition and number sense build on

about: The first sound and the rest of the word are two magnets on a rail: c and at. The gap between them is the pause, drawn as a stretchy dotted line and a row of pause dots. The child pushes the first magnet along until it snaps onto the rest — c … at becomes cat — and then taps the picture of the word. It is an interactive Kindergarten blending activity that plays in the browser.

Three pictures wait: the word, one that rhymes and one that starts with the same sound. Check runs a magnet test on the chosen picture’s own name, part by part. Pick the bat for cat, and the “at” magnets click together while the “b” jumps away: the end is right, the start is not. After two tries every picture shows its first letter. A second level gives one magnet per sound, c · a · t, for blending three or four sounds.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.c, blending onsets and rimes of single-syllable spoken words. No timer and no score.
practices: Blending a first sound and the rest of a word
Telling a rhyming word from the right word by its first sound
Telling a word with the same first sound from the right word by its ending
Blending three or four single sounds into a word
howToPlay: Push the red magnet along the rail until it snaps onto the blue one.
Tap the picture of the word you made.
Press Check and watch which parts stick together and which push apart.
learningGoals: The child blends a first sound and the rest of a word into a whole word
The child uses the first sound to tell a rhyming word from the right one
The child blends three or four single sounds into a word

about: A building of ten floors stands beside two animal passengers, each holding a ticket with a number on it — a pig with 6 and a dog with 9, say. Who goes higher? The child taps the passenger with the bigger number and presses Check. Then the elevator rides up: it stops at floor 6, where one passenger gets off, and carries the other on up to floor 9. It's an interactive Kindergarten activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The building is a number line stood upright: its floor numbers run up the wall in counting order, so a bigger number is a higher floor, and the comparison becomes something the child can see. A child who is not sure can find both numbers on the wall first. A wrong Check says to find both numbers on the building (or, with the numbers hidden, to count the floors from the bottom); after a second, both floors light up, each in its passenger's colour, so the higher one is plain to see. A right Check says it with numbers: “Yes — 9 is bigger than 6!” Some pairs are far apart, like 8 and 2, and some are neighbours, like 7 and 8 — those are the ones that need a careful look. The two numbers are never the same.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.7 — comparing two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals. Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 (a building of five floors) or up to 10, and hide the floor numbers so the floors have to be counted from the bottom. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing two written numbers up to 10
Finding a number in the counting order
Seeing that a number later in the count is bigger
Counting the floors from the bottom when the numbers are hidden
howToPlay: Look at the two tickets. Who goes higher?
Not sure? Find both numbers on the building.
Tap the passenger with the bigger number, then press Check.
Not quite? The hint helps you find both numbers — the one higher up is bigger. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 given as written numerals — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.7
Know that a number later in the count is bigger
Use the order of the numbers to compare

about: Two big number cards stand side by side — 3 and 8, say — each with an empty tower base above it. Which number is smaller? The child taps it and presses Check. Then both towers grow at the same time, one block per beat, while a counting row underneath lights up 1, 2, 3… The tower for 3 stops at three blocks and raises a little flag; the tower for 8 keeps climbing. It's an interactive Kindergarten activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The towers show what each written number means and why one is smaller: counting up from 1, the smaller number is the one you reach first, so its tower stops first. A wrong Check asks the child to count from 1 and notice which of the two numbers comes first; after a second, the towers grow for that look, the flag marking the smaller one, until the child chooses again. A right Check says it with numbers: “Yes — 3 is smaller than 8!” Some pairs are far apart, like 2 and 9, and some are neighbours, like 5 and 6 — those are the ones that need a careful look. The two numbers are never the same.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.7 — comparing two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals. Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 or up to 10, and show or hide the counting row under the towers. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing two written numbers up to 10
Saying which of two numbers comes first in the count
Seeing how many each written number means
Using “smaller” for the number that comes first
howToPlay: Look at the two numbers. Which one is smaller?
Tap the smaller number, then press Check.
Watch both towers grow together: the smaller number’s tower stops first.
Not quite? Count from 1 — the number you say first is smaller. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 given as written numerals — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.7
Know that a number that comes earlier in the count is smaller
Connect each written number to how many it means

about: The printed word is a name tag on a string: cat. Four pictures hang on a cork board, and their names start alike: a cat, a cap, a can and a car. The child hangs the tag on a picture and presses Check, and the tag presses down letter by letter from the left. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

On the cap it sticks c and a, then the corner curls up at t and the tag peels off, back to the tray, with the t ringed. A guess from the first letter fails at the end, and the child sees exactly how far the word matched. Further levels hang rhyming words (cat, hat, bat), join syllable pieces into one tag (pen·cil, beside a pen·guin) and play memory with pictures and tags.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3, knowing and applying grade-level phonics in decoding words. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading a short printed word all the way to the last letter
Telling apart words that start the same way
Reading rhyming words where only the first letter changes
Joining syllables and reading a longer word
howToPlay: Read the word on the tag.
Drag the tag onto its picture, or tap the tag and then the picture.
Press Check and watch the tag stick, or peel off at the first letter that is different.
learningGoals: The child decodes a short word left to right, to the end
The child notices the first letter where two words differ
The child reads rhyming words and longer words in syllables

about: In The Glow Ruler a picture lies on a glass centimeter ruler with its left end exactly on 0: a snail, a seashell, a toy car, a lemon, a key, a centipede, a glue bottle, an ice pop, a kiwi half, a toy train or a toy airplane, each shown at a length the real thing has. The child slides a glow marker under the ruler to where the object ends and presses Check. Then light fills the centimeter spaces one by one from 0, and each lit space shows its count, so the child sees that the number on a ruler counts the spaces before it.

If the marker is too far, the extra spaces glow coral with no object above them. If it is too short, the end of the object stays unlit. This answers the two classic ruler mistakes: counting the lines instead of the spaces, and stopping at a number before the end. After a second miss, a dashed line drops from the end of the object to the ruler. In the setting with only 0, 5, 10 and 15 printed, the child reads an end such as 12 by counting on from the 10, as on a ruler that prints only some of its numbers. Each object measured joins a small chart of today's lengths, shortest first.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.A.1 (measure the length of an object with a ruler). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Read where an object ends on a centimeter ruler that starts at 0
Count centimeter spaces, not tick lines
Count on from 5 or 10 to read an unnumbered mark
Say a length in centimeters
howToPlay: Drag the glow marker under the ruler, or tap the ruler, to put the marker where the object ends; the arrow buttons move it one centimeter.
Press Check and watch the light count the spaces from 0.
In the settings, choose whether the ruler shows every number or only 0, 5, 10 and 15, and whether the light shows a count in every space or only at the end.
learningGoals: Measure the length of an object with a centimeter ruler, the focus of Common Core 2.MD.A.1.
Understand that the number at a mark tells how many centimeter spaces lie between 0 and that mark.
Read a mark with no number printed by counting on from the nearest 5 or 10.

about: A sight word is a word you can read in a blink, so this camera shows the word for exactly one blink. The child presses the big button, the iris spins open and «was» glows in the lens while four cards lie face down. The shutter clicks shut, the cards flip up – saw, was, want and with – and the child taps the word they saw. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

The look-alikes are chosen so that a glance at the first letter is never enough. A wrong card flips back and the camera looks again, a little longer; after two misses a photo of the word sits beside the cards and the letters that differ glow. In Find every one the child brackets every copy of «the» in a grid of twelve tiles – it is there five times – and then says how many. In the story mode the word hides in short sentences next to a picture: “The cat was on the bed. Was it hot?” A capital at the start is still the same word. Every right answer develops into a photo for the album.

It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3.c, reading common high-frequency words by sight. The dial on the camera sets a long, medium or short blink, and the camera can be pressed again at any time. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading common words at a glance
Telling a word from its look-alikes, letter by letter
Noticing letter order, as in was and saw
Finding the same word in sentences, with or without a capital
howToPlay: Press the camera button and look at the word in the lens.
When the cards flip up, tap the word you saw.
Press Check. Not right? Press the camera again and take another look.
learningGoals: The child reads common high-frequency words by sight
The child tells a word apart from words that look almost the same
The child recognises the same word in sentences, also with a capital letter

about: A picture made only of shapes — a house, a rocket, a train, a robot, a lighthouse — waits in plain cream, with two paint tins beside it. The child picks a tin and taps every piece that is the tin's shape.
