The brush runs round the edge of each piece it touches and leaves a bead on every corner and little ticks on sides of equal length, so the corners and sides are drawn right on the piece. It is an interactive Kindergarten geometry activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the paint stays wet until Check. Nothing is judged at the tap, so the child has to decide; then the paint sets one piece after another, and it only stays in a piece that truly is the tin's shape, however it is turned and however small it is. A piece that is not the shape sheds its paint into a puddle, and a figure with a gap leaks through it. The hint names what really differs: count the corners, look at the ticks to see whether the sides match, check for square corners, or notice a bent side. If a piece is still missing, the tin drips on the quarter of the picture where it hides; a second miss makes the missing pieces glow. A finished picture comes alive for a moment.

It is aligned to Common Core K.G.A.2: correctly naming shapes regardless of their orientation or overall size. Every shape a tin asks for comes in more than one size, and the ones with corners also come turned, and the diamond is always a leaning rhombus, never a square on its point. Teachers choose shape pictures, a real-or-not quilt (open, rounded and curved fakes beside real shapes) or count pictures (paint the triangles and squares, then say how many), and whether the tins show the shape, only its name or only a clue. No library pictures, no timer, no score.
practices: Naming shapes that are turned, tiny or stretched
Seeing what makes a shape: corners, equal sides, square corners, closed
Telling real shapes from open, rounded and curved look-alikes
Counting the triangles and squares in a figure
howToPlay: Tap a paint tin to open it.
Tap every piece that is the tin's shape; tap a painted piece again to take the paint back.
In count pictures, set how many with the − and + buttons.
Press Check and watch which paint stays.
learningGoals: Name shapes whatever their turn or size, the focus of Common Core K.G.A.2
Use corners and sides to decide what a shape is
Tell a closed shape from an open figure

about: Each little word is a key, and its letters are its teeth. A sentence has a brass padlock in its gap – “The cat ___ on the bed.” – and the child picks a key from the rail and turns it. Only was opens the lock; saw, war and wax look almost the same, but their teeth sit in the wrong places. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

A wrong key jams and shows why: the teeth that differ glow, an extra tooth sticks out of the lock, a missing one leaves an empty notch. After two jams the lock turns to glass and shows how many letters it needs. In Key ring, three sentences share three keys – was, saw and say – and each key opens exactly one lock, so every look-alike is right somewhere and the child has to read the word and the sentence. In Cut the key, the child cuts the word tooth by tooth from a tray of letters. Every opened lock puts its key on the key ring.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3.c, reading common high-frequency words by sight. A setting hides the pictures for confident readers. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading common words letter by letter, in order
Telling apart words that look alike, such as was and saw
Choosing the word a sentence needs
Spelling a common word from its letters
howToPlay: Read the sentence with the padlock in it.
Tap or drag a key into the lock.
Press Turn. If the key jams, look at the glowing teeth and try another key.
learningGoals: The child reads common high-frequency words exactly
The child tells a word apart from look-alikes with the same letters in another order, one letter more, one less, or one letter changed
The child chooses the word that makes the sentence right

about: The number lives in two glass tubes: rods of ten in the tens tube and single cubes in the ones tube, with a digit under each tube. Both tubes stop at nine under a lid, so pushing the ones up at nine only bumps the lid. That is why 10 more can only ever be one more rod in the tens tube, and the ones tube stays as it was.

In the 10 more, 10 less and 1 more, 1 less rounds the child changes the tubes and presses Check; at 39 + 1 the ones tube is full, so the child lifts a rod into the tens and empties the ones by hand. In arrow rounds each card moves one tube: ↓ and ↑ a rod, → and ← a cube, and a card dragged onto the wrong tube slides back. There are also two trips that land on one number, and rounds where the child first types how many jumps of ten and of one lead from one number to another, then watches the tubes run them. In the number-of-the-day rounds the child makes its four neighbors, which fill a cross: 10 less above, 10 more below, 1 less and 1 more beside it.

With frosted glass the blocks are hidden, so the child works from the digits in their head; the frost clears at Check. After a wrong try in the rounds where the child makes a number, the tube that should change lights up and a see-through block (or a dashed one on its way out) shows the step; after a second, the digit that stays the same is ringed in gold. When a round is solved, ten frames, tally marks and the number in words light up. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.C.5. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding 10 more and 10 less than a two-digit number without counting
Seeing that 10 more changes only the tens digit
Finding 1 more and 1 less, also when the ones tube is full or empty
Following and counting jumps of ten and of one
howToPlay: Press ▲ under a tube to add a block and ▼ to take one out, or drag the glass up and down.
Make the new number and press Check.
In arrow rounds, tap a card to play it on its own tube, or drag it there.
In counting rounds, type how many jumps of ten and of one, press Check and watch the tubes.
In the settings, choose the task (10 more, 10 less · 1 more, 1 less · arrow jumps · number of the day) and the glass (clear or frosted).
learningGoals: Find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number in your head, without counting — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.C.5.
Explain that 10 more changes the tens digit and leaves the ones digit alone.
Find 1 more and 1 less, including across a ten.
Read the arrows of a hundreds chart as moves of tens and ones.

about: Two mats, two groups that belong together — bees and flowers, bunnies and carrots, squirrels and acorns. Which group has more, or are they the same? The child taps “More” on the group with more, or “The same”, and presses Check. It's an interactive Kindergarten activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The spacing is often a trick: in many rounds the smaller group is spread out across its mat while the bigger one huddles together, so the group that looks bigger is the one with fewer — but not always, so the eye can't be trusted either way. That is the classic trap of comparing by eye, and the activity gives the child two honest ways past it. One is matching: a tap on one in the top group and then one in the bottom group gives both the same bow — a colour and a shape — and whoever is left without a bow shows which group has more; if nobody is left over, the groups are the same. The other is counting both groups. A wrong answer brings a hint: pair them up, or look for the ones without a partner. After a second, the rest are paired and the ones without a partner are ringed. A right answer bows every pair, numbers both groups and says it with numbers: “10 is more than 7”.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.6 — saying whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than or equal to the number in another, by matching and counting, up to 10. Teachers can choose groups up to 5 or up to 10, and switch the spacing trick off. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing two groups up to 10: more, fewer or the same
Matching one to one: a partner for each
Counting both groups to compare them
Not letting the spacing fool the eye
howToPlay: Look at the two groups. Which has more, or are they the same?
To find out, pair them up: tap one at the top, then one at the bottom — both get the same bow.
Tap “More” on the group with more, or “The same”, then press Check.
Not quite? The hint says what to try — fix it and press Check again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Say whether one group has more than, fewer than or the same as another, up to 10 — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.6
Compare groups by matching one to one
Compare groups by counting

about: In Chuffer's Switchyard the child splits a number by throwing a railway switch. A load of crates waits in a wagon on top of a hill. Hold the release lever and the crates roll down one at a time; each one goes into whichever car the switch points to as it crosses the fork. Flick the switch halfway and the load splits — 2 crates to the left, 3 to the right. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The child never moves a crate by hand, so every split is a moment of throwing the switch. The two cars are ten-frames, so 3 crates look like 3. The child reads each car and sets the number bond — a whole circle over two part circles, the same diagram as on the worksheets — then pulls the coupler. The coupler only takes a split whose numbers match the cars and that is new; each one lands as a row of a staircase in the route book (1 + 4, 2 + 3, 3 + 2, 4 + 1), so the empty rows show which ways are still missing. The equation, such as 5 = 2 + 3, appears only after the child has set the bond. The back-up button rolls every crate home into the same wagon — the whole never changes — and the turntable turns a banked pair round, so 2 + 3 becomes 3 + 2. A wrong number lights that car's crates; a second one numbers them up to a question mark on the last, so the child still says the number.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.3 — breaking numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way and recording each split. Besides "find every way" rounds there are sealed-car rounds (one car hides its crates under a tarp with its number, such as 5 = 2 + ☐, and the child sends the missing part) and back-up rounds (the crates of two loaded cars roll back into one wagon and the child sets the whole). Teachers can choose up to 5, 6 to 9, or Make ten — nine sealed rounds that fill one staircase with every way to make 10 — and show or hide the turntable. "Shunting yard" is open play with any load from 2 to 10. No timer, no score.

Reading each part on a number bond: 5 = 2 + 3
Finding the missing part and the whole
Seeing that 2 + 3 and 3 + 2 are two ways to make the same whole
howToPlay: Hold the release lever: the crates roll down one at a time. Flick the switch to send them to the left or the right car.
Tap a circle of the number bond and choose the number each car holds.
Pull the coupler (or press Check). A new way goes into the route book; find them all.
Not quite? The car to count again lights up. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.3
Record each split with a number bond and an equation such as 5 = 2 + 3
Know the pairs that make 10

about: Sprocket's Clock is a big clock with a window near the 12. Behind the face turns a day wheel, geared at half the speed of the hour hand: one half is gold, the lap from midnight to noon, and the other half is violet, the lap from noon to midnight. The moon rides the wheel at midnight and the sun at noon. Every round starts at midnight, and the child winds the hour hand round to the time on the card: "You eat breakfast. 7:00."

The hands go round twice a day, so every time on the clock comes round twice. Wind to the first 7:00 and the window is gold, with the badge reading a.m.; wind one more lap and the hands are back at 7:00, but now the window is violet and the badge reads p.m. The same pictures and the same times appear in both laps (the bed when you get up and when you go to bed, the toothbrush after breakfast and before bed), so the clock alone never decides: the child has to think about when the thing happens. A wrong time gets a hint that compares the card and the clock; the right time in the wrong lap asks whether it happens before or after noon; after a second miss a dashed arrow shows the way, one lap on or one lap back.

There are two levels: o'clock times, and half hours with two clock riddles, half an hour after midnight and half an hour after noon. A setting hides the picture and shows the a.m./p.m. label on the card instead, so the child must place the label on the wheel. It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Tell a.m. from p.m.: before noon or after noon
Understand that the hour hand goes round twice a day
Read and set o'clock and half-past times on an analog clock
Place everyday events in the right part of the day
howToPlay: Read the card. Drag the hour hand round the clock from midnight; the day wheel in the window turns with it.
Stop at the card's time in the right lap: gold before noon, violet after noon. Then press Check.
In the settings, choose o'clock or half-past times, and whether the card shows what happens or the a.m./p.m. label.
learningGoals: Use a.m. and p.m. with clock times, the a.m./p.m. part of Common Core 2.MD.C.7.
See that every clock time happens twice a day, once before noon and once after noon.
Read and set times to the hour and the half hour.

about: One time of day can be written two ways. In the 12-hour way the clock's numbers repeat, so the time needs a.m. or p.m.; in the 24-hour way the hours keep counting after noon, so 3 p.m. is 15:00. Sprocket's Clock shows a time on an open card, one way or the other, and the child writes the same time the other way: an hour, minutes, and for the 12-hour way, a.m. or p.m.

Then the clock acts the answer out. The hands run from midnight to the time the child wrote, and the hour hand carries a counting tag. On the first lap the tag says the face's own numbers; at noon a sun pops up over the 12, and on the second lap the tag keeps counting 13, 14, 15 and drops each number into an empty socket under the face's numeral. The given time stays on the face as dashed outlines, so a right answer lands exactly in them, and its number stays in the inner ring: across a session the child builds a 24-hour clock face. Writing 20:00 for 8 a.m. makes the run go round twice, though the open card's time never passed noon; a wrong hour, changed minutes, noon and midnight each get their own hint, and a second miss shows the given time's run with its last number face-down.

There are two levels: o'clock and half past, and five-minute times with noon and midnight. A setting keeps the inner ring or empties it every round, for teachers who want the child to work every answer out. It builds on Common Core 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time using a.m. and p.m.), extended to the 24-hour clock. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Write a 12-hour time the 24-hour way and back
Add or take away 12 for times after noon
Keep morning times and the minutes the same
Write noon and midnight both ways
howToPlay: Read the open card. Tap the hour box and the minute box and write the same time the other way with the number pad; for the 12-hour way, choose a.m. or p.m.
Press Check. The clock runs from midnight to your time; if your hands land in the dashed outlines, you are right.
In the settings, choose the times (o'clock and half past, or five minutes with noon and midnight) and whether the second ring keeps what you built.
learningGoals: Convert times between the 12-hour and the 24-hour clock, building on Common Core 2.MD.C.7.
See that after noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 13, 14, 15.
Write noon as 12:00 and midnight as 00:00.

about: A digital clock and a clock with hands can show the same time, and a child has to learn to see that they do. Sprocket's Clock is a small switchboard: four clocks with hands, each with a socket and a lamp, and three digital cards, each with a cable. The child plugs every card into the clock it thinks shows the same time. One clock matches no card: it is a trap built for one common mistake, such as swapped hands or a short hand drawn on the wrong number.

When the child presses Check, each card draws its own time as dashed hands on the clock it is plugged into. Where the dashed hands sit exactly on the clock's hands, the lamp lights and that pair stays plugged in. Where they do not, two sets of hands share one face, and the hand that disagrees blinks: the short hand when the hour is wrong, the long hand when the minutes are wrong. The hint names what to look at, and a second miss adds dots every five minutes along the dashed long hand and makes the numbers beside the dashed short hand bold. Hour digits and short hands are coral, minute digits and long hands are teal, so the card and the clock use one colour code.

There are two levels: o'clock and half past, then quarter hours and five-minute times. A setting shows all twelve numbers on the clocks or only 12, 3, 6 and 9. It follows Common Core 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Match a digital time to a clock with hands
Tell the short hand from the long hand
See where the short hand sits at half past and quarter to
Count by fives from the 12 to read the minutes
howToPlay: Tap a card, then the clock that shows the same time, or drag the card onto the clock. Tap a plugged card twice to pull its plug out.
Plug in all three cards and press Check. A lamp lights where the dashed hands land on the clock's hands; fix the pairs that stay dark.
In the settings, choose the times (o'clock and half past, or quarter hours and five minutes) and whether the clocks show all twelve numbers.
learningGoals: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes (Common Core 2.MD.C.7).
Read the hour from the short hand and the minutes from the long hand.
Know that at half past the short hand sits halfway between two numbers.

about: Reading a clock to five minutes means two different readings: the minutes are how far the long hand has gone round from the 12, five for every number, and the hour is the number the short hand is on or has already passed. Sprocket's Clock turns the minutes into something a child can build. A toy railway runs round the inside of the rim, and every carriage is exactly one number-gap long: five minutes.

The child taps the tunnel at the 12 to send carriages out one by one. Each new carriage couples behind the last and lights its roof number, so the train counts 5, 10, 15. The long hand is a level-crossing barrier: the train cannot go past it, so the number on the last roof is the minutes. Then the child writes the time on a digital card, hour and minutes, from empty boxes. A wrong answer shows its own mistake. Minutes like 04 make a train that is not even one carriage long. Reading the next hour (5:55 for 4:55) makes the train finish its lap in pale carriages: the short hand only reaches the next number when the ring closes. Any other wrong hour outlines the short hand. After a second miss, the right train is built with a question mark on its last roof, and the number the short hand has passed turns bold.

There are two levels: quarter hours, then five-minute times. A setting shows or hides the numbers on the roofs, so children can count the carriages by fives themselves. Once a time is read, the train becomes a toy: every carriage pushes the clock on five minutes, and when the twelfth closes the ring, the short hand steps to the next number. It follows Common Core 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Read the minutes by counting fives from the 12
Read the hour from the number the short hand is on or has passed
Read quarter past, half past and quarter to
Write a clock time on a digital card
howToPlay: Tap the tunnel or + to send out carriages until the train reaches the long hand; − sends the last one back.
Tap the hour box and the minute box and write the time with the number pad, then press Check.
In the settings, choose the times (quarter hours or five minutes) and whether the roofs show their numbers.
learningGoals: Tell and write time from analog clocks to the nearest five minutes (Common Core 2.MD.C.7).
Count by fives from the 12 to find the minutes.
Know that the hour is the number the short hand has passed, even when it is nearly at the next one.

about: Under Sprocket's clock lies its rim, unrolled into a straight road: thirteen posts from 12 round to 12 again, with a half stone between every two. The child reads both hands and taps one of three digital cards. On Check, Sprocket's marker walks to that time's spot on the road, the road rolls back up into a ring round the dial, and the marker slides in to the tip of the short hand. If the card was right, it lands exactly on the tip, and the clock runs on by half an hour: half a lap of the long hand and half a step of the short hand.

Every wrong card lands a visible distance away, joined to the tip by a dashed arc. If the child chooses 3:00 for 3:30, the marker stops half a step short, because the long hand on the 6 was ignored. If they choose 4:30, the marker lands a whole hour too far, the most common half-past mistake, made because the short hand is already close to the 4. After a second try the marker walks round the ring to the short hand's tip while the long hand turns with it. The setting Half past only gives nine half-past clocks, and Road: Only to check hides the road until Check, so the child reads the clock without it.
Hints talk about the hands and never give the answer. Aligned to Common Core 1.MD.B.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading the long hand: on the 12 for o'clock, on the 6 for half past
Naming the hour by the number the short hand has passed
Seeing half past as halfway between two numbers
Matching an analog clock to its digital time
howToPlay: Look at both hands, then tap the digital time that matches.
Press Check: the marker walks the road, the road rolls round the clock, and the marker lands on the short hand's tip if you were right.
Not yet? The dashed arc shows how far off the time was. Tap another card and check again.
After a right answer, drag the marker along the road and watch the hands move.
In the settings, choose the times (O'clock and half past · Half past only) and the road (Always shown · Only to check).
learningGoals: Tell time in hours and half-hours from an analog clock and match it to its digital time — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.B.3.
Use both hands to tell 3:00 from 3:30.
At half past, name the hour by the number the short hand has passed, not the next one.
See an hour as one step round the clock and half an hour as half a step.

about: Sprocket's clock has an orange short hand and a green long hand, and every digital card is written in the same two colours: the hour in orange, the minutes in green. A digital time is the two hands written down. The child reads the clock and taps a card. On Check the card docks under the clock and its two parts ride out: the hour along the short hand to the number that hand points to, the minutes along the long hand to the small 00 label at the 12. Each part clicks home only on its own number.

Reading the long hand as the hour is the classic mistake. A 12:00 card on a 3 o'clock clock sends its 12 out along the short hand to the 3, where it does not fit, and the 3 lights up. A neighbouring hour does not fit either. When both parts fit, an hour passes: the long hand runs one lap, the short hand steps to the next number and the display flips. After that the child can tap the long hand to make more hours pass. With O'clock and half past, a 30 label appears at the 6; at half past the hour rides out to the rim between two numbers and slides back to the one the short hand has passed. Hand colours: Off draws both hands in black and the cards in one colour, the step to an ordinary clock.
Hints talk about the hands and never give the answer. Aligned to Common Core 1.MD.B.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading the short hand as the hour and the long hand as the minutes
Knowing that the long hand on the 12 means :00
Matching an analog clock to its digital time
At half past, naming the hour the short hand has passed
howToPlay: Look at the clock, then tap the digital time that matches.
Press Check: the orange hour rides the short hand and the green minutes ride the long hand. A part that does not fit stops short of the number.
Not yet? The hand that sent a part back glows, and its number lights up. Tap another card and check again.
After a right answer, tap the long hand to make an hour pass.
In the settings, choose the times (O'clock · O'clock and half past) and the hand colours (On · Off).
learningGoals: Tell time in hours and half-hours from an analog clock and match it to its digital time — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.B.3.
Know which hand shows the hour and which shows the minutes.
Avoid reading the long hand as the hour (12:00 for 3:00).
See an hour passing as one full lap of the long hand.

about: An analog clock shows its minute marks and an exact time like 3:23, 7:47, 10:08, or 12:41, and the child reads the hands and taps the matching digital time from three choices. Sprocket the rooster cheers along in this interactive Grade 3 time activity about reading a clock to the nearest minute, right in the browser with no account.

The challenge is reading past the nearest five: the child finds the closest five-minute mark by counting in fives, then counts the small ticks on to the exact minute, so the long hand just past the 4 reads 23, not 20. The wrong choices sit only a minute or two away, so estimating to the nearest five is not enough — the child has to read the precise minute. This is the most exact clock reading in the elementary grades.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.A.1 — telling and writing time to the nearest minute. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Finding the nearest five-minute mark, then counting on to the exact minute
Reading the small minute ticks between the numbers
Reading the hour hand precisely as the minute hand moves around
Matching the clock to the exact digital time, down to the minute
howToPlay: Look at the clock, count the minutes by fives to the nearest mark, then count the small ticks to the exact minute.
Tap the digital time that matches, then check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Read an analog clock to the nearest minute — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.A.1.
Combine counting by fives with counting single minute ticks to read exact times like 3:23.
Build the precise time-reading skill that elapsed-time and schedule work depend on.

about: The hardest thing about quarter to is the hour. At 3:45 the short hand is nearly on the 4, so children write 4:45. Sprocket's Clock answers that with a machine. A marble run sits on the clock: every time the long hand reaches the 12, a numbered ball rolls down the chute into the cup. The ball in the cup is always the hour that has begun, so at quarter to four the 4-ball is still waiting at the top and the cup still holds the 3.

Each round shows a clock and four flip-clock cards: the right hour or its neighbour, with the right minutes or their mirror (3:15 and 3:45). Every wrong card is a real reading mistake. Tapping a card posts its guess on the clock: its hour as a marble over the cup's closed lid, its minutes as a little pin in the rim. Check opens the lid. A wrong hour bounces off the ball in the cup: a later hour is still waiting at the top of the chute, an earlier one is already in the tray of past hours. Wrong minutes leave the pin standing away from the long hand, with a dotted line showing the gap. After a second miss, the clock runs on to the 12 so the child sees the next ball drop only then, and runs back.

There are two levels: quarter hours, then five-minute times. A setting shows or hides the tray of past hours. Once a time is read, the long hand can be dragged round, and a ball drops at every 12. It follows Common Core 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Read quarter past and quarter to on a clock with hands
Find the hour: the last number the short hand has passed
Tell the long hand on the 3 from the long hand on the 9
Match a clock to a digital time
howToPlay: Look at the clock, then tap the card that shows the same time. Its hour floats over the cup and its minutes go in the rim as a pin.
Press Check. The cup opens: if the ball in the cup and your ball match, and the long hand meets your pin, you are right.
In the settings, choose the times (quarter hours or five minutes) and whether the tray of past hours is shown.
learningGoals: Tell time from analog clocks to the quarter hour and to five minutes, and match it to digital time (Common Core 2.MD.C.7).
Know that quarter to 4 is written 3:45, because the hour changes only when the long hand reaches the 12.
Read the minutes from the long hand: on the 3 it is 15 minutes, on the 9 it is 45.

about: Sprocket the rooster shows a start time on an analog face — say 3:00, 7:20, or 12:10 — and asks either 'What time will it be in 30 minutes?' or 'What time was it 30 minutes ago?' The child reads the hands, counts the minutes forward or back, and taps the matching digital time from three cards, in this Grade 3 time activity that runs right in the browser with no install and no account.

The activity mixes counting on and counting back on purpose, so a child cannot lock into one direction. Several rounds cross an hour boundary in both directions — 3:45 plus 30 lands on 4:15, while 12:10 minus 20 slips back to 11:50 and 1:05 minus 10 becomes 12:55. The three choices are close together, like the right answer, the same shift in the wrong direction, and a near time, so the child has to track which way the question points and roll the hour over correctly rather than nudge the nearest number.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.A.1 — solving elapsed-time word problems in minutes by adding and subtracting on a clock. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Read a start time on an analog clock and count minutes forward or backward
Tell an 'in 30 minutes' question apart from a 'was it 30 minutes ago' question
Roll the hour over correctly when minutes cross 12 — both up and down
Match the worked-out time to its written digital form
howToPlay: Read the start time on Sprocket's clock and the question above it — count on, or count back.
Work out the new time and tap the digital card that matches.
A wrong card simply dims and Sprocket offers a hint, so children try again as often as they like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Add and subtract minutes to find an earlier or later clock time — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.A.1.
Cross the hour confidently in both directions, such as 3:45 + 30 = 4:15 and 1:05 − 10 = 12:55.
Build the elapsed-time reasoning children use to plan and read schedules.

about: Sprocket the rooster shows a start time on an analog clock — 3:00, 7:20, 10:50, 2:15 — and asks, for example, 'What time will it be in 30 minutes?' The child reads the hands, counts on the minutes, and taps the matching digital time from three cards, in this Grade 3 time activity that plays right in the browser with no sign-up.

Every round here counts forward, and most of them cross the next hour, which is the part that trips children up. Three o'clock plus thirty is an easy 3:30, but 3:45 plus 30 must roll past four to 4:15, 10:50 plus 20 jumps to 11:10, and 2:15 plus 45 lands exactly on 3:00. The two wrong cards are deliberately tempting — a time that forgot to roll the hour, or one that added the minutes the lazy way — so the only sure path is to count on carefully and carry the hour.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.A.1 — solving elapsed-time problems in minutes by counting on from a start time. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Read a start time on an analog clock and count the minutes forward
Carry into the next hour when the minutes pass 60, like 3:45 + 30 = 4:15
Choose the worked-out time over a close-but-wrong distractor
Connect a counted-on time to its written digital form
howToPlay: Read the start time on Sprocket's clock and the 'in how many minutes' question.
Count on the minutes, then tap the digital time card that matches.
If a card is not right it dims and Sprocket gives a gentle hint — try again as many times as you like, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count on minutes to find a later clock time — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.A.1.
Carry the hour confidently when minutes cross the top of the clock.
Build the elapsed-time sense children use to figure out 'how long until' in everyday life.

about: Owl's cuckoo clock has a brass spring key on its side. The child drags the key round anticlockwise and both hands run backwards together, one click for every five minutes. The key stops by itself when the long hand reaches the 12, and at that moment the short hand stands exactly on the hour the clock is in, and that number is ringed. Let go and the clock whirrs forward to the real time. Then the child answers: tap the picture card of what Owl is doing at that time, write the time on two wheels, find the clock that matches a digital time, or pull the key out and wind the clock on to Owl's next activity.

The classic mistake at half past is to read the hour the short hand is nearer: 7:30 read as 8:30. Winding back shows it at once, because the short hand lands on the 7, never on the 8. After a wrong answer the spring winds the clock back by itself; after a second one, beads count the minutes in fives from the 12 to the long hand. On a right answer the cuckoo door opens and Owl pops out holding the picture of what she is doing. On the hour she bobs as many times as the hour, a row of dots lighting one per bob, so the count is seen with the sound off. Afterwards the child may wind the clock freely through Owl's day.
Hints talk about the hands and never give the answer. Aligned to Common Core 1.MD.B.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading the hour from the short hand and the minutes from the long hand
At half past, naming the hour the short hand has passed
Writing a time shown on an analog clock as a digital time
Setting a clock to a given time by winding it on
howToPlay: Look at Owl's clock. Drag the key round anticlockwise (or press ◀) to wind both hands back to the hour, then let go.
Answer: tap the picture card with the right time, turn the two wheels, tap the matching clock, or wind the clock on with ▶ to the time on the sign.
Press Check. Not yet? The clock winds back by itself and rings the hour. A second miss counts the minutes in fives.
After a right answer Owl pops out, and you can wind the clock freely.
In the settings, choose the times (O'clock and half past · With quarter hours) and the rounds (Read and set · Read only).
learningGoals: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours from an analog clock — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.B.3.
Know that the short hand shows the hour and the long hand the minutes.
At half past, read the hour the short hand has passed, not the next one.
Set a clock to a time by moving it forward through the day.

about: The child builds the clock. Both hands lie in a tray; each one is put on the clock and pointed, just like drawing the hands on a worksheet. The hands are not linked, so the child has to make them agree. On Check, the part of the face the long hand has swept from the 12 turns green, and a narrow copy of that slice drops into the hour's own slice between two numbers. The short hand has to point at the end of that little slice. A paper receipt prints the time the hands really show.

This catches the classic mistakes. At half past, a short hand placed right on the 7 sits at the start of its little slice, not the end, and the receipt prints 7:30 with a question mark; on the 8 it prints 8:30 with a question mark. Hands put on the wrong way round print a different time, and a long hand put on the 10 for ten past prints 50 minutes. After a second miss, the minutes 5, 10, 15 and on appear round the rim. On a right answer the slices light up, the bell on top rings and the receipt turns green; after that the child can keep turning the hands.
Hints talk about the hands and never give the answer. Aligned to Common Core 1.MD.B.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Placing the short hand for the hour and the long hand for the minutes
At half past, putting the short hand half way between two numbers
Counting the minutes in fives from the 12
Matching a digital time and its words to a clock
howToPlay: Read the time you have to show. Tap the short hand in the tray to put it on the clock, then tap or drag on the clock to turn it.
Do the same with the long hand. Tap a hand in the tray, or the middle of the clock, to choose which hand you turn.
Press Check. The green slices and the paper show what your hands say; a question mark means the short hand is not at the end of its little slice.
After a right answer you can keep turning the hands.
In the settings, choose the times (O'clock and half past · O'clock · Half past · Quarter hours · Five minutes · Mixed) and when the green slice shows (After Check · While setting).
learningGoals: Show a given time on an analog clock by placing both hands — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.B.3.
Know that the short hand shows the hour and the long hand the minutes.
Place the short hand so it agrees with the minutes: on the number at o'clock, half way between two numbers at half past.
Read the minutes by counting in fives from the 12.

about: Setting a clock means placing two hands, and the short one is the hard one: at 9:20 it is not on the 9 but a third of the way to the 10. A digital readout cannot catch that mistake, because a clock with the short hand on the 9 still reads 9:20. Set the Clock catches it with the clock itself.

A time appears on a card, in digits and in words. The child drags the long hand to the minutes and the short hand to the hour; the hands are loose and nothing reads them back. At Check, the readout shows the time the hands make, a brass gear slides into the centre, and the clock runs on to the next o'clock. A clock set right arrives with the short hand exactly on a number, and the bell strikes that hour, one mark per stroke. If the short hand was in the wrong place, the clock arrives crooked, between two numbers, and the bell clanks. Each kind of mistake gets its own help: a ring where the long hand belongs, or the right gap for the short hand shaded. After a second miss, a ring of minutes appears outside the numbers and dashed slots show where both hands go.

There are four levels: o'clock and half past, quarter hours, five-minute times, and a mix. A setting shows the ring of minutes (05, 10, 15 … 55) for children who are new to five-minute times. It follows Common Core 2.MD.C.7 (tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Set the long hand to the minutes, counting by fives
Set the short hand part of the way past the hour
Set quarter past, half past and quarter to
Check a clock by running it on to the next hour
howToPlay: Read the time on the card, then drag the long hand and the short hand (or select a hand and use the arrow keys).
Press Check. The clock runs on to the next hour: if the short hand lands exactly on a number and the readout matches the card, you are right.
In the settings, choose the times and whether the ring of minutes is shown.
learningGoals: Show times on an analog clock to the nearest five minutes (Common Core 2.MD.C.7).
Place the short hand as far past the hour as the minutes say.
Count by fives from the 12 to place the long hand.

about: Clunk the snack-robot is hungry for an exact number, and his lunchbox has a snake-shaped groove with exactly that many cups. Snacks hang on a wall as strands of identical treats — each strand shows one treat, a number tag and a row of dots for its length. Drop a strand in the box and it uncoils and snakes into the next cups, round the bend. The lid only shuts when the groove is exactly full. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the box checks the lunch by itself. Too little and the lid stops above the empty cups; too much and a tail of treats hangs over the rim, so the lid bonks and springs back. Only a box whose lid has shut can be fed: the lever is padlocked until then, so a box that is not exactly full is never fed and the child is never told off. When Clunk eats, his lunch log prints the lunch biggest part first, such as 10 = 6 + 4, and asks for a new way — 4 + 6 is the same lunch, so it needs different snacks. If the child taps the lid three times over a gap, the empty cups count on from the full ones (7, 8, 9, 10). There are rounds with one snack already packed, rounds that allow exactly three snacks (6 + 4 shuts the lid but is refused), boxes that arrive too full, and a "What did Clunk eat?" round where the child counts the cups and sets Clunk's number, such as 6 and 3 making 9.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.3 — breaking numbers up to 10 into pairs (and into three parts) in more than one way, and recording each one. Teachers choose up to 5, 6 to 10 (the default) or Big lunch up to 14, and can hide the number tags so the parts are counted from the dots. "Snack bar" is open play: any box from 2 to 10 and every strand from 1 to 9. No timer, no score.
practices: Making a number up to 10 in more than one way
Seeing when parts are too many or too few for the whole
Finding the missing part and the whole
Writing each lunch as an equation such as 10 = 6 + 4
howToPlay: Look at Clunk's number and the cups in his lunchbox.
Tap a snack strand, or drag it onto the box; tap a treat in the box to take its strand out again.
When the lid shuts, pull the lever to feed Clunk. Then pack the same number a new way.
Not quite? The lid shows what is wrong — empty cups or a snack over the edge. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Decompose numbers up to 10 in more than one way — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.3
Record each decomposition with an equation such as 10 = 6 + 4
Learn the pairs that make 10

about: Knowing what a coin is worth is the whole of money sense, and in the United States it is hard: the coins carry no numbers, and the dime is smaller than the nickel although it is worth twice as much. Pip's Market Stall makes that knowledge the way in.

Pip's till has a cup for every coin's worth — 25¢, 10¢, 5¢ and 1¢ — and a cup takes only the coin it is named for. Drop a nickel into the 10¢ cup and it bounces straight back, however big it looks. Once the money is in the till it already lies biggest worth first, so counting on is the natural way to count. The coins are drawn true to the real coins' sizes and metals.

Three levels: count a spilled till and set the total; pay Pip an exact price, with the fewest coins, in a fair trade or in a second way; then give change, decide whether a purse holds enough, and find the purse with more money. A first miss lines the coins up, worth first; a second adds the running totals. No timer, no score.
practices: Know the worth of a penny, nickel, dime and quarter without a number on the coin
Count a mixed handful of coins by counting on from the coin worth the most
Pay an exact amount, with the fewest coins, and in more than one way
Give change, and decide whether there is enough money
howToPlay: Drag each coin (or tap it, then tap a cup) into the till cup for its worth; the wrong cup sends it back.
Set the total, choose an answer, or give the change, then press Check.
After a miss the coins line up worth first; after a second, with the running totals.
learningGoals: Knowing the worth of each U.S. coin.
Counting a collection of coins by counting on from the largest worth.
Solving money problems: paying, making change, and comparing amounts.

about: In Comet's Big Leaps the numbers live in a stack of ten glass hundred-charts. On each sheet a step to the right is 1 more and a step down is 10 more, and 100 more is the very same square on the next sheet down. Comet the kangaroo sits on a number such as 247, the task asks for 10 more, and the child types where she will land before she leaps.

A wrong number is not just marked wrong: a flag is planted on the square where that number lives. Typing 258 for 247 + 10 puts the flag one square to the right of Comet on 257, so the child sees that the ones digit moved when it should have stayed. For 296 + 10 Comet falls off the bottom edge of the sheet and lands on the top row of the next one, 306; the answer that forgets the carry, 206 plants the flag a whole sheet higher. After a second miss the child moves Comet with the arrows and reads off the landing square.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to a number from 100 to 900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from it. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Add and subtract 10 and 100 to three-digit numbers in your head
See each digit as a direction: ones across, tens down, hundreds one sheet deeper
Cross a hundred correctly, as in 296 + 10 = 306
Follow arrow trails and find how far one number is from another
howToPlay: Read Comet's number and the leap, then type where she will land and press Check.
If the flag lands on another square, look which way it is off and change that digit; after a second miss, move Comet yourself with the arrows.
In the settings, choose 1 and 10, 10 and 100 or arrow trails, and frosted or clear glass.
learningGoals: Mentally add and subtract 10 and 100 within 1000 — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.B.8.
Know which digit a leap of 1, 10 or 100 changes, and when the next digit changes too.
Read a hundred chart as a map: rows are tens, columns are ones.

about: A creek forks twice on its way to a pond where a friend is waiting — a frog, a fox, a hedgehog. At each fork two number buoys float, one in each channel, and a little sign at the top gives the rule for this trip: follow the bigger numbers, or follow the smaller ones. The child taps one number at each fork, the planned route lights up, and Check sends a sailboat down it. It's an interactive Kindergarten activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The rule changes from trip to trip, so the child has to read the sign and the numbers every time — a child who always picks the bigger number will not get through. If the route is wrong, the boat sails as far as it can and stops in the reeds at the first wrong fork, and that fork is ringed: which number there is bigger (or smaller)? After a second try, dots appear under the two numbers at that fork, so the child can count which has more. A right route takes the boat all the way to the friend: “Yes — you followed the bigger numbers, 7 and 5, all the way to the pond!” Some forks are far apart, like 2 and 7, and some are neighbours, like 7 and 8. The two numbers are never the same.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.7 — comparing two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals. Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 or up to 10, and a rule that changes every trip, or always the bigger, or always the smaller. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing two written numbers up to 10
Finding the bigger and the smaller number of a pair
Keeping a rule in mind while choosing
Counting dots to check which number is bigger
howToPlay: Look at the sign: follow the bigger numbers, or the smaller ones?
At each fork, tap the number that follows the rule.
Press Check and watch the boat sail your route to the pond.
Stuck in the reeds? Look again at the ringed fork. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 given as written numerals — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.7
Say which of two numbers is bigger and which is smaller
Check a comparison by counting dots

about: Skip the squirrel welds two word-blocks together — fish and bowl, milk and jug, egg and cup, foot and ball — and the child works out what the new word means from its parts; a fishbowl is a bowl for fish, not a bowl made of fish. Skip's Word-Welding Yard is a Grade 2 vocabulary game about compound words that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

The activity teaches children to read a compound from its pieces instead of memorizing it. Different rounds approach this from several directions: choose the right meaning (a bed for dogs, not made of dogs), pick the correctly-ordered compound (football, not ballfoot or handball), supply the missing part in a frame like 'a bed for ___,' or name which word is the main thing the compound is (a fishbowl is a kind of bowl). The wrong choices are pointed — 'made of' instead of 'for,' the two words reversed, or the wrong first word — so children must reason about how the parts combine.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.d — using knowledge of the meaning of individual words to predict the meaning of compound words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Use the two parts of a compound word to predict its meaning
Tell 'a bowl for fish' apart from 'a bowl made of fish'
Put the parts in the right order — football, not ballfoot
Identify which word names the main thing the compound is
howToPlay: Read the two word-blocks Skip welds together and the new compound word.
Tap the choice that shows what it really means, the right order, or the missing part.
Not quite? Try again as often as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Predict the meaning of a compound word from its parts — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.d.
Understand that the order of the parts changes the meaning.
Build the word-analysis habit that helps children meet new words on their own.

about: Nib the apostrophe-spirit shows two words — do and not, it and is, you and are, I and am — and the child picks the contraction that drops the right letters and puts the apostrophe in exactly the right spot, making don't, it's, you're, and I'm. Nib's Apostrophe Seat is a Grade 2 grammar activity about forming contractions that runs in the browser with no account.

The thing children most often get wrong is where the apostrophe goes, so that is exactly what the choices test: the right answer sits next to a look-alike with the apostrophe in the wrong place. The set also slips in the tricky irregulars — will not becomes won't and can not becomes can't, where more than the obvious letters change — so children learn that an apostrophe marks the missing letters rather than just sitting wherever it looks nice.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.2.c — using an apostrophe to form contractions. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Combine two words into a contraction by dropping letters
Place the apostrophe exactly where the letters were removed
Tell the correct spelling from a look-alike with a misplaced apostrophe
Handle irregular contractions like won't and can't
howToPlay: Read the two words Nib shows you.
Tap the contraction that drops the right letters with the apostrophe in the right spot.
If it is not right, try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Form contractions with an apostrophe — the focus of Common Core L.2.2.c.
Understand that the apostrophe stands in for the missing letters.
Read and write everyday contractions like don't, it's, and won't with confidence.

about: Every letter is a little glass dropper of its own colour of paint. The child looks at the picture (a ship, a chick, a frog, a bell) and pours the letters of its word into six paint wells, one well for each sound. Letters that make one sound together share a well, and letters that keep their own sounds each get a well of their own. Build Blend and Digraph Words is a Grade 1 phonics activity about exactly that decision.

Press Check and a paddle stirs the wells. S and h in one well swirl into a brand-new green, because sh is one sound; f and r in one well refuse to mix and run in stripes, because frog keeps both sounds. An sh broken across two wells leans across the wall, and a wrong letter clouds grey. There are always six wells, so the wells never tell how many sounds a word has, and the tray always holds a trap or two (a c beside the s, an l beside the r). When every well is right, the paint dries into the word's colour strip and goes on the colour shelf, where every sh is the same green wherever it sat. Two more clues: Team jars (pour the missing sh, ch or ck into the empty well) and Sentence (find every word with sh).
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.3: knowing the spelling-sound correspondences for common consonant digraphs, and decoding regularly spelled one-syllable words. No timer and no score.
practices: Hear that sh, ch and ck are two letters for one sound
Hear both sounds of a blend, as in frog, flag and crab
Spell a word one well per sound, from the picture
Tell where a letter team sits: at the start or at the end
howToPlay: Look at the picture and say the word slowly. Tap the picture to hear it.
Tap a dropper to pour it into the next empty well, or drag it onto a well. To put two letters in one well, drag the second one onto the first.
Press Check and watch the paint: one new colour means one sound, stripes mean two sounds. Fix any well and stir again.
learningGoals: Know the common consonant digraphs sh, ch and ck, the focus of Common Core RF.1.3.
Decode and spell words that begin or end with a consonant blend.
Understand that the number of sounds in a word is not always the number of letters.

about: The picture shows a cat; the word is not printed anywhere. The child pulls the knob of a coral elastic, and one bead pops out for each sound: three beads for c · a · t. One letter goes on each bead, then the child lets go, and the beads snap together into the word. It is an interactive Kindergarten phonics activity that plays in the browser.

If the middle bead holds e, the snap kicks that one bead up out of the line, so the child sees exactly which sound to listen for again. Other settings give the first sound, leave one sound missing, add a word bank or a keyboard, let the child decide how many beads to pull out, or turn it round: the elastic arrives lettered and the child reads it and finds the picture. With letter teams, two letters share one bead, as sh does in fish.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.3, knowing and applying grade-level phonics. No timer and no score.
practices: Saying a word slowly and hearing each sound in order
Writing one letter for each sound
Listening hardest for the middle vowel
Spelling a sound with two letters, like sh or ck
howToPlay: Look at the picture and say its name slowly.
Pull the knob: one bead for each sound. Put a letter on each bead.
Press Check and watch the beads snap together, or see which bead is kicked out.
learningGoals: The child segments a short word into its sounds
The child writes the letter for each sound in order
The child blends the sounds back into the word

about: A picture appears (a kite, a cap, a whale, a pot) with its consonants already sitting on a wooden rail and one empty socket for the vowel. The child picks the vowel and then decides whether the word needs the magic e. Add the Magic e is a Grade 1 phonics activity about the final e that makes a vowel say its name.

The e is silent, but it has an arm. Drop it on the end and the arm swings back over exactly one letter and taps the vowel, which flips like a coin from its teal short face to its gold name face: kit becomes kite. Take the e away and the vowel flips back. Four rounds in nine are short-vowel pictures such as cap, pot and pen, where an e would make the word stop naming the picture, so the child has to listen rather than add an e to everything. Cap, cape and cup all share the same rail, so only the picture decides. Finished words hang on a washing line, short and long side by side. In Read and find, the word arrives built and the child taps the picture it names.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.3: knowing the final -e convention for representing long vowel sounds. No timer and no score.
practices: Hear when a vowel says its name and when it is short
Spell words like kite, cake and rose with the final e
Leave the e off short-vowel words like cap, pot and pen
Read cap and cape, cup and cube, and match each to its picture
howToPlay: Look at the picture and say its name. Tap the picture to hear it.
Tap or drag a vowel into the empty socket. If the vowel says its name, add the magic e on the end and watch its arm.
Press Check. If the word is right, it clips onto the picture and hangs on the washing line.
learningGoals: Use the final -e convention for long vowel sounds, the focus of Common Core RF.1.3.
Tell short and long vowel words apart by sound and by spelling.
Read and spell one-syllable words that end in a silent e.

about: At Daisy's diner counter, the ticket shows how many the order needs. The child taps the pile and plates land on the shelf, each with the same picture on it; animal customers sit on stools on the stepped counter. Under the shelf the word stands in wooden letter tiles. With one plate the word is just "cup". The moment the second plate lands, the end of the word slides open: now it needs an ending tile, such as s or es.

Endings are real tiles, never made-up spellings to choose from. A tile with a little hump adds a beat you can hear (peach-es). Words that change themselves, like mouse and mice or knife and knives, have no ending slot: their card flips over. In "Back to one" the child takes plates away until one is left, and the ending has to come off. An ending left on with one plate rattles in its slot.

Five sets of words: first words, s or es, words that change, back to one, and sentences with a gap. Under "Answer" the child can type the ending instead of using tiles. Aligned to Common Core L.K.1.c: form regular plural nouns by adding /s/ or /es/. No timer and no score.
practices: Telling one from more than one
Adding the right ending: s or es
Recognizing words that change themselves, like mice and knives
Taking the ending off to go back to one
howToPlay: Look at the ticket and tap the pile until the shelf has that many.
Put the right ending tile in the open slot, or flip the card if the word changes inside. Then press "Check".
Under "Words" choose a set such as "s or es?" or "Back to one", and under "Answer" choose "Write it" to type the ending.
learningGoals: The child knows that a word usually changes when there is more than one
The child chooses between s and es by listening for the extra beat
The child forms the singular by taking the ending off

about: One writing line, three boxes. The first box shows the whole road of the numeral with a green start dot; the second only a faint line; the third is empty. The child writes the number with a finger in each box in turn — 0 to 9, one numeral per round — and the ink appears only where the finger has actually travelled the stroke, from its start. When the third box is done, the three numerals the child wrote stand on the line and the number is spoken. It is an interactive Kindergarten handwriting activity that runs in the browser on tablets, phones and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is the handwriting-book method — model, trace, copy — with the help fading inside one line, so the last numeral is the child’s own. Stroke order and direction are built in: a stroke only counts when it is drawn from its starting point along its path, so a numeral drawn from the bottom, or flipped, does not pass. The slips young writers make are named from the finger’s own path — started at the other end, flipped the wrong way, went round the wrong way, stopped short — and after three tries the faint line comes back to help, then the whole road. A walker can show the strokes on request, and Rub out starts a box again. Settings keep the full guide in every box for a class that needs it, or remove it for one that is ready to write alone; the paper can show three lines or one.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.3 — writing numbers from 0 to 20 and representing a number of objects with a written numeral. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Form each numeral 0 to 9 from the correct starting point, in the correct stroke order and direction
Move from tracing a full guide to writing the numeral unaided, inside one line
Notice and fix a reversed, flipped or unfinished numeral
Build the fine-motor control and pencil path that neat handwriting needs
howToPlay: Put your finger on the green dot in the first box and follow the road. The ink appears where your finger goes.
Do the same in the second box, where the road is only a faint line, and then in the third box by yourself. Not sure? Press Show me to watch the strokes, or Rub out to start a box again.
When the third box is done, the round checks itself and the number is spoken — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Write every numeral from 0 to 9 with correct, consistent strokes — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.3
Write a numeral without a guide after tracing it
Build the handwriting foundation for recording counts and answers later

about: Every syllable is a little ice floe bobbing on a pond. Three pictures stand on the ice shelf (a pencil, a penguin, a pepper) and their pieces float loose: pen, cil, pen, guin, pep, per. The child pushes the pieces into each picture's slot to build its word. Domino's Two-Part Words is a Grade 1 activity for reading longer words one syllable at a time.

Press Check and a frost sweeps the shelf. Where the pieces really are the picture's word, in the right order, they freeze into one; a wrong piece cracks off and drifts back to the pond. Every slot has three seats, so it never tells how many pieces a word has. On some shelves the words share their first part (pencil, penguin, pepper), so the child has to read every piece, not just the first. Missing piece, Mixed-up word and Read and find give the same skill three more ways, and every finished word goes onto the two-piece or three-piece ice shelf.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.3.e: decoding two-syllable words by breaking them into syllables. No timer and no score.
practices: Read a long word one syllable at a time
Join syllables in the right order to make a word
Read the second syllable when first parts are the same (pencil, penguin, pepper)
Sort words into two-syllable and three-syllable words
howToPlay: Tap a picture to choose its slot and hear its name.
Tap an ice piece and it floats into the glowing slot, or drag it to any slot. Tap a slot to take its last piece back.
Press Check. The right words freeze, and a wrong piece cracks off and floats back.
learningGoals: Decode two-syllable words by breaking them into syllables, the focus of Common Core RF.1.3.e.
Blend syllables in order into a word and connect it to its meaning.
Notice that a long word can still have just two or three parts.

about: Pim shows a rune such as 3 × 4, and the child taps the grove that shows 3 groups of 4 fruits — raspberries, strawberries, apples, lemons, pears, bananas, oranges, or plums. This interactive Grade 3 math activity is about reading multiplication as equal groups, and it runs in the browser on any device with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that the two numbers in a product mean different things: the first factor is how many groups, and the second is how many in each group. The trap in every round is a look-alike grove with the same total but the wrong grouping — for 3 × 4 the decoy might show 4 groups of 3. Both hold twelve fruits, so a child who only counts the total is fooled; the child has to read the grouping itself, which is exactly what 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 record differently.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.OA.A.1 — interpreting products of whole numbers as the total number of objects in equal groups. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a multiplication expression as 'this many groups of this many'
Telling the number of groups apart from the size of each group
Resisting the same-total trap by checking the grouping, not just the count
Connecting 3 × 4 to a real picture of equal groups of fruit
howToPlay: Read Pim's rune, like 3 × 4.
Look at the groves and find the one that shows 3 groups of 4 — not the one with the same total but a different grouping.
Tap your choice; if it is not quite right, try again with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Interpret a product as equal groups, knowing which factor is the number of groups — the focus of Common Core 3.OA.A.1
See why 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 picture different groupings even with the same total
Build the equal-groups meaning of multiplication that division and arrays rely on

about: Fern the fawn works out what a tricky word means by reading the words around it: each round shows a sentence with a word that has more than one meaning — bark, bat, trunk, ring, light, fair, wave, park, or duck — and the child reads the whole sentence and taps the meaning that fits. It's an interactive Grade 2 vocabulary game played in the browser on any device with no sign-up.

The big idea is that many everyday words mean different things, and the sentence tells you which one. In each round one wrong choice is a real, correct definition of the word — just not the one this sentence is using (for 'The puppy began to bark,' the tree-bark meaning is offered as a tempting decoy) — and another choice is simply off. So a child cannot pick by recognizing the word alone; they have to use the context clues to decide.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.a — using sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading the whole sentence before deciding what a word means
Recognizing that words like bark, trunk, and ring have more than one meaning
Using context clues to choose the meaning that fits this sentence
Setting aside a true-but-wrong definition that the sentence does not support
howToPlay: Read the sentence and notice the highlighted word, like 'trunk.'
Think about what the sentence is really telling you.
Tap the meaning that fits — try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use sentence context to determine the meaning of a multiple-meaning word — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.a
Tell a word's intended meaning apart from its other real meanings
Build the context-clue habit that supports independent reading comprehension

about: Detective Dewey's field guide cannot be flipped through. The only way into it is through its own tools: tap a line in the contents and the book opens at that page, tap a heading and its section unfolds, tap a bold word and the book turns to Words to Know. The creatures in the book (the Gribbet, the Wuzzle and the Nim) are made up, so no child can answer from what they already know. The Field Guide is a Grade 1 reading activity about using text features to find a fact.

Send the book to the wrong line and it opens the wrong page, in plain view: asked how the Gribbet can glow, a child who taps "Snoud: all about swimming" lands on a page about swimming. The fact is always the page's second sentence ("At night the frell glows, so the Gribbet can find its way."), so the child reads the page instead of tapping the first line. There are also labelled pictures of real animals, and a closed book with tabs and a screen book with buttons for choosing the right tool.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.RI.5: know and use text features to locate key facts. No timer and no score.
practices: Use a table of contents to find the right chapter
Open the section under the right heading
Look up a word in Words to Know and in the index
Read labels and captions on a picture
Know which part of a book does which job
howToPlay: Read Dewey's question on his card. Then use the book: tap a line, a heading, a bold word, a label, a tab or a button.
When the book opens at a page, read it and tap the sentence that answers. It slides onto Dewey's card.
Choose the tools in the settings: Contents & headings, Words to Know & Index, Picture labels or Which tool?. Help can underline the key words after a miss or from the start.
learningGoals: Use text features to locate key facts, the focus of Common Core 1.RI.5.
Read a line, a heading or a meaning before choosing it, not just match a word.
Know which part of a book answers which kind of question.

about: Every broken gadget on Fixit’s bench has two gauges, one for each side of the equals sign. Under them sits an equation such as 9 + □ = 15 with one number missing. The child puts a number in the empty socket and pulls the lever: each needle sweeps its side number by number, forward for adding and back for taking away, and the gadget only runs when both needles stop on the same number.

The missing number can be anywhere: the answer (8 + 5 = □ or 16 − 7 = □), an addend (9 + □ = 15), the number taken away (13 − □ = 8), the starting number (□ − 6 = 8), or one part of a balance such as 6 + 6 = □ + 4, where both sides must show 12. A wrong number lights the gap between the two needles; after a second try, the gauge marks the steps to count. Nothing shows the answer before the lever is pulled.
The “To 100” setting uses mostly whole tens, a jump of exactly ten (62 + □ = 72) and a chain of three numbers. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.8. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the unknown number in any position: the answer, an addend, the number taken away or the starting number
Reading the equals sign as “both sides show the same number”
Counting on and counting back from a known number
Making both sides of a balance equal, such as 6 + 6 = □ + 4
howToPlay: Read the equation under the two gauges and find the empty socket.
Tap the socket and choose a number. In “To 100”, set the tens and the ones with the arrows.
Pull the lever. If both needles stop on the same number, the gadget runs.
If they don’t, look at the gap between the needles, change the number and pull again. Tap a gauge to watch its needle again.
In the settings, choose the numbers (to 10, to 20 or to 100) and when to show the counting path (only as a help, or always).
learningGoals: Find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction equation, wherever it is
Understand that both sides of the equals sign show the same amount
Count on or back to find a missing part
Make two sides with two numbers each equal

about: Pip the fox takes a chocolate order like three fourths, then the child picks the unit piece by its size — there are no labels to read — and forges it the right number of times along the bar. Rounds cover halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, and eighths, including 3/4, 2/3, 3/8, and 5/6. It's an interactive Grade 3 fractions activity that runs in the browser on any device, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that a fraction is built from copies of a unit fraction: 3/4 is three of the one-fourth pieces. Because the molds are shown by size, not labeled, the child has to judge which piece fits the whole bar the right number of times — one round even offers an unequal mold to reject, and another asks the same 3/4 on a bigger bar to show the share looks larger when the whole is larger. There are also 'name the unit' rounds where the bar is already split and the child picks the fraction for one part.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.NF.A.1 — understanding a fraction 1/b as one part of a whole split into b equal parts, and a/b as a parts of size 1/b. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Choosing a unit-fraction piece by its size, with no labels to lean on
Building a fraction as repeated copies of the unit piece — 3/4 as three fourths
Telling equal partitions from unequal ones, and rejecting the unfair mold
Seeing that the same fraction of a bigger whole is a bigger amount
howToPlay: Read Pip's order, like 'Forge three fourths.'
Pick the piece whose size fits the bar the right number of times.
Forge it that many times to fill the order; try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Understand a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b — the focus of Common Core 3.NF.A.1
Connect the denominator to the size of the equal part and the numerator to how many
Build the part-by-part meaning of fractions that comparing and equivalence rely on

about: Crumb the mouse shows a piece cut one way, then three more cut into more or fewer slices, and the child taps the one that is the same amount — the equivalent fraction — for pairs like 1/2 and 3/6, or 3/4 and 6/8. Each fraction appears as a shaded bar beside its numbers, so the size is visible. It's an interactive Grade 3 fractions activity that plays in the browser on any device, with no sign-up.

The big idea is that different fractions can name the very same amount. The reference fraction (such as 1/2, 1/3, 2/3, or 3/4) sits beside three candidates that are cut into different numbers of slices, and only one shades the same length of bar. The other choices are close but wrong — for 1/2 the decoys might be 2/6 or 5/6 — so the child compares the shaded amounts, not just the numbers, and learns to look past 'different numbers' to 'same size.'
It is aligned to Common Core 3.NF.A.3 — recognizing and generating simple equivalent fractions and explaining why they are equal. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Recognizing that two fractions with different numbers can be the same amount
Comparing shaded bars to judge which fraction matches the reference
Connecting the picture of a fraction to its numerator and denominator
Spotting close-but-wrong fractions that shade more or less of the bar
howToPlay: Look at Crumb's reference piece and how much of the bar it shades.
Compare the three candidates — each cut into a different number of slices.
Tap the one that shades the same amount; try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Recognize simple equivalent fractions like 1/2 = 3/6 — the focus of Common Core 3.NF.A.3
Understand that equivalence is about equal amounts, not matching numbers
Build the equivalence sense needed for comparing and adding fractions later

about: Children tap the dotted lines to split a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares — 2 rows and 3 columns, 3 rows and 4 columns, on up to 4 rows and 5 columns — then type how many squares there are in all. It's an interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that runs in the browser on any device, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that a rectangle can be split into equal squares laid out in neat rows and columns, and the rows-and-columns structure helps you count them. Because the child makes the grid themselves and then counts, they begin to feel that 3 rows of 4 squares means counting by equal groups — the quiet beginning of arrays and multiplication. The squares are all the same size on purpose, so 'how many' is a true total of equal parts.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.2 — partitioning a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and counting to find the total number. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Splitting a rectangle into equal rows and columns of same-size squares
Building a grid by tapping the dividing lines
Counting the squares to find the total in the rectangle
Noticing the rows-and-columns structure that leads toward arrays
howToPlay: Tap the dotted lines to make rows and columns of equal squares.
Build the grid the round asks for, like 3 rows and 4 columns.
Type how many squares there are in all — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Partition a rectangle into same-size squares and count the total — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.2
See a rectangle as rows and columns of equal parts
Build the array foundation that prepares children for multiplication

about: A cardboard shape lies on a green cutting mat: a circle, a square, a rectangle, a triangle, an oval, a rhombus, a hexagon or a pentagon. The child cuts it by dragging a line from one dot on its edge to another, or, for thirds of a circle, triangle or hexagon, from a pin in the middle out to the edge. Then comes the test: tap one piece to lift a glass stamp of it, and stamp it on the other pieces. A piece that is a copy clicks into place and gets the next number; a piece that is not shows where the stamp hangs over in coral and where it leaves a gap in stripes.

On this mat, equal parts are always copies of one piece: the cuts are chosen so that the stamp never disagrees with the sizes: a fair cut always passes and an unfair one never does. The first level asks for halves and fourths of all eight shapes; the second for thirds and for fourths made from halves. The third level shades a fraction by stamping copies (three fourths is three copies of the one-fourth piece), names a shaded fraction on two number wheels, and once asks whether some pieces really are fourths, when they are not. After success, every piece shows its fraction, the shape goes to a little shelf, and the scissors button halves every piece again: more parts, smaller parts.

After a first miss the stamp tests every piece against the biggest one and the hint says what it found; after a second miss gold dots mark the ends of one fair cut. Aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.3, with thirds from 2.G.A.3. No timer and no score.
practices: Cutting a shape into 2, 3 or 4 equal parts
Testing whether parts are equal by checking that each one is a copy of the first
Seeing that more equal parts means smaller parts
Naming and shading fractions like 1/2, 1/3, 3/4 as copies of one unit piece
howToPlay: Drag from a dot on the edge to another dot to cut the shape. In the thirds rounds, drag from the pin in the middle to the edge. Tap a cut to take it away.
Tap a piece to lift a glass stamp of it, then tap or drag onto another piece. A copy clicks and gets a number; coral and stripes mean it is not a copy.
Press Check when every piece should be a copy of the others.
In "Shade and name", stamp as many pieces as the top number on the card, or set the two number wheels to the colored fraction.
In the settings choose the level (Halves and fourths · Thirds · Shade and name), show ruler marks at the halves, thirds and fourths, and let the stamp test by itself when you press Check.
learningGoals: Partition circles, rectangles and other shapes into two, three or four equal shares.
Test whether shares are equal by stamping a copy of one piece onto the others, and see when parts are not equal.
Understand that cutting into more equal shares makes smaller shares.
Describe a shaded part as a fraction such as 3/4: three copies of the one-fourth piece.

about: A circle, triangle, hexagon, square, rectangle, diamond, or ellipse appears, and the child taps the cutting lines to divide it into three equal pieces — thirds. It's an interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that runs in the browser on any device, with nothing to install and no account.
