The big idea is that thirds are trickier than halves because three equal pieces do not fall on an obvious middle line. A circle is split with three lines from the center, a rectangle into three equal strips, a triangle into three matching parts — so the child learns that 'thirds' means three same-size shares however the shape is cut. Making the cuts themselves builds the feel for equal partitioning that just looking at a picture cannot.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.3 — partitioning circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares and describing the shares using the word thirds. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Cutting a shape into 3 equal parts
Making thirds across circles, rectangles, triangles, and more
Keeping all three pieces the same size
Using the word thirds for three equal shares
howToPlay: Look at the shape you need to cut into 3 equal parts.
Tap the cutting lines to make thirds.
Check that the three pieces are equal — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Partition shapes into three equal shares and name them thirds — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.3
Understand that thirds must be three same-size parts, however the shape is cut
Strengthen the equal-partitioning sense that fractions build on

about: Two plates of toys sit one above the other, with a little plank bridge between them — seven balls on top, say, and three below. Which plate has more, or do they have the same? The child taps the plate with more, or “The same”. Then comes the fair part: the child taps a toy to send it walking across the bridge to the other plate, until both plates have the same, and presses Check. It's an interactive Kindergarten activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

Making “the same” by hand is where counting earns its keep. Seven and three do not become five and five with one tap: the child sends a toy across, counts both plates, sends another, counts again — and sees that the plate with more gets smaller while the other grows. A wrong first answer only makes the plate shake, so the child looks again. A Check before the plates are the same says which plate still has more and numbers the toys on both plates for that look; after a second, one toy on the bigger plate lights up to show the next one to send. A right Check says it with numbers: “Fair! 5 and 5.” The totals are always even, so a fair share is always possible, and each plate has room for twelve, so its size never gives the answer away.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.6 — saying whether one group has more than, fewer than or the same as another, by counting, up to 10 — and to what “the same” means. Teachers can choose groups up to 5 or up to 10, and lay the toys out in rows instead of scattered, which makes the comparison easier to see. No timer, no score.
practices: Saying which of two groups has more, or that they have the same
Counting both groups again after every change
Making two groups the same by moving one at a time
Seeing that one group shrinks while the other grows
howToPlay: Look at the two plates. Tap the plate with more, or “The same”.
Tap a toy to send it across the bridge to the other plate.
Keep going until both plates have the same, then press Check.
Not quite? The hint says which plate still has more — send a toy and count again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Say whether one group has more than, fewer than or the same as another, up to 10 — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.6
Compare groups by counting
Make two groups the same

about: Gabby the goose explores funny sayings that don't mean what the words say — the child reads an idiom in a sentence, like 'It's raining cats and dogs,' 'a piece of cake,' 'hold your horses,' or 'let the cat out of the bag,' and taps what it really means. It's an interactive Grade 3 vocabulary game that runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that figurative language carries a meaning beyond the literal words. In every round one wrong choice is the funny literal picture (cats and dogs truly falling, an actual potato on the couch), which is exactly the trap, and another choice is simply off. So the child cannot pick the words at face value — they have to think about what the saying means when people really use it.
It is aligned to Common Core L.3.5.a — distinguishing the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a common idiom inside a real sentence
Choosing what a saying really means, not what the words literally say
Spotting and setting aside the funny literal picture
Understanding everyday figurative language people actually use
howToPlay: Read the saying in Gabby's sentence, like 'hold your horses.'
Think about what it really means, beyond the literal words.
Tap the real meaning — try again freely, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Tell the literal and nonliteral meanings of phrases apart — the focus of Common Core L.3.5.a
Interpret common idioms from how they are used in a sentence
Build the figurative-language understanding that deepens reading comprehension

about: In Gauge's Good Guess every estimate is a promise about size. The child reads a question such as "About how long is an ant?" and taps one of three estimates. The picture then grows or shrinks to exactly that size beside a 30-cm school ruler for centimeters, or a 1-meter stick for meters, drawn to the same scale. Tap 30 cm for an ant and the ant becomes as long as the whole ruler; tap 2 m for a truck and it looks like a toy beside the meter stick. A wrong estimate looks wrong.

The things are an ant, a snail, a spoon, a pencil, a banana, a bed, a door, a house, a truck, a lighthouse, a passenger plane, a ferry and a whale, each with one option that fits the real thing. After a wrong guess, a dashed outline shows the real size next to the guess, with no number on it; after a second, a comparison helps, such as "A truck is about as long as four beds." In the Pick the unit setting the number is given and the child chooses cm or m, with both the ruler and the meter stick in view. Every thing that is solved joins Gauge's size album, ordered from the smallest to the biggest.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.A.3 (estimate lengths using units of centimeters and meters). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Estimate the length or height of familiar things in centimeters and meters
Compare an estimate with a 30-cm ruler and a 1-meter stick
Choose the unit that fits: centimeters for small things, meters for big ones
See the solved things lined up by size in the size album
howToPlay: Read the question, tap an estimate, and watch the picture grow or shrink to that size beside the ruler or the meter stick.
Tap another estimate to compare, then press Check.
In the settings, choose Pick the estimate or Pick the unit, and whether the picture grows when you tap or only after Check.
learningGoals: Estimate lengths using units of centimeters and meters, the focus of Common Core 2.MD.A.3.
Use a ruler and a meter stick as benchmarks to judge whether an estimate makes sense.
Know which unit fits a thing: centimeters for small things, meters for big ones.

about: A bar graph is read against its scale, and that is where children slip: the eye drifts down to the numbers and lands a line too high or too low, and "how many more leaves than raspberries?" gets the taller bar's number instead of the difference. Pip's Stacking Fence gives the child a real tool for both.

The graph is Pip's fence: a number post and up to four pickets of planks, one plank for each one counted. A spirit-level rail hangs on a slider on the post, and its other end rests on a picket's top. Slide the post end up or down until the bubble sits in the middle: only then is the rail level, the post reads that picket's number, and every plank of a taller picket above the rail is striped. That striped part is how many more. Pickets can be stacked to find how many altogether, and planks dropped into Pip's basket to find how many are left.

Three levels: build (pull each picket up to match a tally, a picture card or a table, or fix the one picket that is wrong), read (how many more, how many fewer, altogether, which is the most, how many are left, true or false), and scaled, where the post counts by 2, 5 or 10 and one picture can stand for 2 or 5. The first miss lays the rail where it helps; the second counts it out with the child. No timer, no score.
practices: Building a bar graph and a picture graph from a tally, a picture card or a table
Reading a bar's value against the scale with a level straightedge
Solving how many more, how many fewer, altogether and how many are left from a graph
Reading graphs whose scale counts by 2, 5 or 10
howToPlay: In a build round, pull each picket up until it matches the card.
In a read round, drag the rail's end onto a picket, then slide its other end up or down the post until the bubble sits in the middle.
Tap one picket and then another to stack them; drag planks into Pip's basket to take some away.
Turn the dial, tap True or False, or tap a picket, then press Check.
learningGoals: Drawing a bar graph and a picture graph for up to four categories.
Solving compare, put-together and take-apart problems with the information in a graph.
Reading graphs whose scale counts by more than one.

about: Gus sells snacks from a cart that rides on a number road from 0 to 100. Each round tells a short story — Gus had 45 cookies and sold 8 — and the child types how many Gus has now. Then the cart drives out to that number, turns round, and drives the story back the other way: for 45 − 8 it drives back up 8. Only the right answer, 37, brings it home to its flag at 45.

A wrong answer is a mishap you can see. If the child types 47, the cart drives back up 8 and stops at 55, and a bracket shows the gap of 10 between the cart and its flag — exactly one ten. A second miss replays the story's own hops from the flag, tens first and then ones, to a ghost cart. In the route setting Gus follows three signs in a row, such as 24 → +30 → −6 → +15, and the cart checks each stop. With round first on, the child rounds 38 + 21 to 40 + 20, writes about 60, and then finds the exact 59.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.5: add and subtract within 100 fluently, using the relationship between addition and subtraction. The answer can also be written in columns. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Add and subtract two-digit numbers within 100
Check a subtraction by adding and an addition by subtracting
Cross a ten when adding or taking away
Round to the nearest ten to estimate a sum
howToPlay: Read the story, type how many Gus has now on the keypad, and press Check.
Watch the cart drive out to your number and back. If it misses its flag, the gap shows how far off you were — change the number and try again.
In the settings, choose one stop or a route of three stops, and switch round first on or off.
learningGoals: Add and subtract within 100, with and without crossing a ten.
Understand that subtraction undoes addition and addition undoes subtraction.
Estimate a sum by rounding to tens and check that the exact answer is close.

about: Marina the lighthouse-cat sends each little boat to its nearest round-number harbor: a boat sits at a spot on a number line — 63, 47, 24, or larger numbers like 247, 360, and 480 — and the child taps the harbor it is closest to, rounding to the nearest ten or hundred. It's an interactive Grade 3 math activity that plays in the browser, with no sign-up.

The heart of the activity is the halfway point. Some rounds ask the child to find the buoy in the middle between two harbors first — is 45 the halfway mark between 40 and 50? — so they can see which side the boat falls on. That focus is what makes rounding make sense rather than a rule to memorize, and it handles the tricky case where a number like 75 sits right on the line and rounds up. The child reads the position on the number line and decides; they do not just look at the last digit in isolation.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.NBT.A.1 — using place-value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Locating a number's position between two round-number harbors on a number line
Finding the halfway point between two tens or two hundreds
Rounding to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred
Handling the round-up case when a number sits exactly halfway
howToPlay: Look at where the boat sits on the number line between the harbors.
Find the halfway buoy, decide which harbor the boat is closer to, and tap it.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Round whole numbers to the nearest 10 and 100 using a number line — the focus of Common Core 3.NBT.A.1
Use the halfway point to decide which way a number rounds
Understand rounding as position on the line, not just a digit rule

about: Hattie runs a lost-and-found. An owner stands on a shelf under a brass peg, a lost thing waits in the basket, and the owner's word lies on a word bar with an empty slot. The tray holds two tiles: the hooked 's and a plain s. Hattie's Whose-Is-It is a Grade 1 grammar activity about possessive nouns.

Seat the hooked 's and the ball swings up onto the dog's peg: "dog's ball". Seat the plain s instead and a second dog pops up on the shelf — that is what "dogs" means — and the ball stays in the basket. When two or three owners already stand on the shelf and there is nothing to hang, the plain s is right and the hook dangles empty. Level three adds names on name cards: "This is Mia's kite."
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.b: use common, proper and possessive nouns. No timer and no score.
practices: Tell the possessive 's from the plural s
Build possessive nouns: the dog's ball, the girl's kite
Build possessives of names: Mia's kite
Read a short sentence and decide: one owner, or more?
howToPlay: Look at the shelf and the basket. Tap a tile to put it in the slot; tap it again to take it out.
Watch what it does: the hook hangs the thing on its owner, the plain s makes more owners. Then press Check.
Choose the level in the settings: Things and owners, One or more?, or Names. The hooks can be shown or left off the tiles.
learningGoals: Use possessive nouns, the focus of Common Core L.1.1.b.
Tell apart the possessive 's and the plural s.
Write the possessive of a name.

about: Hazel's river runs down the middle: the first half of a sentence stands on a signboard on one bank, the second half on the other, each with its picture, and a gap waits where a bridge should be. Every joining word is a wooden plank with its own shape. AND is a straight plank, BUT has a turn in it, OR splits into a fork, and BECAUSE and SO are one arrow plank, "because" on one face and "so" on the other, whose arrow always runs from the reason to what happened.

Lay a plank and press Check, and a little car drives the bridge its way: straight across for "The cat and the dog are friends", into the fork for "Is it day or night?", round the turn for a surprise. With the arrow plank the car carries the reason across: "It was cold, so I put on my scarf." Swap the two halves and the arrow plank turns over by itself, so "because" and "so" show up as one link read from two ends.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.g: use frequently occurring conjunctions (and, but, or, so, because). No timer and no score.
practices: Join two parts with "and" when both go together
Use "but" when the second part takes a turn, and "or" for a choice
Use "because" before the reason and "so" before what happened
Say the same thing the other way round: "because" becomes "so"
howToPlay: Read the two halves on the banks and find out how they go together.
Tap a plank onto the bridge; tap the turner to flip the arrow plank between "because" and "so". Then press Check.
In the settings, choose the joining words (from "and, but, or" up to "Turn it round") and whether the pictures show.
learningGoals: Choose the joining word that makes two parts make sense.
Tell "because" (the reason comes next) from "so" (what happened comes next).
Turn a sentence round and keep its meaning.

about: Hopper the frog sits on a row of stepping stones across a pond, and the stones are a number line: equally spaced, some with their numbers. Each story gives a start and a hop, such as "Hopper sits on 43. He hops 12 forward." The child drags Hopper onto his start stone and taps him to turn him the way the story goes, because he only hops the way his nose points. Then the child loads his spring with the size of the hop, built from fat ten-coils and thin one-coils, so 12 is one ten and two ones.

Before he jumps, the child drags a lily pad to the stone where they think Hopper will land. On Let go the spring fires: one arc for every coil, each from one stone to another, so the start stone is never counted. If the pad is under his last landing he lands on it and a lotus opens. If not, he splashes into the pond, and the stones between him and the pad ripple, which shows exactly how far off the guess was. A wrong start, the wrong direction or the wrong load each get their own hint. After a second miss, dotted hops show the true path without naming the last stone.

The lines run within 20, within 100 (windows such as 40 to 60, where only every fifth stone has its number, and a line counted in tens), and equal hops from 0 or back to the bank for multiplication and division. It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.B.6 (represent whole numbers as lengths on a number line diagram with equally spaced points, and sums and differences within 100). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Count on and count back on a number line, starting from the next stone
Build a hop as tens and ones: jump a ten, then the ones
Find numbers between labels on a line that starts at 40, 60 or 80
Predict a landing before checking it
howToPlay: Read the story. Drag Hopper onto his start stone and tap him to turn him forward or back.
Tap ten and one to load his spring with the size of the hop, then drag the lily pad to where he will land. On equal hops, tap how many hops he makes.
Press Let go. In the settings, choose the line (within 20, within 100 or equal hops) and how many numbers the stones show.
learningGoals: Represent sums and differences within 100 as hops on a number line with equally spaced points, the focus of Common Core 2.MD.B.6.
Add by hopping forward and subtract by hopping back, without counting the start.
See equal hops as repeated addition and count the hops back to 0.

about: Inky the octopus prints the pages of a little book, but every page comes out half done: no picture, or no words. The child carries each page to the person who can finish it. The author’s ink only makes words, the illustrator’s ink only makes pictures, and the reader has no ink at all – she enjoys a finished page. Bring “A little boat sailed out.” to the illustrator and the boat appears in the empty frame. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

The wrong person still makes their own mark, in the wrong place: the author crams tiny words into the picture box, the illustrator squashes a picture onto the word lines, and the reader stops at the gap. The ink drips and the page comes back. When a book is done, the child puts the author and the illustrator on its cover. With Name plates only, the desks close and only the words Author, Illustrator and Reader decide.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.6: naming the author and the illustrator of a story and telling what each one does. Eight short books, every page a library picture. No timer and no score.
practices: Telling what an author does: writes the words
Telling what an illustrator does: draws the pictures
Seeing what a page still needs: words or a picture
Reading the words author, illustrator and reader
howToPlay: Look at the page: is the picture or are the words missing?
Drag the page to the person who can finish it, or tap that person.
When the book is done, put the author and the illustrator on the cover.
learningGoals: The child names the author and the illustrator of a book
The child tells what the author and the illustrator each make
The child knows that a story is told by both the words and the pictures

about: The day is a row of windows: "It is raining outside", you want to write your name, it is time to go to sleep. Under each window hangs an empty hook, and below them sits a bag of everyday things, each with a little tag folded shut. The child reads each moment and hangs the thing they would use. Press Go and the sun crosses the sky: the right things click into place, and a thing that does not fit comes back to the bag with its tag flipped open, "for a drink", so the child learns what it is for instead of hearing "wrong".

There are three things to do: pack the day, one thing for each moment; hang one thing on every moment where it helps, because a pencil is for writing and for drawing; and sort things under words that say what they are like, such as soft, hard and loud. The moments can be read as sentences or shown only as pictures.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.5.c: identify real-life connections between words and their use. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Read a short sentence about a moment of the day
Choose the thing you would use
Find every moment where one thing helps
Sort things by what they are like
howToPlay: Tap a thing in the bag, then tap a hook (or drag the thing onto the hook). Press Go.
A thing that does not fit comes back with its tag open: read it and try again.
In the settings, choose what to do, six or eight things in the bag, and sentences or pictures for the moments.
learningGoals: Connect everyday words with how we use them.
Explain what a thing is for.
Describe things with words that say what they are like.

about: A short fable sits in three window panes, and Juniper the hedgehog holds a lantern. The child slides a card into the lantern and presses Check: the light shows what kind of card it is. A real lesson, like "Slow and steady can still win", lights all three panes and shines on into a new little story (Ana practicing the piano every day), because a lesson is something you can take with you. Juniper's Story Lantern is a Grade 1 activity about the central message of a story.

A detail ("Hare stopped for a long nap") lights only the line it came from, and the beam fizzles halfway. A wrong lesson ("The fastest runner always wins") turns the ending pane cold, because the ending says the opposite. With four cards, a lesson from a different fable lights nothing at all. In the Retell task the three panes arrive out of order: the child puts the story in order first, and only then does the lantern open. Each lesson found adds a firefly to the jar.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.2: retelling stories and understanding their central message or lesson. No timer and no score.
practices: Find the lesson a whole story teaches
Tell a lesson apart from a detail that just happened
Check a lesson against how the story ends
Retell the three parts of a story in order
howToPlay: Read the three panes of the story, and the new little story below.
Tap a card: it slides into the lantern. Tap another card to change it.
Press Check and watch the light. In Retell, tap two panes to swap them until the story is in order.
learningGoals: Understand the central message or lesson of a story, the focus of Common Core RL.1.2.
See that a lesson fits the whole story and its ending, and also a new story.
Retell a short story in order.

about: Inchie the little worm can hop only one way: exactly one helper long. The child lays identical green helpers end to end under a picture, such as a car, a fish, a shoe or a ferry, starting at the stone by its tip, then taps the helpers to count. Every tap is one hop. Where the row is right, Inchie lands on the join between two helpers. Where it is wrong, everyone can see it: she drops into a gap, wobbles on two helpers lying on top of each other, lands in the middle of a helper of another size, or finds that the first helper does not start at the stone.

Lay and count starts with an empty path; some rounds offer a second pot of helpers in another size, which do not belong in the row. Fix it lays a row with a mistake to find and repair, and some of its rounds show three rows under one picture, so the child sends Inchie along each and picks the one measured the right way. Line up three measures three things in turn and puts the cards in order by the numbers written on them, shortest first. With Big and small, each thing is measured twice, with helpers two units long and then with one-unit helpers: a smaller helper needs more of them.

Only when Inchie reaches the end does the keypad wake up, and the child writes how many hops it took. After a wrong number the hint points back to the hops, then asks the child to touch each helper and count out loud; a hint never gives the number. Aligned to Common Core 1.MD.A.2. No timer and no score.
practices: Laying same-size units end to end, with no gaps and no overlaps
Starting the first unit exactly at one end of the object
Giving a length as the number of units that fit
Seeing that a bigger unit gives a smaller number
howToPlay: Tap the pot to lay a helper at the end of the row, or drag a helper onto the path. Drag a helper to move it, or drag it off the path to take it away.
Tap the helpers to count: Inchie hops one helper with every tap. If she lands in the wrong place, fix the row and tap Inchie to send her back to the stone.
When Inchie reaches the end, write how many hops it took and press Check.
In the settings, choose the job (Lay and count · Fix it · Line up three) and the helpers (One size · Big and small).
learningGoals: Measure a length as the number of same-size units laid end to end — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.A.2.
Recognise gaps, overlaps, units of another size and a crooked start as reasons a measurement is wrong.
Order three objects by their measured lengths.
Understand that measuring with a bigger unit gives a smaller number.

about: Facts are dominoes on a wooden track. One fact already stands there, and a gap waits next to it. The child reads the cards in the tray, stands the fact that connects in the gap, and Linc the lizard pushes the first domino. The chain keeps falling only across a real connection, and as it falls the facts join into one sentence on the rail, such as "The hot sun shines on the snow, so the snow melts." At a false link the struck domino rocks and stays standing, and the rail shows the two facts with a broken link between them.

The wrong cards are made to teach: a true fact that has nothing to do with the first one, a fact that only shares a word ("The snow falls."), and a fact from the wrong end of the story. In What happens next the gap comes after the fact; in Why it happens the gap can come before it, so the child must find what made it happen; Three in a chain stands two facts in order, and the chain stops at the first one out of place. Choices can be set to Fewer, which keeps only the lure that teaches.

It is aligned to Common Core RI.K.3: describing the connection between two pieces of information in a text. Linc is from the picture library; the dominoes carry words only, so the child reads to connect them. No timer and no score.
practices: Telling what happens next in a short informational text
Finding what one thing makes happen and what made it happen
Noticing that a true fact is not always a connected fact
Putting three facts in an order that makes sense
howToPlay: Read the fact on the track and the cards in the tray.
Drag a card into the gap, or tap it.
Press Check and watch Linc push the dominoes.
If the chain stops, read the two facts together and try another card.
learningGoals: The child says how two facts are connected
The child uses then and so to join facts
The child sees that sharing a word is not the same as being connected

about: A line plot is read by deciding which of its X's a question is about. "How many shells are longer than 5 cm?" is about every X after the 5, not the 5 itself, and "which length is the most common?" is answered with a length, not with how many X's it has. Shelly's Tide-Line puts that decision in the child's hands.

The plot is drawn on a beach. Two wave handles push the sea in from the left and the right (they stop only in the gaps between numbers), and a buoy raises the sea level one row at a time. Shells under water turn blue but stay visible. The child keeps dry exactly the shells the question is about, then answers. Check looks at the tide first, so "longer than 5" with the 5s still dry is not right, even with the right number.

Three levels: read the tide-line (how many at a length, longer, shorter, the most common length, the longest minus the shortest, how many more); measure and plot, where real shells are measured on a ruler from 0 (they do not always arrive there) and dropped as X's; and halves, on a beach marked in half centimetres. A second miss moves the sea to the right place, numbers what to count and rings the answer. No timer, no score.
practices: Read how many measurements are at, above or below a length on a line plot
Find the most common length and the difference between the longest and the shortest
Measure lengths from the 0 of a ruler to the nearest centimetre and half centimetre
Record each measurement as an X above its number
howToPlay: Drag the wave handles to push the sea in from the sides, and drag the buoy to raise the sea level.
Keep dry only the shells the question is about, then tap the answer on a pebble.
In the measuring rounds, slide the shell to the 0 of the ruler, read where it ends and drop it on its length.
Press Check. After a second miss the sea moves to the right place by itself.
learningGoals: Reading a line plot of measurement data.
Comparing data: the most common length, longer and shorter, how many more, the difference.
Measuring lengths and showing them on a line plot.

about: Mama Duck calls the morning roll at the pond. Her card shows dots, and the child sends exactly that many ducklings from the raft to the bank — one tap, one duckling paddling across. Then the child signs the roll: presses the number stamp for how many came and traces the number in the mud with a finger. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

Mama never shows a numeral (unless the teacher chooses it), so the child counts the dots, counts out the same number of ducklings, and writes the number that tells how many — the numeral is the child's own answer. More ducklings wait on the raft than Mama asks for, so the child has to decide when to stop, and a tap on a duckling on the bank sends it back. The ducklings land scattered, so counting them again is real counting. Check reads the bank first, then the signature, and says what is missing: too many, too few, no number yet, a number that is not how many came, or a number not yet traced. After a wrong Check the ducklings on the bank are numbered; after a second, Mama's dots are too. The help never moves a duckling.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer "how many?" and counting out a given number of things — together with writing the numeral that tells how many (K.CC.A.3). Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 or up to 9, and whether Mama's card shows dots or the number itself. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting the dots on a card and counting out the same number of ducklings
Stopping at the right number — the last number counted tells how many
Writing the numeral that tells how many, stroke by stroke
Counting a scattered group again to check
howToPlay: Count the dots on Mama's card.
Tap the raft to send ducklings to the bank, one at a time. Tap a duckling on the bank to send it back.
Press the number stamp that tells how many came and trace the number in the mud, starting at the green dot.
Press Check. Not quite? The hint says what is missing — fix it and press Check again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Count to answer "how many?" and count out a given number of things — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Write the numeral that tells how many objects there are
Know that the last number counted tells how many

about: Mango the monkey knows the special name for a group of animals — a herd of cows, a school of fish, a pack of wolves — so the child looks at the animal, then taps the word that names a whole group of them. It's an interactive Grade 2 grammar activity that plays in the browser, with no account.

The big idea is collective nouns, the focus of L.2.1.a. The three choices are all real group words — herd, flock, pack, swarm, school, pride, bunch — so the child cannot pick by ruling out nonsense; they have to know which group word belongs to which animal. Covering bees in a swarm, lions in a pride, and even grapes in a bunch shows that English has a rich, specific vocabulary for groups.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1.a — using collective nouns. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Naming the group word for a familiar animal
Telling apart real group words like herd, flock, pack, and swarm
Matching the specific collective noun to the right animal
Building precise vocabulary for naming groups of things
howToPlay: Look at the animal Mango shows you.
Tap the word that names a whole group of them, then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Use collective nouns to name groups — the focus of Common Core L.2.1.a
Know which group word goes with which animal
Grow a richer, more exact vocabulary

about: Maple the mouse divides cookies two ways: in sharing rounds the child deals cookies equally onto a set number of plates — 12 cookies onto 3 plates — and in packing rounds the child packs them into boxes that each hold the same number, like 18 cookies into boxes of 6, and finds how many boxes are needed. It's an interactive Grade 3 math activity that runs in the browser, with no sign-up.

The big idea is the two meanings of division. Sharing asks 'how many in each group?' when you know the number of groups, while grouping asks 'how many groups?' when you know the size of each — and seeing both with the same kind of cookie problem shows that 12 ÷ 4 can answer either question. Because the child actually deals or packs the cookies, the division answer becomes a thing they can see and count, not a fact to recall.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.OA.A.2 — interpreting whole-number quotients as objects shared equally into groups or as the number of equal groups. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Sharing a number of objects equally to find how many in each group
Packing objects into equal groups to find how many groups there are
Seeing division as both 'how many in each' and 'how many groups'
Connecting the picture of equal groups to a division answer
howToPlay: Read whether Maple is sharing cookies onto plates or packing them into boxes.
Deal or pack the cookies equally and find the answer — how many on each plate, or how many boxes — then press Check.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Interpret a division answer as sharing or as grouping — the focus of Common Core 3.OA.A.2
Tell apart 'how many in each group' from 'how many groups'
Build the equal-groups meaning behind division and multiplication

about: At Marina the otter's news desk, a good headline says what a story is mostly about — the child reads a short three-sentence article, like how bees make honey or how a frog grows up, then taps the card that names its main topic. It's an interactive Grade 2 reading activity that plays in the browser, with no account.

The big idea is finding the main topic, which means seeing the whole point rather than one part. The three cards are built to test it: one states the topic, one is a true detail pulled from the article, and one is off the page entirely — spiders spin webs, camels rarely drink. So the child cannot win by tapping the sentence that 'sounds like the story'; they have to decide what all of it is about, not just one fact it mentions.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.2.2 — identifying the main topic of a multi-paragraph text. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a short informational passage for its overall point
Naming what the whole text is mostly about
Telling the main topic apart from a single supporting detail
Rejecting a choice that is off-topic, even if it sounds factual
howToPlay: Read Marina's short article all the way through.
Tap the card that names its main topic — not a small detail, not something off the page — then press Check.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry when needed.
learningGoals: Identify the main topic of an informational text — the focus of Common Core RI.2.2
Separate the main topic from the details that support it
Build the comprehension habit of summarizing what a text is about

about: A short story, a claim about its character ("Mira is brave.") and three clue cards. The child puts one clue under Marlo the raccoon's magnifier and presses Check. The lens checks two things, in the order a good reader does: first it sweeps the story looking for the sentence the clue comes from, then it swings up to the claim. Marlo's Magnifier is a Grade 1 reading activity about using details from a story to describe its characters.

A clue that did not happen, like "She ran away from the dark cave.", is found nowhere: the lens fogs, even though the card uses the story's own words. A clue that is in the story but proves nothing, like "A loud growl came from inside.", lights its sentence, but the focus ring around "brave" wobbles. Only "She went right into the dark cave." snaps the ring into gold focus. In the Questions case ("Where did Mira go?") every card is in the story, and only one answers the question.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.3: describe characters, settings and major events in a story, using key details. No timer and no score.
practices: Check whether a detail is really in the story
Tell a proof apart from a detail that proves nothing
Back up a claim about a character with a key detail
Answer who, what, where, when and why questions from the text
howToPlay: Read the story and the claim (or the question) at the top.
Tap a clue card: it goes under Marlo's magnifier. Tap another to change it.
Press Check and watch the lens. Choose the case in the settings: Proof, Proof or just a detail?, or Questions.
learningGoals: Describe a character using key details, the focus of Common Core RL.1.3.
Learn that evidence must come from the text, and that being in the text is not yet proof.
Answer questions about a story with details from the story.

about: The two numbers on every card are blocks of snap-cubes. The child taps a card, then the card they think is its twin: on the way over, the two blocks leapfrog across the plus sign, so 4 + 7 becomes 7 + 4 with nothing gained or lost, and the card settles only onto its true twin. In most rounds all six cards make the same total, so the total alone never finds a twin; a card laid on an impostor shows the very cube where the colours disagree.

Take-away cards carry the other half of every fact family: 11 − 4 = 7 and 11 − 7 = 4 are twins, because the two parts trade places across the equals sign while the whole stays first. Tap the minus sign and the whole tries to jump over its own part, and bounces back. There are numbers to 10 and to 20, and turnaround, take-away or mixed rounds.
It is aligned to Common Core 1.OA.B.3: apply the properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Add the same two numbers in either order
Tell a turnaround twin from a card with the same total
Find the two take-away facts of one whole
See that the whole never moves in a take-away
howToPlay: Tap a card, then tap the card you think is its twin.
If it is not the twin, look at the cube that glows, and try again.
In the settings, choose numbers to 10 or to 20, and turnaround, take-away or mixed cards.
learningGoals: Know that the order of the numbers does not change a sum.
Use a known fact to find its turnaround.
Match the two subtraction facts of one whole.

about: In The Deciding Gate two numbers race through one gate for each place, the biggest place first. At every gate their digits stand as real blocks (flats for hundreds, rods for tens, cubes for ones), and equal digits let both numbers through. At the first gate where the digits differ, the bar drops in front of the smaller number. Before the race the child taps the gate they think will decide, or the finish flag when the numbers are the same, then puts <, = or > in the box.

For 389 and 412 the race is over at the very first gate: three flats against four, so the big 8 and 9 never get a turn. Swapped digits such as 247 and 274 are split at the tens gate, and 504 and 504 run all the way to the flag. A wrong call is answered by the race itself: the bar falls where the race was really decided, and after a second miss the deciding digits grow and the hint names them as blocks, such as 3 hundreds against 4 hundreds. In the order four job the child puts four numbers on a four-step podium from smallest to greatest. After a win the numbers appear as true lengths on a ruler from 0 to 1000 (to 10,000 with four digits).

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.A.4 (compare two three-digit numbers using >, = and <); the four-digit setting goes on to numbers up to 10,000. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Compare three-digit numbers from the biggest place down
Find the place that decides a comparison
Write <, = or > between two numbers
Order four numbers from smallest to greatest
howToPlay: Compare two: tap the gate you think decides the race, or the flag if the numbers are the same, put a sign in the box, then press Check.
Order four: tap a number, then a step (or drag it there), until every step holds a number, then press Check.
In the settings, choose compare two or order four, and three or four digits.
learningGoals: Compare two three-digit numbers by looking at the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.A.4.
Know that one hundred is more than 9 tens and 9 ones together, so 389 is less than 412.
Record a comparison with <, = or >, and order numbers from smallest to greatest.

about: Every equation is a gap in a path beside a stream, and every number card is a plank exactly as long as its number. The child taps an equation’s signpost, then a plank: it unfolds into the gap square by square. Only the number that makes the equation true fits. A plank that is too short falls into the water, and one that is too long sticks out past the far bank.

Each path has four gaps, and the missing number sits in a different place in each: the number added first, the number added second, the number taken away, the starting number, the total or the difference. A missing starting number or total is a slot under the road. The tray holds five planks: the four answers and one that fits nowhere — usually a typical mistake, such as adding the two numbers you see or subtracting the wrong way round. When all four planks fit, the animal crosses to the flag.
In the “Numbers only” setting the path shows no squares until a plank is laid, so the child works the number out first. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.8. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the missing number in any position: an addend, the number taken away, the starting number, the total or the difference
Seeing every equation as two parts and a whole
Checking an answer by fitting it: too short, too long or just right
Spotting the typical mistakes: adding the numbers you see, or subtracting the wrong way round
howToPlay: Tap an equation’s signpost to choose its gap. The next open gap is already chosen for you.
Tap a plank. If its number is right, it fits the gap; if not, it falls in or sticks out and goes back to the tray.
After two wrong planks in the same gap, its squares are numbered so you can count them.
Tap a signpost with a plank in it to take the plank out again.
In the settings, choose the numbers (within 10 or within 20) and the path (with squares or numbers only).
learningGoals: Find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction equation, wherever it is
Understand that the two parts of an equation make its whole
Use addition to solve a subtraction with a missing number
Check an answer instead of guessing

about: The target number is a string of lantern bulbs — exactly that many, with a small gap after the fifth. Tap a number and coral light runs along the string from the left; tap its partner and teal light runs in from the right. If the two lights meet exactly, the whole string flashes gold and the pair hangs on the garland above as two paper lanterns. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the two lights measure each other, so a wrong pair shows its own error. On the string of 8, 4 and 5 leave one bulb lit twice, and it flickers; 2 and 5 leave one bulb dark. A light longer than its string runs on past the far end. The extra or missing bulbs then number themselves, so the child sees by how much a guess is off, not just that it is wrong. A board holds every pair of its number once, and the garland keeps a dashed hook for each pair still to find. Other rounds plug one part in and ask for its partner (7 and 3 make 10), or plug in both parts with no string at all: the child chooses how long the string is, then lights it — 4 and 3 make 7.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.3 — breaking numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way. Teachers choose Up to 5 (the default), 6 to 9 or Make 10, and can switch on Card dots so each card shows its number as dots. "Lantern maker" is open play: any string from 2 to 10 and any two numbers from 1 to 9. No timer, no score.
practices: Making a number up to 10 from two parts in more than one way
Seeing by how much two parts are too many or too few
Finding the missing part and the whole
Reading each pair as an equation such as 3 + 7 = 10
howToPlay: Look at the number on the string's tag and count its bulbs if you like.
Tap a number, then its partner. The first lights the string from the left, the second from the right.
When the lights meet exactly, the pair hangs on the garland. Find every pair on the board.
In some rounds, choose the partner from four cards or choose how long the string is, then press "Light it". No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.3
Read each pair as an equation such as 3 + 7 = 10
Learn the pairs that make 10

about: Children work out cards like 8 + 5, 9 + 7, 14 − 6, and 17 − 8, then tap each fact and the number that is its answer to link the pair and build fluency within 20. It's an interactive Grade 2 math activity that runs right in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is quick, confident recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20. Each round mixes three facts — some plus, some minus — with their three answers jumbled in, so children compute each fact and then locate its matching value. Repeated practice across the rounds nudges facts like 9 + 9 = 18 and 16 − 9 = 7 from counting toward memory.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.B.2 — fluently adding and subtracting within 20 and knowing all sums of two one-digit numbers from memory. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Add and subtract within 20, with and without crossing ten
Match a fact like 7 + 8 to its answer card
Move addition and subtraction facts from counting toward memory
Work fluently with both plus and minus facts in one set
howToPlay: Work out each fact card, such as 6 + 9 or 13 − 4.
Tap a fact, then tap the number that is its answer, and watch the pair link.
Match all three pairs in the round — there is no timer and no score, so take your time.
learningGoals: Fluently add and subtract within 20 — the focus of Common Core 2.OA.B.2
Know the sums of one-digit numbers from memory
Build the fact recall that makes larger-number math easier

about: Each round deals nine cards: three numerals, three number names and three expanded forms, for three numbers made of the same digits, such as 247, 274 and 427. The child puts two cards in the twin stand, and each card pours its hundreds, tens and ones into its own three glass tubes. Two cards clip together only when all three pairs of tubes stand level.

A number name pours into frosted glass: you see the liquid arrive, but not how high it stands, so reading two hundred seventy-four stays the child's job. A clip melts the frost. A miss rings the uneven tube and says what the card with clear tubes has, for example "The tens are not the same. The card with clear tubes has 4 tens." A second miss writes each part over its tube. With zeros, the numbers are 305, 350 and 530, and 300 + 5 leaves the tens tube empty. In the digit-values setting the child finds what a colored digit is worth, such as the 7 in 721 (700).
It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.A.3: read and write numbers to 1000 as base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Match a numeral, its number name and its expanded form
Read three-digit number words such as two hundred seventy-four
Tell apart numbers made of the same digits, such as 247 and 274
Write expanded form when a place is empty, such as 300 + 5
howToPlay: Tap a card to put it in the stand, then tap a second card. Tap a card in the stand to take it out.
When all three pairs of tubes stand level, the two cards clip together. Tap the clipped pair to put it in the stand, then add the third card.
In the settings, choose three ways or digit values, and numbers with or without zeros.
learningGoals: Read and write numbers to 1000 as numerals, number names and expanded form.
See that the same digits in different places make different numbers.
Understand that an empty place has no part in the expanded form, as in 305 = 300 + 5.

about: A storybook page is torn, and Granny mends it with a needle and red thread. The child puts a paper piece into the torn hole and presses Check: the thread runs from the piece to the word the meaning hangs on. In "The puppy was so tiny that Granny had to look ___", carefully holds; quickly makes the thread snap right between tiny and quickly. Granny's Mending Basket is a Grade 1 activity for reading with understanding.

There are six ways to read closely. Fill the gap and Fix the word (a sentence where one word does not fit, like an umbrella that keeps Granny wet). Who is it? asks who did something in the second sentence. Do what it says gives an instruction to follow exactly: color two balloons red, put the cat under the bed. True or not? shows a picture: sew a true sentence in, or cut a wrong one out. Story questions ask about a short story, and the thread looks for the sentence that proves the answer. Every mended page turns from gray to color and joins Granny's book.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.4.a: reading grade-level text with purpose and understanding. No timer and no score.
practices: Choose the word the sentence needs, not just a word that sounds right
Find the word that does not make sense and fix it
Work out who a sentence is talking about
Follow an instruction exactly, and check a sentence against a picture
howToPlay: Read the sentence. Tap a paper piece: it flies into the torn hole. Tap the hole to take it back.
Press Check. The thread holds if the words agree, and snaps between the two words that do not.
In Do what it says, pick a crayon and tap pictures, or tap a sticker and then its place. In True or not?, pick the needle or the scissors.
learningGoals: Read with understanding, the focus of Common Core RF.1.4.a.
Use the word a meaning hangs on to choose, check and fix words.
Prove an answer with a sentence from the text.

about: Hazel the badger has paddock fences to mend, and children pitch in by finding the missing board when the whole fence and one side are known — a 6-by-4 paddock needs a board of 4, not 14 or 8. Along the way they judge which field needs more fence but grows less grass, tell the marks around the edge from the squares inside, and check whether a roll of fence reaches all the way around, in an interactive Grade 3 math activity that plays right in the browser with no install and no account.

The big idea is that perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape — a length — and not the space it covers. The rounds deliberately pit fence against grass: a long, thin 9-by-2 field and a square 5-by-5 field invite children to compare the fence around with the grass inside and discover the two can disagree. By fencing the edge in some rounds and counting inside squares in others, children feel the difference instead of memorizing a rule.

It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.D.8 — solving real-world problems involving perimeter, including finding an unknown side length and comparing shapes with the same perimeter or area. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Find an unknown side length when the perimeter and one side are known
Tell perimeter (the distance around) apart from area (the space inside)
Compare fields with the same area but different perimeters
Check whether a given length of fence reaches around a shape
howToPlay: Read the fence job — mend a missing board, compare two fields, or check whether a roll reaches around.
Work out the distance around the edge, then tap the answer that mends the fence.
Got it wrong? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Solve perimeter problems, including finding an unknown side length — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.D.8
Understand perimeter as a length around a shape, distinct from area
Compare shapes that share a perimeter or an area

about: Sorting things into groups is how a child learns what a word like “animal” or “food” really means. In Mim’s Memory Baskets, Mim the little cloud tips over her basket, and her things spill onto the grass. The baskets below have no labels: the child decides which things belong together.

When a basket holds two or more things of one kind, Mim’s cloud above it rains down a cousin, a new thing of that kind: a dog and a cat bring a rabbit. When the child presses “Check” and a basket mixes two kinds, its cloud splits in two, and each half rains a cousin onto its own family, so the two groups appear side by side. In the color and shape rounds the cousins never share the confusing look: the red apple gets a green kiwi, and the red tractor gets an airplane.

Three kinds of rounds: Sort, with two to four baskets (animals, food, vehicles, toys, clothes, shapes, fruits and vegetables, sea, forest, and farm animals); The stray, where the one thing of another kind goes into the little basket; and Two clouds, where each cloud shows its rule with two pictures and the middle basket is for things that fit both. Aligned to Common Core L.K.5.A: sort common objects into categories. No timer and no score.
practices: Sorting pictures into groups by what they are
Telling a thing’s kind apart from its color or shape
Finding the one thing that is a different kind
Sorting by two rules at once, with a middle place for both
howToPlay: Tap a thing on the grass, then tap a basket (or drag it there). Put every thing in a basket.
Things of one kind go in one basket. Press “Check” when the grass is empty.
Under “Round types” choose The stray or Two clouds; under “Baskets” choose Two; under “Helping rain” choose “Only at Check” to sort without the rain while you play.
learningGoals: The child sorts common objects into categories and meets the name of each category
The child sees that things of one kind can look very different, and that a shared color or shape does not make a kind
The child sorts by two features at once and puts the things that have both in the middle

about: Mochi has ordered a box of treats, and the order ticket shows how many — 7, say. The child taps treats on the tray, and each one drops into a bakery box with the lid on: one tap, one treat out of sight. When the child thinks the box holds exactly the number on the ticket, they press Check and the box opens. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The lid is the point. Once a treat is in the box it cannot be seen, so the count has to stay in the child's head — the last number said is how many are in the box, and the child has to stop there. Counting out a given number is harder than counting a group that is already there, and the closed box makes the child keep the count instead of looking. A tap on the lid lifts it for a short peek, and it drops again by itself; while the box is open, a tap on a treat inside puts it back on the tray. The tray always holds more treats than any order (12, or 7 when the numbers go up to 5), so its size never gives the answer. A wrong Check says too many or too few and leaves the lid off for the rest of the round; after a second, the treats in the box are numbered and the box marks the extra treats or the empty places still needed. The help never moves a treat.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting out a given number of things, up to 10 — and to the idea behind it, that the last number counted tells how many (K.CC.B.4b). Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 or up to 10, and take the lid off so the treats stay in sight. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting out a given number of treats, one at a time
Keeping the count in your head when the treats go out of sight
Stopping at the right number — the last number counted tells how many
Peeking and counting again to check
howToPlay: Read the number on the order ticket.
Tap treats on the tray to put them in the box, one at a time. With the lid on they are out of sight, so keep count.
With the lid on, tap it to peek. While the box is open, tap a treat inside to put it back on the tray.
Press Check. Not quite? The hint says too many or too few — fix it and press Check again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Count out a given number of things, up to 10 — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Know that the last number counted tells how many
Keep track of a count when the objects can no longer be seen

about: Counting a handful of coins means counting on: 25, 35, 40, 41. Most coin games add the money up for the child and show a running total, so the child only watches a number climb. Count Out the Money takes the adding off the screen and puts it in the child's hands.

The bakery's coin box has a slot, a counter with number wheels and a price pin. A coin drops in only when the child has already turned the counter to what the box will hold with that coin inside; any other number flips the coin back out. The wheels stop at the price pin, so paying too much cannot happen, and the coins come from a real purse, so a child who spends the small coins first can be left with coins that no longer fit. The coins are drawn true to the real coins' sizes and metals, each with its worth on it.

Three levels: pay an exact price; pay it with the fewest coins; then top up the coins already in the box, or count two trays to find which holds more money. A wrong count shows the child's number and rolls the wheels back; a second shows the count-on step by step. No timer, no score.
practices: Count a mixed set of coins by counting on from the biggest coin
Pay an exact amount, and pay it with the fewest coins
Find how much more money is needed to reach a price
Decide which of two sets of coins is worth more
howToPlay: Turn the counter to what the box will hold with your coin in it, then tap the coin and the slot, or drag the coin to the slot.
A wrong number sends the coin back out. The lever gives back the last coin; the ring tips them all out.
In the tray rounds, tap the tray you think holds more money, then count both trays into the box.
The bell rings when the box holds exactly the price.
learningGoals: Counting on by the worth of each coin.
Making an amount with coins, and with the fewest coins.
Solving money problems: how much more is needed, and which amount is more.

about: Change is the part of the customer's money that is not the price. Children who are still learning it often hand back the price itself, or count coins instead of their worth. Make Change with Coins shows change as what it is: money taken out of the customer's own payment.

The customer's payment goes into Pip's change box, which rattles and pours out the same money in small coins. The child taps the change into the customer's tray; whatever is left belongs to Pip. At Check, Pip counts his coins onto the price tag: he comes up short if too much went back, and goes past the price if too little did. Pip's count is the only total on the screen, and it appears only at Check. The coins are drawn true to the real coins' sizes, each with its worth on it.

Four shops: give change; decide whether a purse holds enough and add what it still needs; buy two or three toys and give change; or all of them mixed. After a second miss the count runs up from the price to the payment, and the change coins are outlined in the pile. The "as you go" setting shows Pip's count all the time, for a first lesson. No timer, no score.
practices: Give change by counting up from the price to the money paid
Add up two or three prices, then give change
Decide whether a purse holds enough money for a price
Find how much more money is needed to reach a price
howToPlay: Watch the change box turn the customer's money into small coins.
Tap coins into the customer's tray for the change; tap a coin in the tray to put it back.
Press Check: Pip counts the coins left for him against the price.
In the purse rounds, tap Enough or Not enough, or add coins to Pip's dish until he has the price.
learningGoals: Making change by counting up from the price.
Adding prices and giving change from the total.
Comparing an amount of money with a price, and finding how much more is needed.

about: Tessa shows a mosaic — say a 2-by-3 block of 6 tiles — and children find the one made of the same number of unit tiles, which might be a single row of 6 even though it is shaped nothing like the target. It's an interactive Grade 3 math activity that runs right in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is that area is a count of unit squares, the same no matter the shape. One of the look-alike choices is a bigger-looking shape with the wrong count — a 3-by-3 of 9 tiles next to a 2-by-3 of 6 — so a child cannot pick by which looks largest and has to actually count the squares. Matching across different shapes is exactly what makes area click as a count rather than an impression.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.C.6 — measuring areas by counting unit squares. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Measure area by counting unit squares
Match two shapes that have the same area but look different
Resist judging area by which shape looks biggest
Compare rectangles, rows, and L-shapes by their tile count
howToPlay: Look at Tessa's target mosaic and count how many unit tiles it uses.
Tap the other mosaic with the same number of tiles, even if its shape looks different.
Got it wrong? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Measure area by counting unit squares — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.C.6
Understand that area stays the same across different shapes with equal tile counts
Build the unit-square foundation for finding area by rows and columns later

about: A round necklace with a clasp at the top. The child taps the necklace and the next bead slides along the cord to the clasp — beads cannot pass each other on a string, so every bead is counted once and none is skipped. The count shows in the middle of the necklace as the beads slide, then fades: how many beads? This interactive Kindergarten counting activity runs in the browser with nothing to install.

Then the necklace won't hold still. The beads glide apart around the cord, squeeze close together, or one more bead comes on — and the child answers again: how many now? There are three big number cards to choose from. A wrong card is named: the last number counted tells how many; the beads only moved — none came on or fell off; only one bead came on. Count again is always there — recounting to check is a good strategy, not a mistake. The cards are chosen so that the right one is not always the biggest, not always the smallest and not always in the same place.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4 — counting one by one, knowing that the last number said tells how many, that the number stays the same however the objects are arranged, and that each next number is one more. Teachers can choose up to 5 or up to 10 beads, and counting numbers shown or said aloud by the child. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting each bead once, in order, as it slides past the clasp
Answering how many with the last number counted
Knowing the number stays the same when the beads spread out or squeeze together
Seeing that one more bead makes the next number
howToPlay: Tap the necklace: the next bead slides past the clasp. Count each bead as it moves.
When every bead is across, tap the number card that tells how many.
Watch the necklace change, then answer again: how many now? Not sure? Tap Count again and count them.
learningGoals: Connect counting to cardinality: the last number counted tells how many — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.4
Understand that the number of objects stays the same when they are moved apart or pushed together
Understand that each successive number is one more

about: Four flowerpots wait in a row — 6, 9, 2 and 4, say — and they all look exactly the same: only the number painted on each one is different. The child taps a pot and it drops into the nest, growing to the size of its number as it lands: the 9 becomes a big pot, the 2 a small one. A pot only fits inside a pot with a bigger number, so the nest has to be built from the biggest number down to the smallest. It's an interactive Kindergarten activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

Because every pot in the row is the same size, size gives nothing away: the child reads and compares the numbers, and trying a pot shows at once whether it fits. The pots themselves answer back: a pot that is too big sticks out over the rim, wobbles and goes back to the row. Choosing a small pot too early leads to a dead end — put the 9 in and then the 2, and neither the 6 nor the 4 fits any more — so the inside pot glows, and a tap lifts it out again. After two bounces, dots appear on the waiting pots so the child can count which number is biggest. When every pot is in, Check reads the nest out: “Yes — 9, 6, 4, 2: from the biggest number to the smallest!”

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.C.7 — comparing numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals, here three or four at a time. Teachers can choose three pots up to 5 or four pots up to 10, and show the dots only as a help or always. No timer, no score.
practices: Comparing written numbers up to 10
Finding the biggest number in a group
Putting three or four numbers in order, biggest to smallest
Fixing a mistake by taking a step back
howToPlay: Look at the numbers on the pots. Which one is the biggest?
Tap the biggest number first: it is the outside pot.
Then tap the next biggest, and the next — each pot must fit inside the last one.
Too big? It comes back. Stuck? Tap the inside pot to take it out. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Compare numbers between 1 and 10 given as written numerals — the focus of Common Core K.CC.C.7
Order three or four numbers from the biggest to the smallest
See that a bigger number means more

about: Nila the otter has a pond, a rain cloud and four umbrellas. The child reads a short text about an animal, such as "When the cold snow falls, a bear must stay snug.", and its three detail sentences float on the pond as lily pads. Each umbrella carries one idea. Hang one over the pond and it opens to the same size as every other umbrella, so hanging tells the child nothing. Then it rains: the canopy pulls in to exactly what its idea covers. Only the big idea, "staying warm in the snow", keeps every lily pad dry; a detail idea shelters just its own pad, and an idea that is not in the text folds up over open water while the ink on the wet pads runs.

Some rounds go on. A true sentence about the same animal drifts in under the umbrella, and the child pushes it out into the rain because it is not about the big idea; or two new pads float at the edge, and the child pulls the one that belongs under. After a third wrong umbrella, a new text about the same animal takes its place, so trying every umbrella does not work. The twelve texts are about a bear, a bee and a swan. The Reading setting switches between I read it and Read it to me; with Umbrellas set to 3, the idea that is not in the text stays home.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.K.2: identifying the main topic of a text and retelling its key details. Every picture comes from the picture library. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the main topic of a short informational text
Telling a main topic from a single detail
Noticing an idea that is not in the text
Retelling the key details that belong to the topic
howToPlay: Read the text, or tap Nila to hear it.
Drag or tap an umbrella to hang it over the pond, then check.
Watch the rain: the right umbrella keeps every lily pad dry.
In some rounds, push the pad that does not belong out into the rain, or pull the one that belongs under.
learningGoals: The child names what a whole text is about
The child tells the details that belong to the main topic
The child sees that one detail is not the main topic

about: Three numbers sit in a three-part number bond as three glassy drops of beads. Drag one drop onto another, or tap one and then the other, and they melt into one drop that keeps every bead's colour. When a drop holds ten beads or more, the first ten click into a 2 × 5 frame inside a gold ring: the pearl. Any extra beads gather in a small droplet beside it.

Children can join the drops in any order, and every order ends in the same last drop, which rises into the whole circle. Joining the two that make ten first makes the last step easy: a pearl and four more is 14. The child types the total on the number keys, or adds in their head without joining anything.

If the answer is the sum of only two drops, those two join by themselves and the third drop is left out, pulsing. After a second miss, the pearl is labelled 10 so the child can count on from there. After a right answer, “See other ways” shows all three orders reaching the same total. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.A.2. No timer and no score.
practices: Adding three numbers with a total up to 20
Adding in any order and getting the same total
Looking for two numbers that make ten, or a double, first
Reading a ten and some more instead of counting from 1
howToPlay: Drag a drop onto another drop (or tap one, then the other) to join them. Join all three in any order.
Type how many beads there are on the number keys and press the tick. The round arrow undoes the last join.
After a right answer, press “See other ways” to watch the other orders reach the same total.
In the settings, choose the numbers (Within 10 or Within 20) and whether the drops show their beads or only their numerals.
learningGoals: Add three whole numbers with a sum up to 20
Use any order when adding three numbers
Make a ten first to add more easily
See a ten and its extra ones in a teen number

about: Two bowls of things and one basket. The child pours one bowl into the basket: the basket counts the things on its tag as they fall in, then a checked cloth drops over them and only the number stays. The other bowl goes in one thing at a time through a slot in the cloth.

The running count is never shown, so the child cannot count everything again from one. The only way to the total is to start at the number on the cloth and count on as each thing is posted: “8 … 9, 10, 11”. Which bowl to pour first is the child's choice, and pouring the bowl with more is quicker. Children find that out with their own hands.

When the answer is not right, the counting-on numbers appear over the posted things, starting one after the number on the cloth. On a second try the cloth lifts and everything lies in ten-frame rows in two colours. Four tasks: find the total within 20, bonds within 10, make the whole (post until the basket is full), and bigger totals to 20. The parts can be pictures, dots (like dice) or ten frames. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.A.1. No timer and no score.
practices: Adding two parts by putting them together
Counting on from a number instead of counting all from one
Starting with the larger part to count on fewer
Finding the whole of a number bond, and the part that makes a whole
howToPlay: Tap a bowl to pour it into the basket. Watch the tag count the things, then the cloth covers them.
Tap the other bowl to post its things one at a time through the slot. Count on from the number on the cloth.
Type how many there are in all on the number keys and press the tick. A long press on the cloth lifts one corner for a peek; the round arrow empties the basket.
In the settings, choose the task (find the total, bonds within 10, make the whole, bigger totals to 20) and what the parts look like (pictures, dots, ten frames).
learningGoals: Add two numbers within 20 by putting the parts together
Count on from the first part instead of counting all
Find the whole of a number bond within 10 and within 20
Find the part that is missing to make a whole

about: The first number sits in a ten-rack of linking cubes, and the empty slots at its end are the hole. The second number is a stick of cubes. The child taps the stick to snap it and drags a piece into the hole. A piece that is too long bounces back, one that is too short leaves empty slots glowing, and only the exact piece fills the ten.

When the ten is full, the rack turns gold and the equation strip shows the strategy, as in 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 10 + 3. The rest of the stick waits beside the golden ten on the ones shelf, and the child types the total. Where the first number is the smaller one, a swap button lets the bigger number go into the rack instead.

A wrong total is drawn on the shelves as a ghost ten and ghost ones. The common slip of adding the whole second number after making ten (8 + 5 → 15) shows extra ghost places glowing, with a thread into the ten: those cubes are inside the ten now. On a second miss, the ten is labelled 10 so the child can count on. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.C.6. No timer and no score.
practices: Making a ten to add within 20: 8 + 5 = 10 + 3
Breaking a number into two parts so one part makes 10
Knowing the partner that makes 10, such as 7 and 3
Seeing a teen number as a ten and some ones
howToPlay: Tap the stick to snap it into pieces. The round arrow joins it again.
Drag a piece into the hole in the ten-rack. Only the exact piece fits: too long bounces back, too short leaves a gap.
When the ten is gold, type the total and press the tick.
In the settings, choose the level (Make a ten to add or Make 10) and the mode (Snap first or In my head). In “In my head” mode, the child types the total first, and a miss shows the snap by itself.
learningGoals: Add within 20 by making a ten
Break the second number so one part completes the ten
Know the pairs that make 10
Understand a teen number as a ten and some ones

about: A Ferris wheel has exactly ten seats, and some riders are already on — say 7. The child sets a number on the boarding gate's dial, pulls the gate lever, and that many farm animals hop in one by one while the wheel clicks round a seat each time. Then the brake comes off. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the wheel checks the answer by balancing. A full wheel turns a slow circle with its rim lights chasing. Too few riders, and the heavy side swings down: the wheel rocks and settles with the empty seats at the very top, where everyone can count them. Too many, and the riders who do not fit are left standing on the platform; the brake will not release, and they all hop back off so the child can turn the dial down. The seats come in two colours of five, so 7 reads as five and two more. After a second try the empty seats count on (8, 9, 10) and the dial's arrow shows which way to turn it — never the number itself. The number bond beside the wheel records each ride, such as 10 = 7 + 3, and a pass through Make 10 starts once from every number from 1 to 9. Other rounds use smaller wheels, or fill every seat with two kinds of rider and ask for the whole: 5 and 3 make 8.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.4 — finding the number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9 — with number bonds to 5 and within 10 as extra levels. Teachers choose Up to 5, 6 to 9 or Make 10 (the default), and can switch on seat numbers so a child can count on round the wheel. "Fairground" is open play: any wheel from 2 to 10 seats and any number of riders. No timer, no score.
practices: Finding the number that makes 10 with a given number from 1 to 9
Seeing whether a guess is too few or too many
Counting on from the riders already aboard
Reading each ride as a number bond such as 10 = 7 + 3
howToPlay: Look at the riders already on the wheel and the number in the middle.
Turn the dial with the arrows, then pull the gate lever: that many riders hop on.
Release the brake. A full wheel spins; empty seats or riders left standing show what to change.
Tap a rider who just got on to let them off again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Find the number that makes 10 with any number from 1 to 9 — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.4
Decompose numbers up to 10 into two parts
Learn every pair that makes ten

about: The child reads a short story, types the number they think is missing, and presses Replay: the story plays itself out on a measuring track with that number put in. Every number the story told is a little flag the bars must land on. Tom had some marbles, found 17 more and now has 45: type 62 and Tom starts with 62, grows by 17 and sails far past the 45 flag, and the shaded gap shows by how much.

A second miss replays the right story backwards from the told end and outlines where the missing number belongs, without printing it. When the number is right, the flags wave and the track folds into a number bond with the equation underneath, here 28 + 17 = 45. Adding all the numbers or reading only the keyword fails on purpose about half the time, so the child learns to put the answer back into the story.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.A.1: add and subtract within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems with the unknown in any position.
