The settings also cover stories within 20 with pictures and equal groups for multiplying and sharing. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Find a missing total, part, change or starting number in a story
Solve comparison stories with more and fewer
Solve two-step stories
Check an answer by putting it back into the story
howToPlay: Read the story and type the number you think is missing.
Press Replay and watch whether the bars land on every flag. If not, see where it goes wrong and try again.
In the settings, choose stories within 20 with pictures, within 100, two steps or equal groups, and whether the flags show from the start.
learningGoals: Solve add and subtract stories with the unknown in any position.
Not add every number just because the story says more.
Check an answer by replaying the story with it.

about: Each round shows one domino on a green holder. A brass plate above it carries the whole, and the two halves are the parts. One number is hidden: a half lies face down, or a felt lid covers the plate. The equation strip under the domino shows where the ? is, as in 3 + ? = 8, 12 − ? = 7 or ? − 5 = 8.

The child sets the hidden number with + and − and presses Check. Every dot then marches onto the plate’s places. When a half is hidden, a number that is too small leaves empty places glowing, and one that is too big leaves dots hanging off the end. When the lid hides the whole, the number is the size of the plate, so it works the other way round: a plate too small leaves dots hanging off, a plate too big leaves places empty. In a missing-part round, the common slip of adding the two numbers that are shown never fits, and the plate shows why.

After the right number, the hidden half turns over and the domino is whole again. Now the child turns the domino: the addition swaps and the plate stays the same. Tapping a half breaks it off, and what is left on the holder is the subtraction. Fact by fact, the fact house fills with all four facts of the family. On a second miss, the places (or, under the lid, the dots) are laid out to count. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.B.4. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding a missing part: 3 and how many make 8?
Seeing subtraction as a missing part: 12 − ? = 7
Finding the unknown in any place of an addition or subtraction within 20
Building the four facts of a fact family
howToPlay: Look at the equation strip: the ? is the hidden number.
Set the number with + and − and press Check. The dots march onto the plate: every dot needs a place, and every place needs a dot.
With the fact house on, turn the domino with the round arrow and tap a half to break it off or put it back, until all four windows are filled.
In the settings, choose the numbers (Within 10 or Within 20) and switch the fact house on or off.
learningGoals: Understand subtraction as finding a missing part
Find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction within 20
Connect addition and subtraction through the four facts of a fact family
See that swapping the parts of an addition does not change the whole

about: The child is the Judge in Numbers Court. A witness makes a claim such as 6 + 2 = 8 + 1, and the child stamps it = (true) or ≠ (false), then bangs the gavel. In the middle of the courtroom stands the equal sign itself: a fixed top bar with a beam below it, and each side of the claim sits in a pan.

A red court seal holds the beam until the ruling is right. A right ruling cracks the seal: if both sides hold the same amount, the two bars lie flat and read “=”; if not, the light end rises until it touches the top bar, and the bars form a “<” or “>” that opens toward the bigger side. A wrong ruling never moves the beam. Instead the pans show their amounts as dots, and after a second wrong ruling, threads pair the dots one to one.

A false claim is then made true: one crate turns gold, and the child changes its number until the beam lies flat. In the “Make it balance” setting, every claim starts with a missing number, such as 8 + 4 = □ + 5. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.7. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading the equal sign as “both sides hold the same amount”, not “the answer comes next”
Deciding whether an equation with addition and subtraction is true or false
Seeing that 3 + 5 = 5 + 3 and 7 = 3 + 4 are true, whichever way round they are written
Finding the missing number that makes both sides equal
howToPlay: Read the witness’s claim, then tap the = stamp if it is true or the ≠ stamp if it is false.
Tap “Bang the gavel”. A right ruling breaks the seal, and the beam shows whether the two sides are equal.
If the beam stays still, look at the dots under the pans and rule again.
For a false claim, change the number in the gold crate with − and + until the beam lies flat. After a true claim, you can turn the court round to read it the other way.
In “Make it balance”, there is no stamp: set the missing number with − and +, then bang the gavel.
In the settings, choose the claims (“True or false” or “Make it balance”) and the numbers (to 10 or to 20).
learningGoals: Understand the equal sign as “the same amount on both sides”
Tell whether an addition or subtraction equation is true or false
Make a false equation true by changing one number
Find the missing number in an equation such as 8 + 4 = □ + 5

about: Every branch of the tree holds one kind of thing: birds, fruit, vehicles, clothing. The child reads the clue and climbs the picture up to the branch where its kind lives, and a leaf on the trunk spells out the climb. Put the banana on the animals branch and the leaf says so, which a child can tell is wrong; press Check and the branch cannot hold it, so it slides back down to the roots.

There are three things to do: say what kind of thing a picture is; sort nine pictures into three groups; and climb to a definition, where every branch opens three twigs and the leaf grows into a sentence such as "A duck is a bird that swims." The same attribute can grow on different branches (a boat goes on water, and so does a duck), so the kind has to come first.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.5.b: define words by category and by one or more key attributes. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Say what kind of thing something is
Sort pictures into groups
Name one thing that sets it apart from others of its kind
Read a definition and check it
howToPlay: Tap a branch (or drag the picture to it), then press Check.
In the definition level, the branch opens three twigs: tap the one that tells the picture apart.
In the settings, choose what to do, whether the clue comes with a picture, and three or four branches.
learningGoals: Name the category a word belongs to.
Define a word by its category and one key attribute.
Sort words into groups.

about: Every pair of opposites lives on one rod. The rod for hot and cold is painted from red to blue; the child drops a card on it and the card slides to where its meaning lives. "cold" runs all the way to the far end and clicks into the clip. "warm" stops at the middle groove: it is only halfway. A word that means the same parks beside "hot", and a word from another family, like a colour, finds no place and falls off. Up and down stand on an upright rod, and "left" slides onto the crossing rod instead. The pictures are a ball, a jar, a door, a lamp, the sun and the moon from the picture library.

The rod has five levels. Pictures has nine rods and a bedtime scene. Same or opposite? asks the child to put each word at the same end or the other end, then check. Pair up has three rods and three opposites, each with one home. Sentences finishes a sentence with the opposite, by picking a card or, with Write it, by typing the word. Prefixes hangs a clip such as "un" or "dis" at the far end and pushes the word along: only the right clip closes on it and makes "unhappy"; a wrong clip never turns the word into its opposite. The Words setting can hide the pictures (Words only).
It is aligned to Common Core K.L.5.b: relating words to their opposites. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the opposite of a word
Telling a word that means the opposite from one that means the same
Seeing that a middle word like warm is not the opposite of hot
Using an opposite in a sentence and with a prefix
howToPlay: Look at the word at one end of the rod.
Drag a card onto the rod, or tap it, and watch where it slides.
The opposite runs all the way to the other end.
In Prefixes, hang a clip at the empty end and tap the word to push it.
learningGoals: The child names the opposite of a familiar word
The child sorts words into same and opposite
The child uses an opposite to finish a sentence

about: Otto the owl reads with pins. Every important word in his sentence carries a pin, and when the child checks, the pins fly into the picture. A pin sticks only where the picture shows what its word says; where it does not, the pin hangs loose and shows exactly which word did not match. Put “A gust of wind pushes the boat.” under a picture with no wind, and the pin on wind dangles. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

There are four tasks. In Which picture? the child puts the sentence under the one picture of a little story that shows it. In Fill the blank the child picks the word, or spells it with letter tiles, that makes the sentence match the scene. In Read and color the child paints a row of pictures as the sentence says. In True or false? the child decides whether a sentence matches the picture. With Two parts, every round has two sentences or a longer instruction to keep track of.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.7: telling how a story’s pictures and its words go together. Every picture comes from the picture library. No timer and no score.
practices: Matching a sentence to the picture that shows it
Checking each word of a sentence against a picture
Choosing the word that makes a sentence true for a picture
Following a written instruction to color pictures
howToPlay: Choose a task in the settings.
Read Otto’s sentence, or tap the speaker to hear it.
Put the sentence under a picture, choose a word, paint or tap ✓ or ✗, then check.
A pin that hangs shows the word that does not match the picture.
learningGoals: The child finds the picture that shows a sentence
The child tells which word does or does not match a picture
The child knows that the words and the pictures of a story tell the same thing

about: Bramble the beaver runs a parking tower, and the child parks each vehicle where the sentence says: next to the bus, above the van, below the car, between the bus and the van, to the left of the bulldozer. Tap an empty space and the vehicle drives to the glass lift, rides it up or down, and rolls along its floor into the space. It is an interactive Kindergarten activity about position words that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that a vehicle can only ride the lift up and down and drive along a floor, so every position word becomes a route the child can see. Above is always one ride up the lift in the same column, never a drive sideways, and the dotted route that stays after parking is a small diagram of the word the child chose. A wrong space brings help that shows instead of tells: a teal arrow grows from the landmark towards the asked position and a coral arrow points to where the vehicle actually is; the floor between the levels pulses for above and below; a second miss makes the right space glow with a ghost of the vehicle. Some rounds turn it round: Bramble has already parked, and the child taps his truck.

It is aligned to Common Core K.G.A.1: describing the relative positions of objects with words such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind and next to. Teachers choose the near words (above, below, next to, between, left, right), the tower words (on top of, under, beside, inside and outside the tower; the top, middle and bottom level), or the roof plan, which reaches beyond K.G.A.1 to the map skills of second grade: lettered columns and numbered rows on a 6 × 6 or a 10 × 10 grid, codes such as B2 to park in or D3 to read on two dials, and a compass whose north does not always point up. The vehicles and Bramble come from the illustrated library. No timer, no score.
practices: Above, below, next to and between, always from the viewer's side
Left and right of another object
On top of, under, beside, inside and outside; top, middle and bottom level
Reading and writing grid codes (letter across, number down) and the four compass directions
howToPlay: Read the sentence: the teal word is the vehicle to park, the coral word the vehicle it is parked next to.
Tap an empty space; the vehicle drives there by the lift and the route stays.
On the roof plan, tap a square, or turn the letter and number wheels to set a code.
Press Check.
learningGoals: Describe the position of an object relative to another, the focus of Common Core K.G.A.1
Tell above from next to, and between from beside one of them
Find a square from its grid code and use north, east, south and west on a map

about: Sprout the gardener has irregular flower beds — L-shapes, staircases, and crosses — and children carpet each one completely with moss-patch unit squares, leaving no gaps and no overlaps, then count the squares to find the area. It's an interactive Grade 3 math activity that runs right in the browser with no account.

Because the beds are not plain rectangles, there is no length to multiply by a width — the child measures area the real way, by covering the space with unit squares and counting them. The rounds vary the thinking: cover an empty bed, fix a covering that has a gap and an overlap, predict an area before tiling, finish a partly-covered bed, and build a bed of an exact size such as 5 or 6 squares.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.C.6 (with 3.MD.C.5) — measuring area by counting unit squares with no gaps or overlaps. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Cover a shape completely with unit squares, leaving no gaps or overlaps
Count the squares to find the area
Find the area of irregular L-shapes and staircases without multiplying
Fix gaps and overlaps, and build a region of an exact area
howToPlay: Tap inside the flower bed to lay moss-patch unit squares until the whole space is covered.
Cover it with no gaps and no overlaps, count the squares, and check — or fix, finish, or build to the size asked.
Not quite? Add or remove squares and try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Measure area by covering a shape with unit squares and counting them — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.C.6
Understand area as the number of unit squares with no gaps or overlaps
Find the area of irregular shapes that cannot be measured by length times width

about: Pearl the seal runs the opinion page, and each column makes one clear point — "Our town should build a new park," "Everyone should wear a helmet when biking" — so children read the point and tap the card that backs it up with a real reason, like "Children have nowhere safe to play." It's an interactive Grade 2 reading activity that runs right in the browser with no account.

The big idea is that a reason is not the same as repeating the point. In every round the three cards are one true reason, one restatement that just says the point again in different words ("Our town really needs a brand-new park"), and one off-topic card about something else entirely ("The library closes at five o'clock"). The child cannot win by matching words — they have to decide which card actually explains WHY the point is a good idea. That is the difference between supporting a claim and merely echoing it.
It is aligned to Common Core RI.2.8 — describing how reasons support the points an author makes in a text. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Tell a supporting reason apart from a card that just restates the point
Spot off-topic cards that talk about something unrelated
Decide WHY a point is a good idea, not just whether it sounds true
Build the claim-and-reason thinking that opinion reading and writing depend on
howToPlay: Read Pearl's point at the top, like "Our class should grow a garden."
Read the three cards and tap the one that gives a real reason for the point.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify the reason that supports an author's point — the focus of Common Core RI.2.8
Understand that restating a point is not the same as giving a reason for it
Build a foundation for reading and writing opinion pieces with real support

about: Every letter is written in the same window, and the paper moves under it like a typewriter carriage. The child starts on the green dot, traces the letter along its road, then writes it once more with only the lines and the green dot. Each finished letter glides out to the left with three clicks and sits on the line beside the others, so a letter that does not reach its line stands out next to its neighbours.

Tracing only counts where the finger really went: from the green dot, the way the arrow points, stroke by stroke in order. A line drawn from the wrong end stays pale and fades away. In the writing step the road is hidden; if the letter wanders off, "Check" shows a shadow letter over the child's line, and a second time a spark runs along the stroke and the child traces that letter again.

The alphabet wall above the paper fills with the child's own letters in alphabet order: all 26 capitals and all 26 lowercase letters. The paper is ruled like school handwriting paper. Aligned to Common Core L.K.1.a: print upper- and lowercase letters. No timer and no score.
practices: Starting every letter at the right point and writing its strokes in order
Moving the pencil the right way for each stroke
Sizing capitals and lowercase letters on the lines
Writing a letter without the road after tracing it
howToPlay: Put your finger on the green dot and trace the letter in the window.
Write it again with only the lines and the green dot.
Under "Practice" choose "Trace, then write twice" or "Trace only", and under "Letters" a set such as "Vowels" or "First letters".
learningGoals: The child starts each letter at the correct point
The child writes the strokes of each letter in the right order and direction
The child writes capital and lowercase letters on the lines

about: A word sits on a flip card, its sounds on tiles along the bottom: c · a · t. Pepper the parrot brings a new tile, h, for the first sound. The child guesses which picture the card will turn into, then Check plays the swap: the old tile pops out, the h drops in, and the card flips over to a hat. It is an interactive Kindergarten phonemic awareness activity that plays in the browser.

The card always shows the word the tiles really make. Guess the bat and the card still turns into a hat, and the bat shows its own tiles with the one that differs marked. In the swap level the child pushes tiles in from a tray: put b into cat and the card flips to a bat, a real word but not the goal; tiles that make a word with no picture turn the card grey and show only its letters. Further levels change the middle or last sound, follow word chains, and add a sound at the start or the end.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.e, adding or substituting sounds in simple words to make new words. No timer and no score.
practices: Changing one sound in a short word to make a new word
Hearing that the place of a sound matters: first, middle or last
Telling the right new word from one that shares the other sounds
Adding a sound at the start or the end of a word
howToPlay: Look at the word on the card and at Pepper’s new tile.
Tap the picture you think the card will turn into, or swap a tile yourself.
Press Check and watch the card flip to the word the tiles really make.
learningGoals: The child changes one sound to make a new word
The child keeps track of which sound changed and where
The child adds a sound to a word and hears the new word

about: Fable the fox opens a little picture book: three pages (or four) that the child turns one by one, each a scene of library pictures with a caption underneath. A question is printed on a ribbon bookmark – “Where did the mitten slip off?” – and the child answers it by slipping the bookmark into the story, onto the picture, the words or the page that answers it. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

The answer has to come from the book. Who questions are answered with a picture (the robin, wherever it appears), where, when, why and what-were-they-doing questions with the caption words that say it (“by a big rock”), and first, middle and last with a whole page. A wrong mark comes back, and the answer line shows what was marked; after two tries the page that holds the answer lifts up and the words that repeat the question light up. A right answer underlines the proving words in gold and Fable hops for joy. In Caption the pages, the bookmark carries a sentence instead, and the page it belongs to acts it out.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.1, asking and answering questions about key details in a story. Seven short stories, three or four pages each. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the answer to a question in a story
Answering who, what, where, when and why questions with details from the pictures and words
Telling which page comes first, in the middle and last
Matching sentences to the pictures they tell
howToPlay: Read the story and the question on the bookmark.
Tap the answer in the book, or drag the bookmark onto it: a picture, some words or a whole page.
Press Check. If the bookmark comes back, read the page again and try another spot.
learningGoals: The child answers questions about key details of a story
The child shows where in the story the answer is written or drawn
The child tells the beginning, middle and end of a short story

about: Pim the carrier pigeon delivers letters, and a letter needs its commas in exactly the right spot, so children read three ways to write a greeting like 'Dear Sam' or a closing like 'Your friend,' and tap the one punctuated correctly. It's an interactive Grade 2 grammar activity that runs right in the browser with no account.

The big idea is that the comma goes at the END of the greeting and the END of the closing — after the name, not before it. The three choices are built around the common mistakes: the correct form ('Dear Sam,'), a version with no comma at all ('Dear Sam'), and a version with the comma in the wrong place ('Dear, Sam'). The child has to know where the comma belongs, not just notice that a comma is somewhere on the card.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.2.b — using commas in the greeting and closing of a letter. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Place a comma at the end of a letter's greeting, like Dear Grandma,
Place a comma at the end of a letter's closing, like Your pal,
Spot a greeting or closing with a missing comma or a misplaced one
Build the letter-writing punctuation habits of Grade 2 writing
howToPlay: Read the three ways to write the greeting or closing Pim is delivering.
Tap the one with its comma in the right place — at the end, after the name.
Not quite? Try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use commas correctly in the greeting and closing of a letter — the focus of Common Core L.2.2.b
Understand that the comma comes at the end of the greeting and closing, not before the name
Build the punctuation skills that letter and note writing depend on

about: Professor Pip the penguin is opening a new wing of the museum, and the treasures arrive on a conveyor belt: shapes that are turned, tiny, stretched or standing on a corner. Each pedestal carries a brass clasp in its own shape. The child drags a treasure to the pedestal that names it, or taps the treasure and then the pedestal. Treasures that fit no pedestal go through the doorway of the Mystery Gallery. It is an interactive Kindergarten geometry activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is the clasp. Nothing is judged while the child sorts; at Check every clasp closes round its treasure and only holds a shape that truly is its shape, however it is turned and however small it is. A treasure that does not fit rides back to the belt wearing a ghost of its own clasp: sides of equal length in the same colour, square corners marked with a lock, a gap where a figure is open and a bent rod where a side is curved, so the child sees what really makes it different. A second miss makes the right pedestal glow for the treasure the child picks up. The look-alikes are deliberate: a rhombus beside the square, an oval beside the circle, a pentagon beside the hexagon, an open square, a rectangle with rounded corners.

It is aligned to Common Core K.G.A.2: correctly naming shapes regardless of their orientation or overall size. The last round of the shape hall ends with counting: when every clasp has closed, the child sets how many triangles and how many squares now stand in the hall. In the hall of solids, each pedestal shows an everyday object such as a ball, a dice, a can or a book in a wire cage, and the child brings each solid, standing, lying or turned, to the object with the same shape; cones, pyramids and any solid with no matching object belong in the Mystery Gallery. Teachers choose the hall and whether the plates show the names or riddles. No timer, no score.
practices: Naming shapes that are turned, tiny, stretched or upside down
Using sides and corners to decide what a shape is
Telling real shapes from look-alikes: a rhombus, an oval, an open square
Matching spheres, cubes, cylinders and boxes to everyday objects
howToPlay: Drag a treasure from the belt to a pedestal, or tap the treasure and then the pedestal.
Put treasures that fit no pedestal in the Mystery Gallery.
Press Check and watch which clasps close.
In the last round, set how many triangles and squares there are with − and +.
learningGoals: Name shapes whatever their turn or size, the focus of Common Core K.G.A.2
Tell a shape from a look-alike by its sides and corners
Recognize the same solid in everyday objects

about: A street of five houses, each with a printed number plate over its door, and a post van with three letters. The address on every letter is written by hand — in the same hand children learn to write their numerals — while the plates are printed, so the child cannot match shapes: the number has to be read. The child drags each letter to a house; it goes through one slot only. When the right door opens, the neighbour steps onto the doorstep, the number is spoken, and the next letter pops up. When the third letter is posted, the round checks itself. An interactive Kindergarten numeral-reading activity that runs in the browser on tablets, phones and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is reading numerals 0 to 20 as numbers, not as pictures. Every street carries the mix-ups young readers make: 13 lives next to 31, so the order of the digits matters; 14 sits among 13 and 11, so the last digit has to be read; 14 stands beside 4, so one digit is not two; and 6 sits near 9, 2 near 5, 1 near 7. A wrong door answers with its own number beside the letter's and names the slip — the same digits the other way round, look at the last digit, two digits not one — and after two misses the right plate glows. Settings keep the numbers to 10 for a class that is starting, or switch the address from written to spoken so the child listens for the number, with a Show button for a quiet room.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.3 — reading written numerals from 0 to 20. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Read written numerals 0 to 20, including zero and the teen numbers
Tell 13 from 31: the order of the digits changes the number
Tell 14 from 13 and 14 from 4: read the last digit, and count the digits
Read a handwritten number and find it in print
howToPlay: Take the letter from the van and read the number written on it.
Drag it to the house whose plate shows that number — it only fits through that letterbox.
Post all three letters; the round checks itself and Next brings a new street.
learningGoals: Read numerals 0 to 20 — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.3
Understand that 13 and 31 are different numbers because digit order matters
Recognise a number whether it is handwritten or printed

about: Tuck the hamster has a vice that only locks shut on a perfect square. Behind its bed stands a square plate ruled into ten stripes, and a ten-rod is exactly as long as the square is wide. The child taps the tens column to lay rods on the bed and cranks the handle: the jaw comes down onto the stack, and its catch drops into the notch only when the stack is exactly ten rods high. Out comes a hundred-flat, which slides into the hundreds column.

For 160 + 50 there are eleven tens. Nine rods leave one bare stripe and the vice will not lock; eleven stick out over the top. Ten lock into a hundred and one rod stays behind, so the total is 210. For 320 + 80 the tens make exactly ten, and the tens box gets a 0: 400. The child types the total into three boxes under the columns, and Check will not take a column that still holds ten or more, because one digit cannot describe it. After a miss each column counts its pieces in hundreds, tens or ones; after a second miss the right digits appear in pencil and the written sum shows its carried 1. Other settings offer sums where nothing reaches ten (34 + 25 = 59) and sums where both the ones and the tens trade (268 + 157 = 425), and a written column sum can be shown beside the blocks.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.7: add within 1000 using models and place value, understanding that sometimes you compose a hundred or a ten. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Adding within 1000 when the tens add up to ten or more.
Trading ten tens for one hundred, and ten ones for one ten.
Seeing why a column with ten or more pieces cannot be written with one digit.
Matching the carried 1 in a written sum to the hundred made in the vice.
howToPlay: Tap a column to move its pieces into Tuck's vice one at a time (press and hold for a handful), then crank the handle down — it locks only on exactly ten.
Type the total in the three boxes under the columns, then press Check.
In the settings, choose sums with no trading, tens that make a hundred, or ones and tens that both trade, and show or hide the written sum.
learningGoals: Add within 1000 with regrouping — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.B.7.
Understand that ten tens make exactly one hundred, and ten ones one ten.
Connect the carried 1 in written addition to a real hundred.

about: Every column of Tuck's bench has a mat with exactly ten wells, and the tenth well hangs out over that column's answer box. The first number is already on the bench; the child brings the second number's blocks over from the bin. When a mat is full, its tenth block lies on the answer box, so the digit cannot be written. The child rolls the full mat up into one ten and it lands on the shelf next door, where the little 1 appears in the written sum. Tapping the shelf drops the ten into that column's mat.

The answer boxes open by themselves from right to left: a box opens only when its own column and every column to its right are settled. So the ones are written first because of how the bench works, not because of a rule. In take-away rounds the child takes blocks away, and when a column has too few, pulls one down from next door: the ten unrolls into a full mat of ten, and in a column sum the digit is crossed out and rewritten.

Settings: + one digit (like 27 + 5), two digits or three digits, and add, take away or both. A wrong digit makes its column light up so the child can count what is left there; a second wrong try points to the two halves of five on each mat. Tuck keeps a little stack of every ten the child rolled up. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.C.4, with the column method for two- and three-digit numbers. No timer and no score.
practices: Adding a two-digit and a one-digit number when the ones make ten or more
Rolling ten ones into one ten and carrying it to the tens
Writing the column method ones first, with the carried 1
Taking away by unrolling a ten when there are too few ones
howToPlay: Tap the bin to bring the blocks over, one at a time (hold to pour).
When a mat is full, roll it up: the ten jumps to the shelf next door. Tap the shelf to put it in.
Tap an answer box that is open, type the answer and press Check.
To take away, tap a mat. If a column runs out, use the arrow to pull one down from next door.
In the settings, choose the numbers (+ one digit, two digits, three digits) and add, take away or both.
learningGoals: Add within 100 by composing a ten when the ones make ten or more — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.C.4.
Understand the carried 1 as a real ten moved to the tens.
Add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers in columns, ones first.
Take away by breaking a ten into ten ones when needed.

about: In Tuck the hamster's stock room a hundred is a crate packed with ten boxes, and every box is packed with ten cubes — you can see them through a window in the crate and as outlines on each box's lid. Each round is a customer's order: an order slip with one empty cell for every crate, box or cube that is taken away. The child can only open what lies on a shelf: a crate opens into ten boxes on the tens shelf, never into loose cubes, and a box opens into ten cubes on the ones shelf.

For 302 − 5 there are two cubes and no boxes at all. The slip wants five cubes, so after two the ones shelf is empty. A crate must open first, then one of its boxes: nine boxes and twelve cubes, five go on the slip, and what is left is 297. A child who writes 307 has taken ten ones out of nowhere; the two crates and nine boxes left on the shelves show why. After a miss, each shelf with a wrong digit counts what is left in hundreds, tens or ones; after a second miss the written subtraction appears with its marks — the 3 crossed out to a 2, 10 written over the 0 and crossed out to 9, and 12 over the 2. The other setting takes away a three-digit number, such as 400 − 136 = 264, and the written subtraction can stay on the screen, writing each mark as its package opens.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.7: subtract within 1000 using models and place value, understanding that sometimes a hundred is decomposed into ten tens and a ten into ten ones. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Subtracting within 1000 when the tens place is zero.
Opening a hundred into ten tens, and then a ten into ten ones.
Seeing why nine tens are left after taking a few ones from a number with no tens.
Matching each crossed-out digit in a written subtraction to a package that opened.
howToPlay: Tap the cubes to put them on Tuck's order slip (press and hold for a handful), or drag any piece onto the slip. Not enough? Tap a crate to open it into ten boxes, then tap a box to open it into ten cubes.
When the slip is full, type what is left on the shelves in the three boxes under them, then press Check.
In the settings, take away a few ones or a three-digit number, and show or hide the written subtraction.
learningGoals: Subtract within 1000 with regrouping across a zero — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.B.7.
Understand that a hundred holds ten tens and each ten holds ten ones.
Connect the crossed-out digits of written subtraction to real regrouping.

about: In this activity the number you take away is a scoop: a tray built to match it — one cup for every one, a long slot for every ten, a square slot for every hundred. Held over Tuck the hamster's shelves, its cups light up where they find a block underneath, and the scoop only lifts when every cup is full. Then it carries its number away to Tuck's bowl, and the child types what is left on the shelves.

For 342 − 5 the ones shelf holds only two cubes, so two cups light up, three stay dark, and the scoop will not lift. The child taps a ten on the tens shelf: it snaps like a chocolate bar into ten cubes, and now all five cups are full. The scoop lifts five away and 337 is left. A child who answers 343 has taken the smaller digit from the bigger one — but the scoop always takes its own five, so that answer never lies on the shelves. After a miss, each shelf with a wrong digit counts what is left; after a second miss the shelves count on from the biggest pieces to the last cube, and the written subtraction shows its marks: the 4 crossed out and replaced by 3, and 12 written over the 2. A warm-up setting has take-aways with nothing to snap, such as 58 − 23 = 35, and the bigger-numbers setting has bigger take-aways, such as 627 − 346 = 281, where a hundred must be snapped into ten tens.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.7: subtract within 1000 using models and place value, understanding that sometimes a ten is decomposed into ten ones or a hundred into ten tens. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Subtracting within 1000 when there are not enough ones.
Snapping a ten into ten ones, or a hundred into ten tens, only when it is needed.
Seeing why the smaller digit cannot simply be taken from the bigger one.
Matching the crossed-out digits of written subtraction to the snapped ten.
howToPlay: Tap the scoop, or drag it over the shelves, to lift its number away. If some cups stay empty, tap a ten (or a hundred) to snap it first.
Type what is left on the shelves in the three boxes under them, then press Check.
In the settings, choose nothing to snap, ones only, or bigger numbers, and show or hide the written subtraction.
learningGoals: Subtract within 1000 with regrouping — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.B.7.
Understand that a ten can be broken into ten ones and a hundred into ten tens.
Connect the crossed-out digits of written subtraction to real regrouping.

about: The Value-Key Adding Machine has a column of keys for each place, and every key is labelled with what it is worth: 100 to 900 in the hundreds, 10 to 90 in the tens, 1 to 9 in the ones. To make 247 the child presses 200, 40 and 7 and pulls the crank; the drums add the keys up and the paper tape prints 200 + 40 + 7 = 247. Making the number is writing its expanded form.

There is no zero key. A zero place is a column where nothing is pressed, so 305 is made with 300 and 5, and the tape prints 300 + 5. A key pressed in the empty place makes the drums show another number (355 instead of 305), and pressing 30 in the tens instead of 300 gives 35, not 305. In the other jobs the child presses the keys a set of blocks is worth, finds what one bright digit is worth (the 7 in 472 is worth 70), or picks which of three sets of rods and cubes shows a two-digit number. After a second miss the ticket opens into its places with each digit's blocks, the blocks are numbered, or the right column of keys lights up.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.A.3 (read and write numbers to 1000 in expanded form), and the tens-and-ones setting covers 1.NBT.B.2. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Write three-digit numbers in expanded form, such as 247 = 200 + 40 + 7
Leave out a zero place: 305 = 300 + 5
Read base-ten blocks as the values of their places
Say what a digit is worth in its place, such as the 7 in 472
howToPlay: Make: press one key in each place the number needs, then pull the crank or press Check, and read the tape.
Read the blocks and what is it worth: press the keys the blocks or the bright digit are worth. In which set?, tap the set that shows the ticket and the machine presses its keys by itself.
In the settings, choose tens and ones or hundreds, tens and ones, and the job.
learningGoals: Write a three-digit number as the sum of its hundreds, tens and ones — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.A.3.
Know that a zero place adds nothing and is left out of the expanded form.
Know that a digit is worth its face value times its place: the 7 in 472 is worth 70.

about: The Capped Mat is a place-value mat with three columns, hundreds, tens and ones, that only closes when every column wears a numeral cap. A cap holds one digit, so a column can take at most nine blocks: the tenth cube is refused, because ten ones make one ten. The child builds a number such as 604 with flats, rods and cubes, and at Check the caps drop onto the columns and read back exactly what was built.

The heart of it is the empty column. A column with no blocks still needs its 0 cap. Leave it bare and it folds shut, the other caps slide together, and 307 reads 37 on the screen. That is the mistake children make when they write numbers with a zero, made visible. In the read job the child caps a set of blocks, and in the match job she drags the number ticket onto the tray of blocks that shows it. After a second miss, outlines show the missing blocks, crosses mark the extra ones and a faint 0 cap appears on the empty column.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.A.1: the three digits of a three-digit number stand for amounts of hundreds, tens and ones, including numbers with a zero such as 307 and 604. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Build three-digit numbers with flats, rods and cubes
Read a set of base-ten blocks as a three-digit number
Use a 0 to show an empty place, as in 307 and 604
Match a number to the blocks that show it, even when the blocks lie out of order
howToPlay: Build: tap + and − under each column until the mat shows the number, then press Check and read the caps.
Read: tap a column's seat, then the cap with its digit; an empty column gets the 0 cap. With jumbled blocks, first tap each pile to put it in its column.
Match: drag the ticket onto the tray that shows the number, then press Check. In the settings, choose the job and tidy or jumbled blocks.
learningGoals: Understand that the digits of a three-digit number stand for hundreds, tens and ones — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.A.1.
Know that a place can hold at most nine, and that ten of one place make one of the next.
Write a 0 for an empty place and see why leaving it out changes the number.

about: Numbers are built from cards on a stand that is exactly two digits wide. A long tens card, such as 40, fills the whole stand; a short ones card, such as 7, only stays when it is laid on the 0 of the tens card. Then the 0 disappears under it, the stand reads 47, and four rods and seven cubes pour out onto the mat below. A ones card laid beside the tens card, or over its tens digit, tips off the stand, so 407 can never be made.

In the build rounds the number is shown as a numeral, in words, as tens and ones, as ten frames or as tally marks, and the child builds it with cards; some numbers can also be heard aloud. In read-the-blocks rounds the rods and cubes already lie on the mat and the child finds the cards that match them. In stretch rounds the child builds a number and pulls the ones card to the side, so 43 opens into 40 + 3, or pushes 60 + 7 back together into 67. In which-blocks rounds the cards are given and the child picks the tray of rods and cubes that shows them; the trays include the number with its digits swapped.

After a wrong try the half of the mat that differs lights up, the rods or the cubes; after a second, the number's own rods and cubes appear see-through beside the child's, and extra blocks are outlined. When a round is solved, the rods count themselves 10, 20, 30… and then the cubes. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.B.2. No timer and no score.
practices: Reading and building two-digit numbers as tens and ones
Seeing why 47 is written 4 then 7, not 40 then 7
Teen numbers as one ten and some ones, and 10, 20 … 90 as tens with no ones
Writing a number as tens + ones, such as 47 = 40 + 7
howToPlay: Tap a tens card and a ones card, or drag them onto the stand. The ones card stays only on the 0 of the tens card.
Tap a card on the stand to take it back. Build the number and press Check.
In stretch rounds, drag the ones card to the side or press ⟷ to pull the number apart, and again to push it together.
In which-blocks rounds, tap the tray that shows the cards, then press Check.
In the settings, choose the task (build it · read the blocks · stretch it · which blocks?) and the numbers (to 20, to 50 or to 99).
learningGoals: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for tens and ones — the focus of Common Core 1.NBT.B.2.
Build a number from its name, its tens and ones, ten frames or tally marks.
See that 11 to 19 are one ten and some ones, and that 10, 20 … 90 have no ones.
Write a number as tens plus ones and put it back together.

about: Foot becomes feet, mouse becomes mice, and child becomes children — but deer and sheep stay exactly the same. At Pearl's Doubling Pond, the child reads a word and taps its correct plural, resisting the pull of the ordinary '-s' ending, in an interactive Grade 2 grammar activity.

The big idea is that not every plural is made by adding -s. There are two wrong choices each time, and they pull in opposite directions: for 'mouse' the child sees 'mice', 'mouses' and 'mouse' — one has added an s that does not belong, and the other has changed nothing at all. Adding an s is the healthy over-application of a rule the child has just learned, so the round is not about avoiding a bad habit; it is about knowing which words are exceptions. The child has to know the special plural rather than reach for the default ending, which is the whole point of learning irregular plurals.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1.b — forming and using frequently occurring irregular plural nouns. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Form irregular plurals like feet, teeth, geese, men, women, and mice
Use the special plural 'children' for child
Recognize words that stay the same, like deer and sheep
Tell an added -s apart from the plural a word actually takes
howToPlay: Read the question, like "What is the plural of “mouse”?"
Tap the form that means more than one. A wrong tap dims that choice and you pick again.
Not quite? Try again — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Form and use frequently occurring irregular plural nouns — the focus of Common Core L.2.1.b
Understand that some nouns change their spelling or stay the same instead of adding -s
Build the plural-noun knowledge that careful writing depends on

about: Three creatures look out of Lumen's lighthouse: one from a high window, one from the middle and one from the bottom. Tap a window and the harbor appears exactly as that creature sees it. From the top, the boat is a tiny dot far below; from the middle, it is straight across; from the bottom, it is so huge it is cut off by the frame. Lumen's Lighthouse Windows is a Grade 1 reading activity about who is telling a story.

The storyteller says "The boat looked like a tiny dot, far below me." Only one window's view matches those words, so the child finds the teller by reading. In Who tells each part?, three lines of one story are told by different creatures: "I flapped my wings and landed on the very top." can only be the gull's, because only the gull has wings. One creature may tell two parts.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.6: identify who is telling the story at various points in a text. No timer and no score.
practices: Use the words "I" and "me" to find who is telling
Match a storyteller's words to what they could see
Use a body clue to tell who says a line
Notice when the teller changes inside one story
howToPlay: Read what happened and what the storyteller says.
Tap a window to see the harbor through that creature's eyes, then press Check. Lumen's lamp shines on the right window.
Choose the task in the settings: From which window?, or Who tells each part?. The three views can also stay side by side for the whole class.
learningGoals: Identify who is telling the story at various points in a text, the focus of Common Core RL.1.6.
Use the storyteller's own words (tiny and far, straight across, huge and close) as evidence.
Know that one story can have more than one teller.

about: Pippa the frog runs a pond-juice stand where a customer orders by feel — "a dragonfly wants about six cups!" — and the child pours into a frosted beaker, then taps Pour or Look to reveal where the juice really landed on a 0-to-10 scale and taps that number. It's an interactive Grade 3 measurement activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The activity is built so reading the scale is the only thing being judged — not how carefully you pour. The level stays invisible during the pour, so there is no line to chase, and the answer is the revealed level, never the order: when the customer asks for 'about six' but the juice reaches 5, tapping 6 is wrong. Some rounds show two beakers — including a tall-thin one beside a short-wide one, or scales that go to 10 next to one that goes to 20 — so the bigger-looking cup is not always the one with more; the number decides.
It is aligned to Common Core 3.MD.A.2 — measuring and estimating liquid volumes using a scale. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Reading a liquid level off a numbered measuring scale, mark by mark
Telling an estimate ('about six') apart from the real measured amount
Comparing two amounts by their scale numbers, not by which container looks bigger
Reading scales that count by ones and by twos, including to 20
howToPlay: Read the order, then tap Pour or Look to reveal where the juice reached on the scale.
Read the number the juice reaches and tap it on the strip — or, with two beakers, tap the one that holds more.
Pour and serve another glass; there is no timer and no score, so you can read carefully each time.
learningGoals: Measure and estimate liquid volume by reading a scale — the focus of Common Core 3.MD.A.2
Understand that the measured level, not a guess or a container's shape, gives the amount
Build the careful scale-reading habit that later measurement and data work depend on

about: Posy packs her eggs in cartons of ten, and the child counts them the fast way. Tap each carton on the shelf and it gets a tag with the running total — 10, 20, 30 — so the fourth carton says 40 and the last carton tells how many eggs; then tap that number on the rail. In a packing round the shelf starts empty and the child adds cartons until the last one says the number asked for. It runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

A carton is drawn as a lidded tray with two rows of five egg cells, so one carton plainly stands for ten, not one. The tags make counting by tens visible: each carton wears the total so far, which is what counting by tens means. The two usual slips get their own help — tapping 10 as if the shelf held one egg per carton brings the reminder that a carton is ten eggs, and picking the wrong number is caught on the rail. Count again clears the tags for a second run.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.1 — counting to 100 by tens, both reading a group of tens and building one. No timer, no score — just calm, hands-on counting.
practices: Tagging each carton with the running total — 10, 20, 30 — instead of counting by ones
Reading the last carton as the total number of eggs
Packing a given number of eggs with cartons of ten
Building the ten-counting sequence up to 100
howToPlay: Tap each carton on the shelf. A tag with the next ten lands on it: 10, 20, 30…
When every carton has a tag, the last one tells how many eggs — tap that number on the rail and press Check.
In a packing round, add cartons from the crate until the last one says the number; tap a carton to take one off. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Count to 100 by tens — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.1
See that a carton of ten is counted as ten, and the last carton names the total
Build a number of eggs from cartons of ten

about: In Hattie's hat shop every person is a wooden prism with three faces: the doer (he), the one the action lands on (him) and the owner (his). A name block says who the gap stands for, with a thread down to the gap. The child lays a prism in the gap and turns it until the right face is up. The Borrowed Hat is a Grade 1 grammar activity about personal and possessive pronouns.

Check fires the sentence's action arrow. In "Pat saw him at the park" the arrow flies from saw and lands in the face with the target; in "He ran to the den" it flies out of the face with the bow; in "That is his red ball" a string from ball ties to the face with the knot. The wrong person or the wrong face lets the arrow drop. Later levels add I, me, my and we, us, our (with the "Sam and I" trap), swapping a name for a prism, tying a pronoun to the names it stands for, sorting names into he, she and they, and owner words on their own: mine, hers, theirs.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.d (use personal, possessive and indefinite pronouns); this activity practises personal and possessive pronouns. No timer and no score.
practices: Choose he, she or they for the person on the name block
Use he when the person does it, him when it happens to them, his when it is theirs
Use I and me correctly next to another name
Tell which name a pronoun stands for
howToPlay: Read the name block: who does the gap stand for?
Tap a prism to lay it in the gap and press the round button to turn it, then press Check.
In the settings, choose the level and whether the faces show their bow, target and knot.
learningGoals: Use personal pronouns for one person or more.
Choose the doer, done-to or owner form by the job in the sentence.
Link a pronoun to the name it stands for.

about: Rhyme lives in the ear, so this activity turns it into something a child can hold. Rosa the raccoon pulls a wagon with a chain of rings behind it. The child taps a picture to hear its name, then drags it to the end of the chain, or taps it and then the empty ring. It is an interactive listening activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install; headphones help.

The invention is the ring itself: a ring only closes on a ring whose word ends with the same sound. Whale closes on snail, and both rings glow the same pattern; bee springs its ring open and drops back onto the grass. The chain judges by sound, never by spelling, so bear and ear, which look alike in print, do not link, while snail and whale do. After a second slip every ring shows its pattern, so the child can see which sounds belong together.

It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.a: recognizing and producing rhyming words. The rounds mix seven kinds of rhyme work: deciding whether two words rhyme, picking the rhyme from three pictures, finding the one that does not rhyme, sorting pictures onto two chains, finishing Rosa's rhyming line, finding every rhyme in a group, and building a rhyme chain. After each chain an open ring invites the child to say a new rhyming word aloud. Teachers can show each picture's name and the patterns from the start. No timer, no score.
practices: Hearing whether two words rhyme
Picking the rhyming word from three pictures
Spotting the word that does not rhyme
Saying a new word that rhymes
howToPlay: Tap a picture to hear its name.
Drag it to the end of Rosa's chain, or tap it and then the empty ring.
A ring that rhymes closes; one that does not falls back onto the grass.
When the chain is finished, pull the wagon.
learningGoals: Recognize rhyming words by their ending sound, the focus of Common Core RF.K.2.a
Tell a rhyme from words that are only spelled alike or only start alike
Say a new word that rhymes

about: A glass jar of toys with an empty label on its lid. The child counts — every toy takes a mark when it is tapped — and writes how many on the number keys; the digits appear on the label. Check lays the label against the jar: the toys file into as many places as the label says, and if the label is right it turns gold and sticks while the number is spoken. In the other kind of round the label is already written and the jar is empty: the child taps toys on the shelf to drop them in until the jar holds that many. An interactive Kindergarten counting-and-writing activity that runs in the browser on tablets, phones and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is the two-way link in numeral work: a count of things becomes a written number, and a written number becomes a count of things. Up to ten the toys sit loosely; from eleven to twenty they stand in rows, so the eye can keep its place. A wrong label is answered by the jar, not by a cross: a label too small leaves toys standing without a place, a label too big leaves empty dashed places, and the slip is named — the digits the other way round (41 for 14) or only the ones (4 for 14). Settings keep the numbers to 10 for a class that is starting, or choose only the counting rounds or only the filling rounds.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.3 — writing numbers to 20 and representing a number of objects with a written numeral. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count a set of up to 20 toys, keeping track with a mark on each one
Write the numeral that tells how many, including the teen numbers
Read a numeral and put that many toys in the jar
Check a written number against the real count and see where it is off
howToPlay: Tap each toy as you count it, then write how many on the number keys.
Press Check: if the label is right, it sticks; if not, the jar shows the toys left over or the places still empty.
When the label is already written, tap toys on the shelf until the jar holds that many; Next brings a new jar.
learningGoals: Write numbers to 20 and represent a count with a written numeral — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.3
Understand that 14 and 41 are different numbers
Move both ways between a group of objects and the number that names it

about: Roary the lion's roar can be soft or mighty, and so can words: shown big, large, huge, the child taps the strongest one — or, in other rounds, the weakest. It's an interactive Grade 2 vocabulary activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is shades of meaning: near-synonyms are not interchangeable, because some are stronger than others. Across the rounds children rank heat (warm, hot, boiling), loudness (talk, shout, scream), tiredness (tired, sleepy, exhausted), and feeling words like good/great/amazing, like/love/adore, and sad/upset/miserable. The prompt switches between asking for the strongest and the weakest, so a child has to think about the whole little scale rather than reaching for one habit answer.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.5.b — distinguishing shades of meaning among closely related words. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Ranking three near-synonyms from weakest to strongest in meaning
Picking the strongest word in a set — like huge over big and large
Picking the weakest word when the prompt asks for it
Noticing that similar words carry different amounts of strength
howToPlay: Read the three words, which all mean nearly the same thing.
Tap the strongest one — or the weakest one, depending on what Roary asks.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Distinguish shades of meaning among related words — the focus of Common Core L.2.5.b
Understand that near-synonyms can be milder or stronger than one another
Build the word-choice sense that makes speaking and writing more precise

about: Robin holds up a mirror to show how a reflexive pronoun points right back at the doer: "Mia poured the juice ___" or "I made this card all by ___," and the child taps the word that matches the subject — herself, myself, themselves. It's an interactive Grade 2 grammar activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The whole idea is agreement: the reflexive pronoun has to match who the subject is — Mia takes herself, Sam takes himself, I takes myself, the twins take themselves, and the cat takes itself. The choices are all reflexive words but only one matches the subject, so a child cannot pick by 'which one is a real word'; they have to read who is acting and choose the mirror-word that points back to that same person or thing.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1.c — using reflexive pronouns correctly. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Matching a reflexive pronoun to the subject of the sentence
Choosing herself, himself, myself, themselves, ourselves, yourself, or itself correctly
Reading who is doing the action before picking the mirror-word
Understanding that a reflexive pronoun points back to the doer
howToPlay: Read the sentence with the blank in it.
Tap the reflexive word — myself, herself, themselves, and friends — that matches who is acting.
A warm check confirms a correct match and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use reflexive pronouns correctly — the focus of Common Core L.2.1.c
Understand that a reflexive pronoun must agree with the subject
Build the grammar foundation for clearer speaking and writing

about: Rusty the robot's machine turns today's verbs into yesterday's: shown go, the child taps went — never 'goed.' Each round offers the real irregular past beside the tempting made-up '-ed' form, in an interactive Grade 2 grammar activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is that some common verbs are irregular: they do not just add -ed to talk about the past. Each round shows three choices — the correct irregular past (went, ran, ate, saw, gave, took, came, swam), the present-tense word itself, and the tempting made-up '-ed' form (goed, runned, eated, seed, gived, taked, comed, swimmed). Because the made-up form is right there, a child has to know the real past-tense word rather than reaching for the regular -ed pattern.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1.d — forming and using frequently occurring irregular past-tense verbs. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Forming the past tense of irregular verbs like go, run, and eat
Telling the real past-tense word apart from a made-up -ed form
Resisting the over-regularized 'goed' or 'runned' habit
Connecting a present-tense verb to its yesterday form
howToPlay: Read the verb and think about how to say it about yesterday.
Tap the correct past-tense word — like went or ran — not the present word or the -ed look-alike.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Form and use common irregular past-tense verbs — the focus of Common Core L.2.1.d
Understand that some verbs do not follow the add-ed pattern
Build the grammar foundation for correct past-tense speaking and writing

about: Sage the tortoise grows word families from one root: from farm the child taps the bigger word that grows out of it — farmer — while dodging look-alikes like former and forest. It's an interactive Grade 2 vocabulary activity that runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is using a known root as a clue to a word's meaning: farm grows into farmer, help into helper, paint into painting, care into careful, play into player, teach into teacher. The two wrong choices are deliberately tricky look-alikes and sound-alikes — former and forest beside farmer, hammer and hello beside helper, pointing and planting beside painting — so a child cannot win on the first few letters; they have to find the word that truly contains the whole root.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.4.c — using a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word in the same family. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Recognizing the smaller root word inside a bigger word
Choosing the word that grows from a given root, like player from play
Telling a true root-family word apart from look-alikes and sound-alikes
Using a familiar root as a clue to a new word's meaning
howToPlay: Read the root word at the start of the round.
Tap the bigger word that grows from it, watching out for words that only look or sound alike.
A warm check confirms a correct choice and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Use a known root word as a clue to a related word's meaning — the focus of Common Core L.2.4.c
Understand that words grow into families from a shared root
Build the word-analysis habit that vocabulary growth depends on

about: A sentence is a script, and a little toy theatre acts it out word by word. The word with the capital letter opens the curtain, a number word lights that many spotlights, a describing word makes the light big or small or gives it a colour, the naming word brings the actor on, the doing word makes it act, and the full stop closes the curtain.

The child taps the scrambled words onto the script line and presses Check. If a word is in the wrong place, the show freezes right there and that word flickers: in "The dog big runs." the dog has already walked on, and "big" has nothing left to describe. Only "The big dog runs." plays to the end, with a bow. Later the child finds the start and the end, asks and shouts ("Can the cat jump?", "The dog runs so fast!"), and at last writes a sentence about a photo, such as "The yellow duck walks.", and sees whether the stage shows what the photo shows.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.j: produce and expand complete simple sentences, statements, questions and exclamations. No timer and no score.
practices: Start a sentence with a capital letter and end it with an end mark
Put a naming word and a doing word in every sentence
Put scrambled words into the order the language uses
Write a true sentence about a picture
howToPlay: Tap a word and it goes onto the first empty place of the script line; tap it there to send it back.
Press Check and watch the stage act out your sentence; it stops at the first word that is out of place.
In the settings, choose the sentences (from "With clues" to "About the photo") and the speed of the show.
learningGoals: Build complete sentences with someone and what they do.
Use capital letters, full stops, question marks and exclamation marks.
Check a sentence against a picture.

about: Gentle Dr. Plume's patients are muddled sentences, each with one ailment — a missing capital in "my dog is happy," no end mark after "The sun is hot," or "She run to school" — and the child finds the trouble and makes the repair. It's an interactive Grade 2 grammar activity that runs in the browser with no account.

Each round practices a different convention, so children meet the real range of fixes: capitalizing the first word, adding the right end mark (a period, not a comma or question mark), correcting subject-verb agreement (run to runs), adding a missing verb ("The cat ___ milk" to drinks), reordering jumbled words into "The dog runs fast," removing an extra word in "My mom she cooks," and splitting a run-on into two sentences. The wrong options are real near-misses, so the child has to diagnose what is actually wrong.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1 — demonstrating command of standard English grammar and usage. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Capitalizing the first word and ending a telling sentence with a period
Fixing subject-verb agreement, like 'She runs' instead of 'She run'
Adding a missing verb and removing an extra or repeated word
Reordering jumbled words and splitting a run-on into two sentences
howToPlay: Read the muddled sentence and find what is wrong.
Make the repair — capitalize, add a mark or word, fix the verb, reorder, delete, or split.
A warm check confirms a correct fix and offers an easy retry, with no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Apply the conventions of standard English grammar and usage — the focus of Common Core L.2.1
Recognize and repair common sentence problems in writing
Build the editing habit that clear writing depends on

about: Tilly's ribbons live in places that can never meet: one hangs from a hook, one lies on a high shelf, one lies on the counter, and each starts somewhere else. So the eye cannot line them up, and the hanging one often looks longer than it is. The same cord, always the same length, is carried to each ribbon: its clip goes on the ribbon's start pin, it lies along the ribbon, and it leaves a tag that shows shorter than the cord, just as long, or longer.

In the mixed rounds the child finds the longest, the shortest or the ribbon just as long as the cord; in the order rounds the child puts the three on a rail, shortest first. In every round exactly one ribbon is longer than the cord, or shorter, or just as long, so the tags alone decide: longer than the cord, and the cord longer than another, means longer than that one too. Tall things work the same way: three candles or three bottles stand on a stool, a box and a high shelf, and the cord is held up from each one's foot, so the one that reaches highest is not always the tallest.

Check works once the cord has been to all three. After a wrong try the hint points back to the tags; after a second, the ribbons' three tags line up: shorter, just as long, longer. When a round is solved, Tilly's reveal lays the three ribbons side by side from one pin with the cord beneath them, and tall things all step down to the floor, exactly as the tags said. No numbers and no rulers. Aligned to Common Core 1.MD.A.1. No timer and no score.
practices: Comparing two lengths through a third object that stays the same
Ordering three objects by length, shortest first
Seeing that where a thing starts and which way it lies change how long it looks, not how long it is
Comparing heights from each object's own foot
howToPlay: Tap the cord's basket, then tap a ribbon, or drag the cord from the basket to the ribbon's start. The tag shows shorter, just as long or longer than the cord.
Do it for each ribbon, then tap your answer and press Check.
In order rounds, tap a ribbon and then a step on the rail, or drag it there: the shortest goes on the first step.
With tall things, the cord is held up beside each one from its foot.
In the settings, choose the question (Longest, shortest, as long · Put in order) and the things (Ribbons · Tall things).
learningGoals: Compare the lengths of two objects indirectly, using a third object — the focus of Common Core 1.MD.A.1.
Order three objects by length.
Judge length from the start to the end, not by where an object sits or which way it points.
Compare the heights of things standing at different levels.

about: Pesto's stove knob has a word on every click. Turn it up and the flame grows one tongue per click, while the soup in the pot takes the strength of the WORD on that click. When the words stand in the right order (warm, hot, boiling), flame and soup rise together; a word in the wrong place makes the soup jump, so the child sees which word to move.

There are four things to do: order a ladder of close words from a little to a lot; read an order ticket and turn the knob to the word it needs, or find the word that goes between two others; put twin words that mean the same on one click; and sort going words and looking words onto two knobs, each by how fast or how long. The soup colours can stay hidden until the knob is turned up, so the order has to come from reading.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.5.d: distinguish shades of meaning among verbs and adjectives that differ in manner or intensity. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Put close words in order from a little to a lot
Choose the word of just the right strength for a sentence
Find words that mean the same
Tell going and looking words apart by how fast or how long
howToPlay: Tap a word, then a click on the knob (or drag the word there). Press Turn it up.
Where the soup jumps, a word is in the wrong place: swap it and try again.
In the settings, choose what to do, three or four words on the knob, and whether the soup colours show all the time.
learningGoals: Order words by strength.
Choose the word that fits a sentence best.
Recognise words that mean the same.

about: Mim the glow-smith fills lanterns with coloured glass. Behind every empty frame a lamp is burning, so every gap between the pieces shines as a bright gold sliver, and every piece that sticks out of the frame throws a dark shadow on the workshop wall. The lantern only glows when it is sealed: no light gets through and nothing sticks out. The child builds rhombuses, trapezoids, triangles, hexagons and a long bar from pattern blocks, picks the one piece that fills a hole exactly, and builds tangram shapes.

Some rounds ask for the same lantern a new way: the lines of the last one stay faintly in the frame, and a filling along the same lines does not count. In the missing-piece rounds size matters as much as shape: a small triangle leaves a gap of light in a medium hole. In the shadow rounds, a tangram pane that is turned or flipped leaks on one side and throws a shadow on the other. After a first miss the lamp blazes every gap; after a second, a dotted piece shows one piece that fits. A sealed lantern keeps its seams etched in silver and rises to the garland, and the child can take it apart and build it again.
The first hint only says what the light shows; after a second miss the lamp points to one piece that fits. Aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.2 and K.G.B.6. No timer and no score.
practices: Putting shapes together to fill a bigger shape exactly: no gaps, no overlaps, nothing sticking out
Building the same shape in more than one way
Seeing a big shape as smaller shapes and the lines where they meet
Choosing a piece by its shape and its size, and turning or flipping it to fit
howToPlay: Drag a glass piece from the tray into the lantern. Tap a piece in the tray to choose it, and tap it again to turn it.
Tap a piece in the lantern to turn it. Drag it off the bench to put it back in the tray.
Gold light means a gap; a shadow on the wall means a piece sticks out. Press Check when the lantern looks sealed.
In "The missing piece", drag in the one spare that fills the hole. In "Tangram", build the shape, or slide the pane that matches the shadow into the frame.
In the settings, choose the level (Glass pieces · The missing piece · Tangram), clear or coloured glass, and whether pieces turn themselves to fit.
learningGoals: Compose two-dimensional shapes into a larger shape that is filled exactly.
Compose the same shape in different ways and compare the lines where the pieces meet.
Choose the piece that fits a gap by its shape and its size.
Turn or flip a piece so it fits a fixed outline, and see that the wrong turn leaves a gap and sticks out.

about: Pim the hedgehog and Bo the mouse each have a glass jar of beads, and a gold ribbon is tied across both jars at the fair height. The child says a number first by tapping a tile, then presses Check, and exactly that many beads move. The right number stops the beads on the ribbon and the two friends lean in. Too few leaves a gap under the ribbon or beads still above it; too many pushes past the ribbon, and now the other friend has less.

There are five kinds of story: how many more one jar needs (3 + □ = 5), how many more one friend has (6 − 2 = □), how many Pim must give back (7 − □ = 4), how many go back in the pile (6 − □ = 4), and how many Bo had at the start (□ + 4 = 7). In a start round the child’s number tints that many beads from the bottom, and they must meet the glowing new beads exactly. After a second try, the beads that were missing or too many are numbered, so the child can count the difference.

Clear jars go to 10; frosted jars go to 20, with each jar’s number on its lid and the frost wiping clear on Check. Tap a jar to light its beads one by one. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.D.8. No timer and no score.
practices: Finding the unknown number in an addition or subtraction story: the part to add, the difference, the number taken away or the starting number
Comparing two amounts and making them equal
Counting on from the smaller amount to the larger one
Checking an answer by seeing what that many beads actually do
howToPlay: Read the question and look at the two jars and the gold ribbon.
Tap the number tile you think is right, then press Check.
Watch the beads: they stop on the ribbon when the number is right. If there is a gap, or beads go past the ribbon, choose another number and check again.
Tap a jar to light its beads one by one and count them.
In the settings, choose the jars (clear, to 10, or frosted, to 20) and the stories (all kinds, or only “how many more”).
learningGoals: Find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction story, wherever it is
Understand “how many more” as the difference between two amounts
Make two amounts equal by adding to one or taking from the other
Work out a starting amount from what was added and the total

about: Every lily pad in the pond shows its number on split-flaps, like an old station board. The empty pad arrives showing the number Hopper the frog is sitting on, and the child flips it forward by one hop. A hop of 10 flips the tens flap and a hop of 100 the hundreds flap, so the place that changes is right there to see.

The flaps never carry. Going from 95 to 100, flipping the ones flap past 9 leaves the tens alone, so the child has to flip the tens and the hundreds as well, which is exactly the regrouping in a count. A wrong pad brings up a leap meter: Hopper's hop says +5, and the child's hop says +1 or −5. On a second try, the pad before lines up above the flaps with the hop written under its place. Chains that start at their own step, such as 10, 20, 30, sit on a number line from 0 with a group of dots on every pad, and the find-the-hop rounds ask the child to set Hopper's sign, for example +25 or −50.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.A.2: count within 1000 and skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s. The settings add counting by 2s, 3s and 4s, and by 25s, 50s and 100s, forward and back. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s within 1000
Count forward and backward from any number
Cross a ten or a hundred while counting
Find the size of each hop in a pattern
howToPlay: Tap the top of a flap to flip it forward and the bottom to flip it back.
Make the empty pad show the next number in the chain and press Check.
In the settings, choose what to count by and whether the chain also goes down.
learningGoals: Skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s, forward and back.
See that adding 10 changes the tens and adding 100 changes the hundreds.
Regroup when a count crosses a ten or a hundred, such as 95, 100.

about: The child writes a letter, and the letter is recorded as it is written. Then it plays back next to Snippy's letter, and the snail on the rail under the two pads is the knob of both replays: drag Snippy back and forth and the two letters un-write and re-write themselves in step.

The rail fills with one colour band for each stroke, the child's on the top track and Snippy's below. When the letter was made the same way, the two tracks match. A stroke that went the other way carries arrows pointing back, and strokes written in another order show their colours in another order. A wobbly letter with the right start, the right direction and the right order counts as a perfect letter.

Each letter has three steps: first with numbered dots and arrows on the road, then with the road only, then on your own, with every start dot shown but no road and no numbers.
