Only the last step is checked. Lowercase and capitals come in eight families, from "Snippy's letters" to "Capitals: the right way round". Aligned to Common Core L.K.1.a. No timer and no score.
practices: Starting each letter at the right point
Moving the right way along every stroke
Writing the strokes of a letter in the right order
Writing a letter from memory after tracing it
howToPlay: Start at dot 1 and follow the arrows, then follow the road, then write the letter on your own.
Press "Check" and watch your letter play back next to Snippy's. Drag Snippy along the rail to see it again.

Under "Letters" choose a family such as "Round and down" or "Capitals: curves", and under "Steps" choose "On my own only". On a tablet or computer, tap a letter in the row at the bottom to watch Snippy write it.
learningGoals: The child starts each letter at the correct point
The child moves in the right direction and writes the strokes in the right order
The child writes lowercase and capital letters from memory

about: Shadow stands inside a dark cupboard and cannot see the coral ring Sock has stuck on the glass. The child is Sock's voice: every word they say lights up only the things it fits, and the little door in the curtain lets just one thing through. Saying what you mean so that a listener who cannot see your world understands it is the heart of speaking clearly.

The cupboard pushes back on the two real reasons young speakers are misunderstood. Say too little (“the car” when there are three cars) and every car stays lit, and two jam side by side in the door. Say too much and Shadow's three memory pegs fill up: one bead too many knocks the first word off, and the cupboard lights up again. A word that fits nothing turns every lamp off.

Two kinds of rounds: Fetch it (tap a thing to say its name, then add the word that tells it apart: big, small, on the top shelf, next to…) and Tell how you feel (tap the face that shows Sock's feeling and add the reason, “I feel sad because it is raining”, so Shadow can hold up the face and bring the right help). Aligned to Common Core SL.K.6: express thoughts, feelings and ideas clearly. Saying the words out loud is practised with a grown-up. No timer and no score.
practices: Naming the thing you mean
Adding the one detail that tells it apart
Saying just enough words, not too many
Saying a feeling together with its reason
howToPlay: Tap a thing in the cupboard to say its name. Tap the word cards (big, small, on the top shelf, next to…) to add a detail. Watch which lamps stay on.
Press the speaking tube to tell Shadow. One lit thing slides through the door; if two are still lit, they jam. Tap a word in your sentence to take it back.
In “Tell how you feel”, tap the face that shows how Sock feels, then add a “because…” card. Shadow holds up the face and brings the help.
In the settings, choose the round types, give Shadow a memory of 3 or 2 words, and choose whether the lamps light up as you tap or only after you speak.
learningGoals: Speak so that a listener who cannot see understands which thing you mean
Use size and position words to tell things apart
Express a feeling and give its reason in one sentence
Notice when a message is too short or too long

about: Every shape here is built like a construction kit: straight wooden sticks joined at brass corners. Tap a shape and it comes apart on a tray. Its sticks line up from the longest to the shortest, and its corners drop into cups. A triangle is always three straight sticks and three full cups, however it is turned, painted, stretched or squeezed. The child sorts real triangles, four-sided shapes, pentagons, hexagons and circles from look-alikes, names a shape, or solves a shape riddle.

The look-alikes are the cases that trip children up. A triangle with one bent side drops a bent stick. A triangle that is not closed leaves one cup empty. A circle has one round hoop and no cups at all. Upside-down, tiny and skinny triangles are real triangles, and an L shape can be a hexagon. After a first miss, the misplaced shape lies taken apart on the tray. After a second, the shape the box asks for lies beside it, stick for stick. When every shape is right, the box closes and its shapes come apart into equal bundles of sticks. A paint pot, a turn knob and a stretch handle then let the child try to change a shape, and the sticks stay the same.
Hints ask about the sticks and never give the answer. Aligned to Common Core 1.G.A.1. No timer and no score.
practices: Telling a shape by what it is made of: closed, straight sides, how many
Seeing that colour, size and turning do not change a shape
Spotting look-alikes: open shapes, bent sides, one side too many
Naming triangles, squares, rectangles, pentagons, hexagons, circles and half-circles
howToPlay: Tap a shape to take it apart on the tray, and tap it again to put it back together.
Drag each shape into a box, or tap a shape and then tap a box.
Press Check. A shape in the wrong box comes apart on the tray, and a question about its sticks helps you look again.
In "Name it", tap the name of the shape. In "Riddles", put the shape that fits the riddle in the frame.
In the settings, choose the level (Real or not? · Name it · Riddles), whether the tray is open or only used as help, and 6 or 4 shapes.
learningGoals: Tell defining attributes (closed, number of straight sides) from non-defining ones (colour, size, turn).
Recognise triangles, four-sided shapes, pentagons and hexagons in any position and size.
Explain why an open shape or a shape with a bent side is not a triangle.
Tell a square from a rectangle and a rhombus by its side lengths and square corners.

about: Each round drops a jumble of shapes — right and obtuse triangles, squares, rhombuses, irregular pentagons and hexagons — and the child counts the sides of each and drags it into the matching bin. It's an interactive Grade 2 geometry activity that plays in the browser with no sign-up.

The key move is counting the sides rather than matching a remembered picture, because a stretched or tilted five-sided shape is still a pentagon. By facing irregular and rotated shapes alongside the tidy ones, the child practices using the number of sides as the rule that names a polygon. That builds the vocabulary — quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon — and the habit of analyzing shapes by their parts.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.G.A.1 — recognizing and drawing shapes with specified attributes such as a given number of sides, and identifying triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count the sides of a shape to decide which polygon group it belongs to
Tell triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons apart by their number of sides
Recognize the same polygon when it is irregular, stretched, or rotated
Use the words quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon correctly
howToPlay: Look at each shape and count how many sides it has.
Drag it into the matching bin — triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, or hexagons.
Not quite? Try again as many times as you like — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons by their sides — the focus of Common Core 2.G.A.1.
Understand that the number of sides, not the look, names a polygon.
Build the shape vocabulary and side-counting habit that later geometry depends on.

about: A short word sits in sound boxes, one box for each sound: c · a · t. The child drops a picture on the boxes, and the lids pop open wherever its sounds are the same as the target’s, in the same place. Drop the hat on cat and the a and the t pop open together, but the first box stays shut: the sounds match, just not at the start. It is an interactive Kindergarten phonemic awareness activity that plays in the browser.

The boxes listen; they do not read. Cat and kite pop open together at the first box although one says c and the other k, and a team of letters such as sh sits in one box because it is one sound. Three tasks share the boxes: find the picture with the same first, middle or last sound; tap the box where a sound lives; and sort pictures by whether the word has the sound at all.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.K.2.d, isolating the first, middle and last sounds in three-sound words. No timer and no score.
practices: Hearing the first, middle and last sound of a short word
Matching two words by the sound in the same place
Telling a sound in the right place from the same sound in another place
Finding where a sound sits in a word, and whether it is there at all
howToPlay: Look at the target word in its boxes; the arrow shows the box to listen for.
Drag a picture onto the boxes, then press Check.
Watch which lids pop open: the asked box must pop for the right picture.
learningGoals: The child isolates the first, middle and last sound in a short word
The child matches words by a sound in the same place, not just any shared sound
The child knows a sound by how it sounds, not by its letter

about: In Span's Length Gap two real things lie on two lanes, both against a wooden zero wall, with one yellow tape measure between them. The child slides the orange clip to the end of the top thing and the green clip to the end of the bottom thing. A dashed line drops from each clip to its own thing, so the child sees the clip meet the end. As soon as both clips are on the tape, the stretch of tape between them glows: the gap is something to look at before it has a number.

The child types how many centimeters longer the longer one is and presses Check. The glowing piece is snipped out of the tape and lands in the tray, where it counts itself from 0. If the number is wrong, a dashed strip as long as the typed number lies beside the piece, so an answer such as the longer length or the sum of both sticks out far past it; after a second miss, one dot appears in every centimeter space of the piece. A clip in the wrong place shades the part of the thing it missed. In the loose setting the things start away from the wall, and nothing is checked until both are pushed against it: lengths are compared from the same start.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.A.4 (measure to find how much longer one object is than another, in a standard unit). It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Measure two things in centimeters on one tape measure
Find how many centimeters longer one thing is than another
See the difference as a piece of the tape: the longer length minus the shorter one
Compare lengths from the same starting point
howToPlay: Slide the orange clip to the end of the top thing and the green clip to the end of the bottom thing, or tap the tape to move them.
Type on the keypad how many centimeters longer the longer one is, then press Check.
In the settings, choose a ruler from 0 to 12 cm or from 0 to 20 cm, and whether the things start at the wall or loose.
learningGoals: Measure two objects in centimeters and find how much longer one is, the focus of Common Core 2.MD.A.4.
Understand the difference as the part of the longer length that the shorter one does not reach.
Line lengths up at the same start before comparing them.

about: A night sky full of numbered stars, and one of them is awake — a 7, say, or a 12, never a 1. The child counts on from it by tapping the star that comes next, then the next: each right star wakes with a gold glow, a thread runs to it and the number is spoken, until the thread has drawn a picture — a kite, a cup, a crown, a staircase. It is an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser on tablets, phones and computers, with nothing to install and no account.

The big idea is counting forward from a number you are given instead of starting over at one. The sky also holds stars numbered below the start — 1 is always there — and tapping one is answered by name: that number comes before yours, you don’t have to go back, count on from where you are. A star too far ahead is named too: one at a time. Nothing lights for a wrong tap, so the picture only ever exists when the count is right, and the strip under the sky reads the run so far — 7, 8, 9 — so the spoken sequence stays visible. Settings go to 10 or to 20 (through the teens), and the extra stars can be switched off for a class that still needs a clear sky.
It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.2 — counting forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Count forward from a given number instead of starting at one
Find and read the numeral that comes next among many
Keep a run going, one number at a time, to 10 or to 20
Refuse a number that comes before yours, and one that skips ahead
howToPlay: Look at the star that is awake and read its number. That is where you start.
Tap the star that comes next, then the next one, and the next. Each right star wakes and the thread grows.
When the last star lights, the picture closes and the round checks itself. Not sure? The strip tells you the number you are on — there is no timer and no score.
learningGoals: Count forward from a given number — the focus of Common Core K.CC.A.2
Understand that counting can begin anywhere, not only at one
Build the counting-on fluency that addition and later number work depend on

about: A story is a book that breaks and gets mended. The child puts three tabs – START, TROUBLE and FIX – on the loose pages of a short picture story and presses the gold Read the book button: the book reads itself. The start page plants a green pennant, the trouble page cracks open (“The wind blew the nest down!”), and the fix page sends a bandage across that seals the crack. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

A bandage only seals a crack its fix really mends. A calm page put in the trouble place cannot crack; a page that makes something else better sends a bandage that peels off and flutters down; a page where nothing has changed sends nothing at all. In Find the trouble the child chooses the middle page, in Find the fix the end page, and in Match the sentences each sentence goes under its picture. Every mended book stands on the shelf, and the retell ribbon tells it back: First, Then, At the end.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.3: identifying the characters, the setting and the major events of a story. Nine short stories, every page made of library pictures. No timer and no score.
practices: Telling the start, the trouble and the fix of a story apart
Finding the page where something goes wrong
Choosing the page that really fixes that trouble
Matching sentences to the pictures they tell
howToPlay: Put the START, TROUBLE and FIX tabs on the pages, or put a page in the empty place.
Press Read the book.
If the reading stops, look at the page it stopped on and change it.
learningGoals: The child names the start, the trouble and the fix of a short story
The child sees that the fix has to answer the trouble
The child retells a story with first, then and at the end

about: A music-box roll you punch with your own finger: one hole for every sound in the word. A tap on the big round punch makes a round hole; hold the punch down and the hole grows under your finger into a long slot, with a click at the stretch mark. That is how a child shows a long vowel, the one that says its name, like the a in cake or the ee in bee, against a quick one like the a in cat. Turn the crank and the box plays the roll back: a short plink for each round hole, a held note for each slot, and the giraffe on the lid rises on tiptoe for every long one.

There are three clues. Long or short? shows three pictures, each with its own roll whose other sounds are already punched; the child says each word and punches only its vowel. Count the sounds shows one picture and a blank roll: one hole for every sound, not every letter, so fish is three holes and frog is four. Blend shows a roll with letters under its holes: crank it, read the sounds, and tap the picture they make. Every word and every split comes from the platform's sound-box word bank, and finished words become little punched cards in a song book.

After a first miss the word's own roll slides up under the child's: holes that agree shine gold, holes that do not are coral, so a slot over a round hole is plain to see. After a second miss the hint points at what to look for. Aligned to Common Core RF.1.2.a, distinguishing long from short vowel sounds. No timer and no score.
practices: Hearing whether a vowel is long (it says its name) or short
Counting the sounds in a word, not its letters
Blending sounds read from left to right into a word
Seeing that how many sounds a word has and how long one sound is are two different things
howToPlay: Tap a picture to hear its name.
Tap the punch for a quick, round hole; hold it until it clicks for a long slot. Tap a hole to close it.
Turn the crank or press Check: the box plays your roll and shows the word's own roll under it.
In Blend, crank the lettered roll, read the sounds, then tap the picture and press Check.
In the settings choose the clue (Long or short? · Count the sounds · Blend) and whether letters show under the holes.
learningGoals: Distinguish long from short vowel sounds in spoken one-syllable words.
Segment a one-syllable word into its separate sounds.
Blend sounds, including two-letter sounds such as sh and ee, into a word.
Recognize that a word can have fewer sounds than letters.

about: A whole sentence has a beginning, its parts joined, and an end. At the Sunny-Side Diner the parts of an order are plates on a brass rail, and the plates are magnets that push each other apart: only a golden “and” holds two of them together.

First the child gathers the order from the ticket onto the tray: the right food and the right number of each. The tray turns into plates on the rail, between the beginning “I would like” and the kitchen hatch. The child puts the golden “and” into the gap between the plates and the end “please.” at the end of the rail; only then does the hatch roll up and the sentence light up word by word.

Four kinds of rounds: gather the order and say it; the missing “and”; fix the robot waiter’s order, where one plate is wrong; and “one more thing!”, when a third plate arrives and the first “and” turns into a comma. With “Listen” the ticket folds shut after a few seconds. Aligned to Common Core L.K.1.f: produce and expand complete sentences. No timer and no score.
practices: Saying an order as one complete sentence
Joining two parts of a sentence with “and”
Giving a sentence its beginning and its end
Adding a third part with a comma and “and”
howToPlay: Look at the ticket. Tap the bins until the whole order is on the tray, then press “Check”.
Tap the golden “and”, then the gap between the plates. Put the end at the end of the rail and press “Check”.
Under “Round types” choose another kind of round; under “Order” choose “Listen” and the ticket folds shut.
learningGoals: The child says an order as one complete sentence with a beginning and an end
The child joins two parts of a sentence with “and”
The child expands a sentence with a third part, using a comma and “and”

about: The picture's word is a stencil with its letters cut out as windows. The child lays a word card in the frame and presses Check: the stencil drops onto it. On books, under a picture of a book, every window frames its own letter and the leftover s slides into a gold ending sleeve. On boots, one window shows a t where the stencil needs a k, and the stencil rocks. Build Words with Endings is a Grade 1 reading activity about finding the root word inside a longer word.

Every round mixes in other words with endings (boots, stamps, calling), so spotting an ending is not enough: the child has to find the picture's word inside. The Tricky look-alikes add a trap that starts with the whole root, like catch under a cat: every window fits, but ch is not an ending, so no sleeve takes it. Peel the ending asks where the root stops (jump | ing), and Add the ending gives a sentence that decides the ending: two cats, Mia is jumping now, it rained yesterday. Each word made hangs on its ending's hook: -s, -ing or -ed.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.3.f: reading words with inflectional endings. No timer and no score.
practices: Find the root word inside a longer word
Tell a real ending (-s, -ing, -ed) from leftover letters that are not an ending
Split a word into its root and its ending
Choose the ending a sentence needs: more than one, happening now, or already happened
howToPlay: Look at the picture and tap the word card you think is built from its word. It goes into the frame.
Press Check. The stencil drops onto the word: a coral window shows a letter that does not belong.
In Peel the ending, tap where the picture's word ends. In Add the ending, read the sentence and tap the ending it needs.
learningGoals: Read words with the endings -s, -ing and -ed, the focus of Common Core RF.1.3.f.
See that the root word keeps its letters when an ending is added.
Link each ending to what it means: more than one, happening now, already happened.

about: A picture appears (a boat, a train, a sheep, a leaf) with its consonants already seated on a wooden rail and a wide socket where the vowel team goes. The child pinches the team in the socket: put one vowel in, then another. Build Vowel-Team Words is a Grade 1 phonics activity about the vowel teams oa, ai, ee and ea.

Only a real team locks. Put o and then a in the socket and a brass clasp snaps over them: oa. Put a and then o and they bump apart, because ao is not a team, so the order matters. A locked team lights up the letter whose name you hear (in oa the o says its name) while its partner goes quiet. In the Same sound? clue both ee and ea say E, and the word decides which spelling it uses: the right sound with the other spelling turns the word's own spelling card over instead of counting as a plain mistake. Finished words pin under their team on the team board, so boat, goat and coat stack under oa, and leaf and seal under ea.
It is aligned to Common Core RF.1.3: knowing common vowel-team conventions for representing long vowel sounds. No timer and no score.
practices: Spell long vowel sounds with the teams oa, ai, ee and ea
Find that the order matters: oa is a team, ao is not
Hear which letter of the team says its name
Choose between ee and ea when both say E
howToPlay: Look at the picture and say its name. Tap the picture to hear it.
Tap or drag a vowel into the wide socket, then a second one. A real team locks under the clasp; two vowels that are not a team bump apart.
Press Check. If the word is right, it pins under its team on the board. Tap a locked team in the socket to open the clasp and try again.
learningGoals: Read and spell words with the vowel teams oa, ai, ee and ea, the focus of Common Core RF.1.3.
Understand that two vowels can spell one long vowel sound.
Learn that the same sound can be spelled two ways, and the word decides.

about: Tally the squirrel keeps acorns in baskets, and every basket holds cups of ten plus some loose acorns. The child tips each basket onto Tally's sieve and shakes it: the loose acorns drop through the holes into a tray with grooves of ten, while the cups of ten are too long to fit and stay on top. So for 15 + 22 + 34 + 11, all the tens end up together on the sieve (7 cups, 70) and all the ones end up together in the tray (12 acorns). The child writes the cups, the loose acorns and the total, 82.

A wrong window is easy to see. If the child writes 10 loose acorns for 23 + 14, the tray holds only 7. After a miss the cups count themselves in tens and each groove shows how many acorns it holds; after a second miss every basket splits into its tens and its ones, and the two small sums appear beside the sieve and the tray. A full groove of ten acorns rolls up into a cup, which is the ten hiding inside the ones. With the cloth on, the sieve is covered: the child works it out from the numbers, and Check lifts the cloth. Other settings offer three small baskets (3 + 4 + 3 = 10) and a number wall where each brick is the two below it (12, 15, 21 → 27, 36 → 63).
It is aligned to Common Core 2.NBT.B.6: add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Adding up to four two-digit numbers within 100.
Adding all the tens, then all the ones, then putting them together.
Seeing that ten loose ones make one ten.
Building a number wall where each brick is the sum of the two below.
howToPlay: Tap each basket to tip it onto the sieve, then shake the sieve with its handle.
Write how many cups of ten, how many loose acorns and how many in all, then press Check.
In the settings, choose three small baskets, two or three, up to four, or a number wall, and turn the cloth on or off.
learningGoals: Add up to four two-digit numbers using place value — the focus of Common Core 2.NBT.B.6.
Keep tens with tens and ones with ones, and regroup ten ones as a ten.
Check a total by seeing where every ten and every one actually went.

about: Tempo's day is a road that runs from morning to evening, and every event on it is a stone tunnel with its picture above the arch: the run, the show, the bath. What you do on the road in front of the tunnel happens "before", what you do inside the tunnel happens "during", and what waits past the exit happens "after".

An action card already stands on the road. The child picks the words that name its place, and a lantern walks the road and lights the stretch those words mean: in "We clap during the song" it goes into the tunnel and the little windows glow. Later the child reads a whole sentence such as "We wash our hands before lunch" and puts the card on the road, and at last plans a day with two tunnels.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.i: use frequently occurring prepositions (here before, during and after). No timer and no score.
practices: Use "before" for what happens first, in front of the event
Use "during" for what happens while the event is going on
Use "after" for what happens once the event is over
Read a sentence and show where its action belongs in the day
howToPlay: Look where the card stands: in front of the tunnel, inside it, or past it.
Tap the words that fit, then press Check; the lantern lights the stretch they mean.
In the settings, choose the level (from "Where is it?" to "Day plan") and whether to show the three stretches on the road.
learningGoals: Tell "before", "during" and "after" apart.
Understand that "during" means the whole time the event lasts.
Put the things we do in the order of the day.

about: A fact such as 3 + 2 or 5 − 2 appears, and below it stand five chunky bars, numbered 1 to 5 — each bar exactly as many blocks tall as its number. The child taps the bar that answers the fact. A right bar punches a hole in its own row of a paper music-box strip, and the next fact slides in. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the answers are notes. Each round is one phrase of a real song — Frère Jacques, Ode to Joy, Lightly Row — and its facts are chosen so that their answers, in order, are the notes of the tune. While the child is answering, every bar makes the same soft knock, so the melody cannot give the maths away. When the strip is full the child turns the crank: the holes play the song at its own steady tempo, never faster for a faster child, and the song's picture pops up. A wrong bar punches nothing. Instead the fact's own rods lie against that bar, and the child can see by how many blocks they stick out or fall short; in a take-away fact the blocks taken away break off the top. After a second wrong bar, a five-frame opens with the fact as counters, so the child can count and try again.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.5 — adding and subtracting fluently within 5 — with a To 10 level for facts up to ten. Teachers choose the level, Add and subtract or Add only, and whether facts appear as numbers, dots (dominoes and dice) or pictures of fruit. "Notes: As you go" lets the bars ring their notes during the round, for a music-and-maths lesson. The Music box is open play: tap any bars, then crank your own tune. No timer, no score.
practices: Adding and subtracting within 5 without counting from 1
Seeing how far a wrong answer is from the right one
Recognising the same fact as numbers, dots and pictures
Linking a number to a length, so 5 is the longest bar
howToPlay: Look at the fact on the card.
Tap the bar that answers it. A right bar punches a hole in the strip.
If the rods beside a bar do not match its height, try another bar. The frame button shows the fact as counters.
When the strip is full, turn the crank to hear the song. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Add and subtract fluently within 5 — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.5
Know facts such as 3 + 2 and 5 − 2 without counting
See addition and subtraction as lengths that fit together

about: The Stamp Frame turns an equation into something a child prints. There are three rubber stamps — an orange dot, a green dot and a big cross — and an empty ten-frame. For 3 + 2 the child stamps 3 orange counters and 2 green ones; for 8 − 3 they stamp 8 orange counters and cross 3 of them out. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that the equation checks the printing. When the child presses Check, the counters slide into order and every number in the equation drops a bracket over its own counters. A counter sticking out of its bracket, or an empty dashed place inside it, is seen at once, and the hint names the number to look under. Only when the printing is right is the answer asked: for an addition the two brackets join into one round all the counters, "How many altogether?"; for a take-away the crossed counters peel off into a dish, "How many are left?". The answer is tapped on a number strip where each number sits in its own place, so the strip itself cannot give it away. In an addition, tapping one of the two parts gets the hint that it is only a part; in a take-away, tapping a number of the equation sends the child back to the counters still on the frame; a second wrong answer numbers the counters up to a question mark on the last one, so the child still says the number.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.1 — representing addition and subtraction with objects, drawings and expressions; the cross-out is the picture model children later draw on paper. Teachers can choose numbers within 5, within 10 (the default) or within 20 on two ten-frames, and show the numbers as numerals or as dice and domino dots. "Stamp anything" is open play: all three stamps, and the equation writes itself from what is stamped. No timer, no score.
practices: Showing an addition as two groups of counters in two colours
Showing a take-away by crossing counters out of the first group
Checking each number of an equation against its own counters
Counting how many altogether, or how many are left
howToPlay: Read the equation, such as 4 + 3 or 8 − 3.

Tap a stamp to lift it, then tap places on the ten-frame. Orange is the first number, green the second; for a take-away, cross counters out with the cross stamp. Tap a counter again with the same stamp to wipe it.
Press Check. The brackets show what is missing or too many — fix it and press Check again.
When the printing is right, tap how many on the number strip. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Represent addition and subtraction with counters and an equation — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.1
See an addition as two parts that make a whole
See a take-away as crossing out and counting what is left

about: The Story Stage turns a word problem into a little play. "3 birds sit on a branch. 2 more birds land. How many birds are there now?" The first line acts itself out: three birds arrive one by one on a stage that is a ten-frame. Then it is the child's line — they bring the 2 more birds from the pile themselves. Only then does the question wake the number keys. It's an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is that every sentence is a stage direction, so the operation comes from what happens, not from a sign. A take-away story has no pile at all: "7 balloons float in the air. 3 balloons pop." The child taps 3 balloons, and each one pops and stays behind as a pale crossed outline — what was there and what is left, side by side. Put-together stories bring two kinds onto one stage: 4 birds and 3 bunnies, how many animals? The next line waits until the child has made a move on the stage, so the story is played, not just read. A wrong number replays the story at its true numbers, each arriving or leaving picture numbered as it moves, and leaves the stage telling the story right — if the child brought one bird too many, the note says so. A second wrong answer numbers the pictures still there up to a question mark on the last one, so the child still says the number.

It is aligned to Common Core K.OA.A.2 — solving addition and subtraction word problems within 10 by acting them out with objects. Teachers can choose stories within 5, within 10 (the default) or within 20, where two ten-frames hold counters and a picture shows what the counters stand for, and turn reading aloud on or off; with it off, each line waits a moment before it acts. "Tell your own" is open play: a pile, the stage, and a story that writes itself as the child plays. No timer, no score.
practices: Acting out a story problem one sentence at a time
Adding to, taking from and putting together within 10
Telling what went away apart from what is still there
Counting the result and typing the number
howToPlay: Read the story. Its first line acts itself out on the stage.
Act out your line: tap the pile (or drag from it) to bring more, or tap things so they go away. Then press Next.
Count the pictures still on the stage, type the number on the keys and press Check.
Not quite? The story plays again with its true numbers — count again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Solve add-to, take-from and put-together word problems within 10 — the focus of Common Core K.OA.A.2
Work out what a story does to a group by acting it out
Count only what is left after some go away

about: Lily the frog crosses a pond on a number line from 0 to 20. The number to add or take away hangs above the pond as a rope of beads. The child pulls Lily back like a slingshot, one bead for each stone, and lets go, or taps a stone ahead of her. Every leap uses up the beads it jumps.

The stones on the far side of ten are under water until Lily stands on the golden Ten Stone. A leap across ten splashes and Lily swims back, which never counts as a miss. So 8 + 6 has to become 8 + 2 to the Ten Stone, then the 4 beads that are left. The equation strip writes down each leap, and the child types the stone where Lily lands.

Some rounds take away (13 − 4 is 13 − 3 − 1), some let the child choose the easier start (3 + 8 or 8 + 3), and bank rounds ask how far it is to the bank at 20. After a first miss, the stones between the Ten Stone and Lily are counted; after a second, her leaps appear as arcs with their lengths. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.C.6. No timer and no score.
practices: Adding within 20 by stopping at ten: 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4
Taking away within 20 by going back to ten: 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − 1
Choosing the easier start: 3 + 8 is the same as 8 + 3
Finding the number bonds to 20
howToPlay: Pull Lily back, away from where she must go, and let go: she leaps one stone for each bead on the spring. You can also tap a stone ahead of her.
If she splashes, that stone was under water: leap to the Ten Stone first. The round arrow takes back a leap. In bank rounds, a splash in the reeds means the leap was too long.
When the rope is empty, type the stone Lily is on and press the tick. In bank rounds, type how far she leapt altogether.
In the settings, choose the facts (Adding, or Adding and taking away) and the stone numbers (Every 5 or Every stone). Every stone is the easier setting: the numbers can be read off.
learningGoals: Add within 20 by making a ten
Subtract within 20 by going back to ten
Use the link between addition and subtraction
Know the number bonds to 20

about: Dewey the duckling has a tank full of glowing bubbles that drift slowly about, so they cannot be counted where they float. The child catches them onto Dewey’s raft, one per seat, with a tap or a drag; on the tenth seat the ten bubbles melt into one golden ten-raft, Dewey hops aboard, and every bubble still loose hooks onto the raft’s tow-line in a single row. Now 13 is one raft and a row of three. It is an interactive Kindergarten math activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install.

The invention is the ghost bay beside the tank. Number cards are the answers, and a wrong card builds its own meaning there: drop 31 for the tank that shows 13 and three ghost rafts and one ghost bubble appear; drop 6 for 16 and six ghost bubbles appear with no raft at all. A second miss puts a 10 on the raft and counts the row on from 11. Other rounds build the number from the reeds (a ready raft and spare bubbles: make 17), fix a tank that starts at 10 + 2 until it shows 14, pop a raft with a long press and see that 12 is still 12, or compare two tanks, 13 and 18: the same ten, but 8 more instead of 3. Every success writes the record, 10 + 3 = 13, and Dewey paddles a lap.

It is aligned to Common Core K.NBT.A.1, composing and decomposing the numbers 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, and recording each as 10 + N. Teachers can choose numbers up to 15 or up to 19, and number cards in digits or in words, taken from the same reviewed number-word tables as the printable worksheets. "Ghost bay" is open play: catch, pop and summon the ghost of any number up to 99. No timer, no score.
practices: Catching ten ones and seeing them become one ten
Seeing 11–19 as a ten and some ones
Telling 13 from 31 by what each number builds
Writing a teen number as 10 + N
howToPlay: Tap or drag the bubbles onto Dewey’s raft until ten seal into one raft.
Tap the number card that tells how many bubbles there are.
A wrong card shows its ghost: compare it with the tank.
No timer, no score: try another card or another move.
learningGoals: Compose and decompose 11–19 as a ten and some ones, the focus of Common Core K.NBT.A.1
Record a teen number as 10 + N
Explain why 13 and 31 are different numbers

about: The verb's form tells when something happens, and here every form turns into a thing you can hold. A sentence card has a time word and a gap; under it lie the verb cards, and below stands a clock tower with three openings: an album sleeve for the past, a window for right now and a post slot for tomorrow.

Drop a card into the gap and press Check: the card develops. A past form becomes a still photo, a present form becomes a window where the picture keeps moving, a future form folds into a sealed envelope. Then it goes to the opening the time word names, and only the right kind fits: "Yesterday the boats sailed on the lake" files a photo into the album, "Tomorrow the dogs will play in the park" drops an envelope through the slot. Later levels bring the tricky verbs (went, ran, was), then the child reads the verb and picks the time word, matches each verb to its past, finds the verb in a sentence and writes its base form.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.e: use verbs to convey a sense of past, present and future. No timer and no score.
practices: Choose the past, present or future form that fits the time word
Use the tricky past forms: went, ran, rode, was, did, had
Read a verb and tell whether it happened, is happening or will happen
Match a verb to its past form and find the base form of a verb in a sentence
howToPlay: Read the time word (Yesterday, Right now or Tomorrow) and look at the cards.
Drag or tap a card into the gap, then press Check and watch where it is filed.
In the settings, choose the level: from yesterday, now and tomorrow up to writing the base form.
learningGoals: Match the verb's form to the time it talks about.
Use common irregular past forms such as went and was.
Find the verb in a sentence and name its base form.

about: In Tildy's Tailor Shop a strip of ribbon, leather, yarn, cord, denim, felt, lace, braid or elastic lies on the cutting table, and Knot the cat has just bumped the ruler off its place. The child slides the ruler until its 0 meets the start of the strip, then taps the number at the other end. On Check, Tildy's cutter rides along the ruler from its 0 and snips at every centimeter: the pieces drop into the jar, and whatever the ruler missed stays lying on the table.

That makes the two classic ruler mistakes visible. If the 0 sat inside the strip, a stub is left over before it. If the 0 sat before the strip, the cutter snips thin air first. In the Tricky rulers setting there are broken rulers that do not start at 0, where the child taps each centimeter space the strip covers. Tildy also makes mistakes for the child to fix, and on a shelf of rulers only one is long enough. Each finished strip is hung on Tildy's rail with its length.

It is aligned to Common Core 2.MD.A.1 (measure the length of an object by selecting and using a ruler). Nothing lights up when the ruler is close: the result shows only after Check. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Line up a ruler's 0 with the start of an object
Read the number at the end of an object in centimeters
Measure with a broken ruler by counting centimeter spaces
Choose a ruler that is long enough
howToPlay: Drag the ruler along the table until its 0 is at the start of the strip, then tap the number on the ruler at the strip's end.
On a broken ruler, tap each centimeter space the strip covers; with a shelf of rulers, tap a ruler to put it on the table first.
Press Check and watch the cutter. In the settings, choose Line up the 0 or Tricky rulers, and whether the ruler shows every number or only 0, 5, 10 and 15.
learningGoals: Measure the length of an object with a ruler, starting at 0, the focus of Common Core 2.MD.A.1.
Understand that starting at the 1 or at the ruler's edge gives the wrong length.
Measure from any mark by counting the centimeter spaces, and choose a ruler that reaches the whole object.

about: A storm has torn up the railway in Whistle Valley, and the track is a number line: every tie stands for a number. The child drags number plates onto the ties where they belong (or taps a plate, then a tie). One plate on the trolley does not belong on this stretch at all, so the child has to decide, not just fill gaps. Then the engine checks the work by counting on from the station: its headlamp lights each tie's number as it rolls, and it stops at the first plate it disagrees with.

There are three tracks. On Hops the train is at a number and goes a few ties on or back; the child plants the red flag where it will stop, and the engine puffs once for each hop, so counting the start tie as “one” is easy to see. On Find the spot the child bolts plates onto ties, sometimes types the number for a tie with an arrow, and sometimes places plates on an open rail with only the two end numbers shown. On Mileposts the posts go up or down in equal jumps, and every jump shows its own size, so the plate that breaks the step stands out.
Numbers go to 50 or to 120. After a second try the lamp leaves a number on every empty tie. Aligned to Common Core 1.NBT.A.1. No timer and no score.
practices: Counting on and back from any number up to 120
Placing numbers on a number line from the nearest printed number
Reading and writing numbers across a ten or a hundred (39, 40 … 99, 100, 101)
Finding and continuing a pattern with an equal step
howToPlay: Read the task and look at the numbers already on the track.
Drag a plate onto the tie where its number belongs, or tap a plate and then a tie. Leave the plate that does not belong on the trolley.
On Hops, plant the red flag on the tie where the train stops. When a tie has an arrow, tap it and type its number.
Press Check and watch the engine count on. If it stops at a plate, move that plate and check again.
In the settings, choose the track (hops, find the spot or mileposts) and the numbers (to 50 or to 120).
learningGoals: Count to 120, starting at any number
Locate a number on a number line by counting on from a known number
Count on and back in hops to add and subtract
Recognise and continue a number pattern with a constant step

about: Two rock pools sit side by side (one above the other on a phone). The first holds sea creatures — seven crabs scattered about, say, or six starfish in a ring. The child counts them, then fills the empty twin pool with just as many, but of a different kind: seven starfish for seven crabs. When the twin pool is ready, the child presses Check. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

Both halves of counting are in one move: count how many there are, then count out that many. The creatures in the first pool come in a line, a ring, rows or a scatter, and a tap on one marks it as counted, so the child can keep track of which ones are done; the mark is never a number. In the twin pool the child taps an empty place to put a creature in and taps a creature to take it out. Because the twin creatures are, by default, a different kind and lie in a different shape, only the number can match. The twin pool always has more places than any round needs (12, or 8 when the numbers go up to 5), so its size never gives the answer. A right Check ties a string from every creature in the first pool to one in the twin pool, with none left over on either side, which is what “the same number” means. A wrong Check says too many or too few and numbers the creatures in the twin pool; after a second, the strings tie as many pairs as they can and ring the creatures left without a twin. The help never moves a creature.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting how many things there are in a line, a ring, rows or a scatter, and counting out a given number, up to 10. Teachers can choose numbers up to 5 or up to 10, and put the same kind of creature in the twin pool to make the match easier to see. No timer, no score.
practices: Counting how many there are in a line, a ring, rows or a scatter
Marking each one as it is counted, so none is counted twice or missed
Counting out the same number with different things
Seeing that two groups are the same number when every one has a twin
howToPlay: Count the sea creatures in the first pool. Tap each one to mark it as you count.
Tap empty places in the twin pool to put in just as many. Tap a creature in the twin pool to take it out.
Press Check. If they match, a string ties every pair.
Not quite? The hint says too many or too few — fix it and press Check again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Count how many there are, up to 10, in a line, a ring, rows or a scatter — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Count out a given number of things
Know that two groups are the same number when each thing in one can be paired with a thing in the other

about: Two little picture books lie open on Mossbeard the turtle's table, one under a gold moon and one under a silver moon. Each tells a short story in three pages, with one picture and one sentence a page. Every experience card is a wooden plank. Lay it across the two books and each end walks its own book page by page, looking for the page that shows that experience. Two Moons is a Grade 1 reading activity about comparing the experiences of characters in two stories.

If both books show it, the plank lies flat like a bridge and Mossbeard walks across. If only one does, the other end finds nothing and the plank tips into that book. If neither does, it drops through the gap. "Lost it, then found it" needs the found page too: Kiki loses her ball and never finds it ("She looked, but she could not find it."), so half the experience cannot hold the plank.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.1.9: compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in stories. No timer and no score.
practices: Read two short stories and notice what happened to each character
Find an experience the two stories share
Find an experience only one story has
Show the page that proves it in each book
howToPlay: Read both little books. Tap a page to make its picture move.
Tap a plank, then tap where it goes: across the books, on one book, or in the basket for "in neither story". Then press Check and watch the ends walk.
Choose the task in the settings: What is the same?, What happened in only one?, or Sort every plank. Books can have three pages or two.
learningGoals: Compare and contrast the experiences of characters in two stories, the focus of Common Core RL.1.9.
Back up "same" and "different" with a page from each story.
See that half an experience is not the whole experience.

about: Every verb is a gate in the hedge. The sentence lies on a strip with a gap, the subject's house stands at the start of a garden path, and three gates hang on a rack: a brass turnstile (is), a wooden double gate (are) and a round star door (am). Vera's Verb Match is a Grade 1 grammar activity about making the verb agree with its subject.

Hang a gate and press Check: the subject walks out of its house. The turnstile lets exactly one through and locks, so in "The dogs are in the yard" the wrong gate leaves two dogs sitting behind it. The double gate only opens when two or more push, so a single dog waits alone in front of it. The star door spins only for the star that means I: "I am ready to play". Later levels move to was and were, then to has and have, goes and go, and to any verb: "The dog runs" but "The dogs run".
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.1.c: use singular and plural nouns with matching verbs in basic sentences. No timer and no score.
practices: Use am with I, is with one, are with more than one
Use was with one and were with more than one
Use has, goes and does with one; have, go and do with more than one
Put the s on the verb for one: the dog runs, the dogs run
howToPlay: Read the sentence and find who is coming: I, one, or more than one.
Tap a gate to hang it in the hedge, then press Check and watch the crowd walk through.
In the settings, choose the verbs (am, is, are up to any verb) and whether to show who is coming before Check.
learningGoals: Make the verb agree with a singular or plural subject.
Choose between am, is and are, and between was and were.
Notice that the s goes on the verb for one, but on the noun for many.

about: A patient comes to the vet as an x-ray, and its problem is a number story: “12 geese are on the pond. Some fly away. Now there are 8.” Under the story is the x-ray light box, a film with a frame for each part of the story. The child puts the story's numbers on the frames where they belong, marks the frame we don't know, and dials how many.

Then the child presses Diagnose and the film plays their own model, sentence by sentence. If a number sits on the wrong frame, the film stops there: the frame and its sentence glow together. If the dialled number is wrong, the last frame shows it, with dots spilling over the rim or sockets left empty. One of the three number cards is a decoy, often the number you get with the wrong operation: adding when the story takes away, or the other way round.

When the film fits the story, the fog lifts, the patient heals and the equation appears (“12 − 4 = 8”). There are add-to, take-from, put-together and compare stories with the unknown in every place, plus a Groups level for equal groups and sharing. Aligned to Common Core 1.OA.A.1. No timer and no score.
practices: Deciding which part of a word problem each number belongs to
Finding the unknown at the start, in the change or at the end of a story
Comparing two amounts: how many more, how many fewer
Writing the equation that matches the story
howToPlay: Read the story (or press the speaker). Tap a number card, then tap the frame where that number belongs in the story.
Tap the frame we don't know to mark it with a question mark, then press − and + on that frame to set how many.
Press Diagnose and watch your film. If it stops, look at the glowing frame and its sentence, change something and try again.
In the settings, choose the stories (Within 10, Within 20 or Groups) and whether the story is read aloud.
learningGoals: Solve add-to, take-from and put-together problems within 20 with the unknown in any position
Solve compare problems: how many more and how many fewer
Model a word problem and write an equation with the unknown
Solve equal-groups and sharing problems

about: A short story plays in a little flipbook – “Mira the mouse’s kite is stuck in a tall tree.” – and then its pages fall out. The child puts the pages back in order and presses Flip!: the book riffles through the stack and the pictures glide from page to page, so the kite really floats down into Mira’s paws. Sleepy Pip the hedgehog lies under his blanket in the corner. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

In the wrong order the story runs backwards and the flip stops right there: the kite jumps back up into the tree and the two pages that broke it jiggle. In The missing page, all the pages but one are already in the book and the child chooses among three loose pages: one moves the story, one shows something true but unimportant (nothing in the story moves), and one shows something that never happened. In Fix the flipbook, two pages are swapped or one page does not belong. When the story plays through, Pip sits up and the retell ribbon tells it back: First, Next, Then, At the end, each over its page’s own sentence. A setting adds the sentences as strips to lay under the pictures.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.2, retelling familiar stories, including key details. Eight short stories, three or four pages each. No timer and no score.
practices: Putting the pictures of a story in order
Telling what happens first, next and at the end
Telling a key page from one where nothing in the story happens
Matching sentences to the pictures they tell
howToPlay: Watch the story in the flipbook.
Tap or drag the pages into the slots in story order.
Press Flip! If the story runs backwards or stops, look at the pages that jiggle and change them.
learningGoals: The child retells a short story in order
The child tells the key details apart from details that do not move the story
The child uses first, next, then and at the end to retell

about: Wally the walrus runs a crane that lifts a small letter up into a big CAPITAL. In each sentence — "We celebrate halloween," "She lives in texas," "I love lego blocks" — one special name has been left lowercase, and the child taps the word that needs Wally's capital. This interactive Grade 2 grammar activity runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is that proper nouns always begin with a capital letter. The sentences mix holidays (Halloween, Christmas), places (Texas, Paris, Canada), and product names (Lego, Oreo, Disney), each set among ordinary words that stay lowercase. The child has to recognize WHICH word names a particular holiday, place, or brand — not simply pick the first word or the longest one.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.2.a — capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Spot the special name in a sentence — a holiday, a place, or a product
Tell a proper noun like Texas, Halloween, or Lego from the ordinary words around it
Know that holidays, places, and brand names always take a capital letter
Leave common words lowercase
howToPlay: Read the sentence and look for the word that names a holiday, place, or product.
Tap that word so Wally's crane lifts its first letter into a capital.
A warm check confirms the choice and offers an easy retry; no timer, no score.
learningGoals: Capitalize holidays, product names, and geographic names — the focus of Common Core L.2.2.a
Recognize proper nouns inside a sentence
Understand why special names are capitalized while common words are not

about: Willow the tortoise reads two short stories, panel by panel. Then each question becomes a tooth of a big zipper between the two stories. Put “Who lost something?” in the middle if it happens in BOTH stories, on one side if it happens in only that story, or in the pocket if it happens in neither. Then pull the slider. It zips past a tooth the pictures prove, and the panels that show it light up; at a tooth in the wrong place it jams. It is an interactive Kindergarten reading activity that plays in the browser.

Each pair of stories fills one zipper with five teeth: something both stories share, something only one has, something neither has, and one of those kinds twice, so the last tooth can never be guessed by leaving it for the empty spot. When the fifth tooth closes, the whole zipper zips shut. In the settings, Two stories or Two animals: with two animals the child compares two library pictures (which one has a beak, stripes, a mane). Listen first decides whether Willow reads the stories at the start or only when the child taps her.
It is aligned to Common Core RL.K.9: comparing and contrasting what happens to characters in familiar stories. No timer and no score.
practices: Comparing what happens in two stories
Telling what is the same in both and what is different
Checking an answer against the pictures and the words
Comparing two animals: what both have and what only one has
howToPlay: Listen to Willow read both stories, or tap a picture to hear it again.
Read the question on the tooth.
Put the tooth on one side, in the middle or in the pocket, then pull the zipper.
If the zipper jams, look again at both stories.
learningGoals: The child tells what happens in both stories
The child tells what happens in only one of them
The child checks an answer against the story pictures

about: The squirrel's acorns lie in rows on a wooden tray. The child cuts the rows into piles by tapping the gaps for twigs, then taps the tree stump: the piles slide over and lie on top of one another. Snow falls, and it can only lay one flat lid on a fair stack. If one pile is bigger, its extra acorns stick out of the stack in coral and the lid slides off into the snow.

Fairness is checked by stacking, a direct way to compare piles, so equal groups are something the child can see rather than a rule to remember. Once the stack is fair, the child types how many are in each pile and the equation appears: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, or 6 + 6 = 12. Two more levels turn the same apparatus into division: cut piles that fill a hole of a given size and say how many holes, or share a loose heap one acorn at a time into the holes and say how many each gets.
It is aligned to Common Core 2.OA.C.4: partition a rectangular array into equal groups and write the total as a sum of equal addends. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Cut an array into equal groups
Write the total as a sum of equal addends
Find how many groups of a given size
Share a quantity fairly and say how many each gets
howToPlay: Tap a gap between two rows to put in a twig; tap it again to take the twig out.
Tap the tree stump to stack the piles: a fair stack takes a flat lid of snow.
Type the number and press Check. In Level 3, tap a hole to give it an acorn and hold it to take one back. In the settings, choose the level and whether the equation is shown.
learningGoals: Split a set into groups that are all the same size.
Write equal groups as an addition like 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Begin to see sharing and grouping as two sides of the same idea.

about: An All-About page tells about ONE thing. In Bram's museum each room is all about one thing, and every sentence card hangs on the wall by a string. The child hooks each card's string to what the card is about: the room's big sign, or the sign of the next room, seen through the doorway.

The traps are the real reasons children drift off topic: a card that names the other thing but is still about the room (“Frogs swim in lakes.”), two cards that share a word (“loud”), and a card that says only “They”. When the strings are wrong, each card's about-word lights up, and the “They” card points back to the card it means. At Check the card about something else is pulled out through the door into its own room, and the room's cards become a page in a book: “All about frogs”.

Three kinds of rounds: Catch the drift (hook every string); Make the page (choose the cards that belong from a cart); and Name the room (three cards say only “They” or “It”, and the child puts the right picture in the empty frame). Aligned to Common Core W.K.2: name what you are writing about and give some information about it. No timer and no score.
practices: Deciding what a sentence is about
Keeping only the facts about the topic on the page
Seeing what a word like “they” or “it” points back to
Naming the topic of a set of facts
howToPlay: Tap a card, then tap the sign it is about (or drag its string onto the sign). Press “Check” when every card hangs by its string.
In “Make the page”, tap a card on the cart to hang it on the wall; in “Name the room”, tap a picture to put it in the frame.
Under “Words that help” choose “On” to underline the word each card is about; under “Cards” choose 3 for a smaller wall.
learningGoals: The child tells what a sentence is about, even when it names something else
The child keeps only on-topic facts on an All-About page
The child names the topic of a set of facts

about: A jar is packed with bugs — ladybugs, bees, snails — heaped over each other, so nobody can count them through the glass. Beside it stands a jar with exactly ten of the same bugs. The child guesses first: fewer than in the jar of ten, or more? Then the child pours the jar out, the bugs land on a tray where they can be counted, and the child finds out. It's an interactive Kindergarten counting activity that runs in the browser with nothing to install and no account.

The jar of ten is the yardstick. Both jars are packed the same way, so the fuller one really holds more, and a child learns to judge an amount against a number they know before counting it. After the pour the bugs lie in rows, a rectangular array, a ring or a scatter — the arrangements of K.CC.B.5 — up to 16. A tap on a bug ticks it as counted, so the child can keep track of which ones are done; the tick is never a number. The child sets the jar's label with − and +, and the label starts at ten, so counting on from ten ("ten, eleven, twelve…") is one way to reach a teen number. A wrong Check says whether some bugs still have no tick or whether the number is too big or too small; after a second, the bugs are numbered up to the last one, which shows a question mark, and the child names the last number — that is how many. A right Check numbers the bugs in the order the child ticked them and holds the count against the guess: "More than 10, just as you guessed" or "more than you guessed". A guess is never marked wrong.

It is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5 — counting to answer "how many?" about things in rows or an array (the standard runs to 20; here up to 16), in a ring (here up to 9) and up to 10 in a scatter. Teachers can choose numbers up to 10 (the yardstick is then a jar of five) or up to 16, and turn the guess off. No timer, no score.
practices: Judging an amount against a jar of ten before counting
Counting up to 16 bugs in rows, an array, a ring or a scatter
Ticking each bug as it is counted, so none is counted twice or missed
Knowing that the last number counted tells how many
howToPlay: Look at the two jars and guess: fewer bugs than in the jar of ten, or more?
Pour the jar out. Tap each bug to tick it as you count.
Set the jar's label to how many with − and +, then press Check.
Not quite? The hint says what to look at — fix it and press Check again. No timer, no score.
learningGoals: Count to answer "how many?" up to 16 in rows or an array, up to 9 in a ring, and up to 10 in a scatter — the focus of Common Core K.CC.B.5
Know that the last number counted tells how many
Compare an amount with ten before counting it

about: The patient on the doctor's chart is a picture, and the child spells its name. Then the doctor's mirror clears and shows only what the letters really spell. Spell "cup" for the cap and a cup appears; spell "map" for the mop and the mirror shows a map; spell letters that make no picture word and the mirror stays foggy, with the letters written in the fog.

The patient is healed when the mirror shows the same picture. First the child heals one sick sound from a tray of three tiles; then writes whole words with the help the teacher picks (letter boxes, the first letter, a word bank or a plain line); then chooses the rule letters (ck or k, as in "duck" and "desk"); and last spells plurals for two patients, where the singular shows only one picture.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.2.e: spell untaught words phonetically, drawing on phonemic awareness and spelling conventions. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Spell a word by its sounds, one sound at a time
Hear that changing one letter changes the word
Choose between ck and k by the sound before it
Add the right plural ending
howToPlay: Put a tile in the empty box (or type the word), then press Mirror.
Look at the mirror: the same picture as the patient means healed; another picture or fog means a letter is sick.
In the settings, choose what to do (the sick sound, write the word, rule letters, plurals) and how much help the word gets.
learningGoals: Spell picture words by their sounds.
Check a spelling by what it really says.
Use simple spelling rules and plural endings.

about: Glim the light-wisp needs help finishing each sentence with the right describing word. Given "The ___ rabbit hopped away" or "The rabbit hopped ___," the child chooses between two forms of the same word — the adjective quick or the adverb quickly. This interactive Grade 2 grammar activity runs in the browser with no account.

The big idea is that an adjective describes a thing while an adverb tells how an action happens. Each round pairs the very same idea two ways — a quick rabbit versus hopping quickly, a loud bell versus ringing loudly — so the child cannot rely on the word's meaning and must instead ask what the blank is describing: a noun or a verb. A guiding question ("Which word describes the rabbit?" or "Which word tells how the rabbit hopped?") points to what to look for.
It is aligned to Common Core L.2.1.e — using adjectives and adverbs and choosing between them depending on what is to be modified. No timer, no score — just calm, playful practice.
practices: Choose an adjective to describe a thing, like a quiet mouse
Choose an adverb to tell how an action happens, like walked slowly
Decide whether the blank describes a noun or a verb
Tell the related forms apart, like loud and loudly
howToPlay: Read the sentence and the guiding question — is the blank describing a thing or an action?
Tap the adjective if it describes a thing, or the adverb if it tells how an action happens.
A warm check confirms the choice and offers an easy retry; no timer, no score.
learningGoals: Use adjectives and adverbs and choose between them — the focus of Common Core L.2.1.e
Tell what describes a noun from what describes a verb
Recognize how an adjective becomes an adverb, like soft and softly

about: Every question word is a lamp that shines on one kind of answer: who on a person, what on a thing, where on a place, when on a time, why on a reason and how on the way something is done. At Wren's window the answer stands under a lamp rail as picture cards, and one card wears a gold frame.

The child puts a question word in the gap and presses "Check". The brass lamp swings along its rail and drops its beam on the card that word asks about: on the gold card when the word is right, on another card (or on nothing at all) when it is not. Every round has exactly one right word. After a right answer the lamp visits every picture card in turn, each with the question word that asks about it.

Five sets: who, what and where; adding when; adding why and how; matching a question to its answer; and sorting answers under three lamps. Under "Answer" the child can type the question word instead. Aligned to Common Core L.K.1.d: understand and use question words. No timer and no score.
practices: Knowing what each question word asks about
Choosing who for a person and what for a thing
Telling where (a place) from when (a time)
Choosing why for a reason and how for a way
howToPlay: Look at the gold card. Tap the question word that asks about it, then press "Check".
Watch where the lamp shines. If it lights another card, that word asks about something else.
Under "Question words" choose a set such as "Add when" or "Sort", and under "Answer" choose "Write it" to type the word.
learningGoals: The child knows that each question word asks for one kind of answer
The child picks the question word that fits a given answer
The child sorts answers by the question they answer

about: The camera only takes a sharp group photo when everyone on the bench is the same kind of thing. The child sends the one that doesn't belong to the step and presses the red shutter. If the group is right, the photo comes out sharp and its name is written underneath: animals, food, birds, insects. If not, the photo comes out cloudy, because the camera sorts by kind, not by look: the yellow banana does not belong with the bee, and the bat flies but is not a bird.

There are five things to do: find the odd one out of four pictures; trickier groups of five, each with a look-alike; what things are made of (glass, plastic, paper, metal); word groups (ways to move and ways to look); and a seat plan, where clue cards say which friend has which thing, a tick pushes crosses along its row and column, and two true-or-false sentences are read off the finished plan. With "I name it", the child picks the group's name from three name tags.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.5.a: sort words into categories to gain a sense of the concepts they represent. It works with the sound off, and there is no timer and no score.
practices: Find the one that is not the same kind
Name a group with one word
Sort things by what they are made of
Reason with yes, no and either-or clues
howToPlay: Tap a picture to send it to the step, then press the red shutter.
A sharp photo with a name means the group is right; a cloudy photo means someone still doesn't belong, so tap anyone in the photo to send them instead.
In the settings, choose what to do (odd one out, trickier groups, materials, word groups, seat plan) and whether the camera writes the name or you pick it.
learningGoals: Sort pictures and words into categories.
Name the category with one word.
Use clues to give each friend the right thing.

about: Cleo packs her case one list at a time, and every comma drops a little wooden wall into it, so each thing in the list gets its own pocket. The words of the list stand right over the case, and every gap between two words is a place where a comma, and its wall, can go.

When the child presses Pack, each thing falls out of its word into the pocket below. A missing comma squashes two things into one pocket: in "We saw cats dogs, and pigs." the cat and the dog land together. A comma before the first thing leaves an empty pocket at the left end. In English "and" is a ribbon tied to the last thing, not a wall, so a comma goes before "and" too: only "I packed apples, pears, and cherries." gives every thing its own pocket, and then the lid shuts. Later the child builds lists of four things, makes their own lists from a shelf of pictures, and fixes lists that came with the wrong commas.
It is aligned to Common Core L.1.2.b: use commas to separate single words in a series. No timer and no score.
practices: Put a comma between the things in a list
Put a comma before "and" in a list of three or more
Leave out a comma before the first thing
Find and fix missing and extra commas
howToPlay: Tap a gap between two words to put in a comma; tap it again to take it out.
Press Pack and watch each thing drop into its pocket: one thing in every pocket shuts the lid.
In the settings, choose what to do (place the commas, make your own list, fix the list), the length of the lists and when the walls drop.
learningGoals: Use commas to separate the things in a list.
See that each comma keeps two things apart.
Check a list and fix its commas.
